1.1.440: 'And rive the stones asunder, though the prize
1.1.441: ' Were Rome herself.' His comrades lift their hands
1.1.442: And vow to follow wheresoever he leads.
1.1.443: And such a clamour rends the sky as when
1.1.444: Some Thracian blast on Ossa's pine-clad rocks
1.1.445: Falls headlong, and the loud re-echoing woods,
1.1.446: Or bending, or rebounding from the stroke,
1.1.447: In sounding chorus lift the roar on high.
1.1.448: When Caesar saw them welcome thus the war
1.1.449: And Fortune leading on, and favouring fates,
1.1.450: He seized the moment, called his troops from Gaul,
1.1.451: And breaking up his camp set on for Rome.
1.1.452: The tents are vacant by Lake Leman's side;
1.1.453: The camps upon the beetling crags of Vosges
1.1.454: No longer hold the warlike Lingon down,
1.1.455: Fierce in his painted arms; Isere is left,
1.1.456: Who past his shallows gliding, flows at last
1.1.457: Into the current of more famous Rhone,
1.1.458: To reach the ocean in another name.
1.1.459: The fair-haired people of Cevennes are free:
1.1.460: Soft Aude rejoicing bears no Roman keel,
1.1.461: Nor pleasant Var, since then Italia's bound;
1.1.462: The harbour sacred to Alcides' name
1.1.463: Where hollow crags encroach upon the sea,
1.1.464: Is left in freedom: there nor Zephyr gains
1.1.465: Nor Caurus access, but the Circian blast
1.1.466: Forbids the roadstead by Monaecus' hold.
1.1.467: Left is the doubtful shore, which the vast sea
1.1.468: And land alternate claim, whene'er the tide
1.1.469: Pours in amain or when the wave rolls back
1.1.470: Be it the wind which thus compels the deep
1.1.471: From furthest pole, and leaves it at the flood;
1.1.472: Or else the moon that makes the tide to swell,
1.1.473: Or else, in search of fuel for his fires,
1.1.474: The sun draws heavenward the ocean wave; -
1.1.475: Whatever the cause that may control the main
1.1.476: I leave to others; let the gods for me
1.1.477: Lock in their breasts the secrets of the world.
1.1.478: Those who keep watch beside the western shore
1.1.479: Have moved their standards home; the happy Gaul
1.1.480: Rejoices in their absence; fair Garonne
1.1.481: Through peaceful meads glides onward to the sea.
1.1.482: And where the river broadens, neath the cape
1.1.483: Her quiet harbour sleeps. No outstretched arm
1.1.484: Except in mimic war now hurls the lance.
1.1.485: No skilful warrior of Seine directs
1.1.486: The chariot scythed against his country's foe.
1.1.487: Now rest the Belgians, and th' Arvernian race
1.1.488: That boasts our kinship by descent from Troy;
1.1.489: And those brave rebels whose undaunted hands
1.1.490: Were dipped in Cotta's blood, and those who wear
1.1.492: No longer listen for the trumpet's call,
1.1.493: Nor those who dwell where Rhone's swift eddies sweep
1.1.494: Saone to the ocean; nor the mountain tribes
1.1.495: Who dwell about its source. Thou, too, oh Treves,
1.1.496: Rejoicest that the war has left thy bounds.
1.1.497: Ligurian tribes, now shorn, in ancient days
1.1.498: First of the long-haired nations, on whose necks
1.1.499: Once flowed the auburn locks in pride supreme;
1.1.500: And those who pacify with blood accursed
1.1.502: And Taranis' altars, cruel as were those
1.1.503: Loved by Diana, goddess of the north;
1.1.504: All these now rest in peace. And you, ye Bards,
1.1.505: Whose martial lays send down to distant times
1.1.506: The fame of valorous deeds in battle done,
1.1.507: Pour forth in safety more abundant song.
1.1.508: While you, ye Druids, when the war was done,
1.1.509: To mysteries strange and hateful rites returned:
1.1.510: To you alone 'tis given the heavenly gods
1.1.511: To know or not to know; secluded groves
1.1.512: Your dwelling-place, and forests far remote.
1.1.513: If what ye sing be true, the shades of men
1.1.514: Seek not the dismal homes of Erebus
1.1.515: Or death's pale kingdoms; but the breath of life
1.1.516: Still rules these bodies in another age-
1.1.517: Life on this hand and that, and death between.
1.1.518: Happy the peoples 'neath the Northern Star
1.1.519: In this their false belief; for them no fear
1.1.520: Of that which frights all others: they with hands
1.1.521: And hearts undaunted rush upon the foe
1.1.522: And scorn to spare the life that shall return.
1.1.523: Ye too depart who kept the banks of Rhine
1.1.524: Safe from the foe, and leave the Teuton tribes
1.1.525: Free at their will to march upon the world.
1.1.526: When strength increased gave hope of greater deeds
1.1.528: His countless bands, and filled the neighbouring towns.
1.1.529: Then empty rumour to well-grounded fear
1.1.530: Gave strength, and heralding the coming war
1.1.531: In hundred voices 'midst the people spread.
1.1.532: One cries in terror, ' Swift the squadrons come
1.1.533: ' Where Nar with Tiber joins: and where, in meads
1.1.534: 'By oxen loved, Mevania spreads her walls,
1.1.536: ' With all his eagles and his standards joined
1.1.537: 'He leads the throng that sweeps along the land.'
1.1.538: Nor as they knew him do they paint the chief,
1.1.539: But stronger than the truth, and pitiless
1.1.540: And fiercer far-as from his conquered foes
1.1.541: Advancing; in his rear the peoples march,
1.1.542: Snatched from their homes between the Rhine and Alps,
1.1.543: To sack the city while her sons look on.
1.1.544: Thus each man's panic thought swells rumour's lie:
1.1.545: They fear the phantoms they themselves create.
1.1.546: Nor did the terror seize the crowd alone:
1.1.547: But fled the Fathers, to the Consuls first
1.1.548: Issuing their hated order, as for war;
1.1.549: And doubting of the peril, doubting too
1.1.550: Where safety lay, through all the choking gates
1.1.551: In dense array they urged the people forth.
1.1.552: Thou wouldst believe that blazing to the torch
1.1.553: Were men's abodes, or nodding to their fall.
1.1.554: So streamed they onwards, frenzied with affright,
1.1.555: As though in exile only could they find
1.1.556: Hope for their country. So, when southern blasts
1.1.557: From Libyan whirlpools drive the boundless main,
1.1.558: And mast and sail crash down upon a ship
1.1.559: With ponderous weight, but still the frame is sound,
1.1.560: Her crew and captain leap into the sea,
1.1.561: Each making shipwreck for himself. 'Twas thus
1.1.562: They passed the city gates and fled to war.
1.1.563: No aged parent now could stay his son;
1.1.564: Nor wife her spouse, nor did they pray the gods
1.1.565: To grant the safety of their fatherland.
1.1.566: None linger on the threshold for a look
1.1.567: Of their loved city, though perchance the last.
1.1.568: Ye gods, who lavish priceless gifts on men,
1.1.569: Nor care to guard them given! thus was Rome
1.1.570: Teeming with conquered nations, whose vast walls
1.1.571: Had compassed all mankind, by coward hands
1.1.572: To coming Caesar left an easy prey.
1.1.573: The Roman soldier, when in foreign lands
1.1.574: Pressed by the enemy, in narrow trench
1.1.575: And hurried mound finds guard enough to make
1.1.576: His tented sleep secure: thou Rome alone
1.1.577: Upon the rumour of advancing war
1.1.578: Art left a desert, and thy battlements
1.1.579: Not trusted for a night. Yet for their fear
1.1.580: This one excuse was left; Pompeius fled.
1.1.581: Nor found they room for hope; for nature gave
1.1.582: Unerring portents of worse ills to come.
1.1.583: The angry gods filled earth and air and sea
1.1.584: With frequent prodigies; in darkest nights
1.1.585: Strange constellations sparkled through the gloom:
1.1.586: The pole was all afire, and torches flew
1.1.587: Across the depths of heaven; with horrid hair
1.1.588: A blazing comet stretched from east to west
1.1.589: And threatened change to kingdoms. From the blue
1.1.590: Pale lightning flashed, and in the murky air
1.1.591: The fire took divers shapes; a lance afar
1.1.592: Would seem to quiver or a misty torch;
1.1.593: A noiseless thunderbolt from cloudless sky
1.1.594: Rushed down, and drawing fire in northern parts
1.1.595: Plunged on the summit of the Alban mount.
1.1.596: The stars that run their courses in the void
1.1.597: Of night, came forth at noontide, and the moon
1.1.598: Whose orb complete gave back her brother's rays,
1.1.599: Hid by the shade of earth, grew pale and wan.
1.1.600: The sun himself, when poised in mid career,
1.1.601: Shrouded his burning car in blackest gloom
1.1.602: And plunged the world in darkness, so that men
1.1.603: Despaired of day-like as he veiled his light
1.1.604: From that fell banquet which Mycenae saw.
1.1.605: The jaws of Etna were agape with flame
1.1.606: That rose not heavenwards, but headlong fell
1.1.607: In smoking stream upon th' Italian flank.
1.1.608: Then black Charybdis, from her boundless depth,
1.1.609: Threw up a gory sea. In piteous tones
1.1.610: Howled the wild dogs; the Vestal fire was snatched
1.1.611: From off the altar; and the flame that crowned
1.1.612: The Latin festival was split in twain,
1.1.613: As on the Theban pyre, in ancient days;
1.1.614: Earth tottered on its base: the mighty Alps
1.1.615: From off their summits shook th' eternal snow.
1.1.616: In huge upheaval Ocean raised his waves
1.1.617: O'er Calpe's rock and Atlas' hoary head.
1.1.618: The native gods shed tears, and holy sweat
1.1.619: Dropped from the idols; gifts in temples fell:
1.1.620: Foul birds defiled the day; beasts left the woods
1.1.621: And made their lair among the streets of Rome.
1.1.622: All this we hear; nay more: dumb oxen spake;
1.1.623: Monsters were brought to birth and mothers shrieked
1.1.624: At their own offspring; words of dire import
1.1.625: From Cumae's prophetess were noised abroad.
1.1.626: Bellona's priests with bleeding arms, and slaves
1.1.627: Of Cybele's worship, with ensanguined hair,
1.1.628: Howled chants of havoc and of woe to men.
1.1.629: Arms clashed; and sounding in the pathless woods
1.1.630: Were heard strange voices; spirits walked the earth:
1.1.631: And dead men's ashes muttered from the urn.
1.1.632: Those who live near the walls desert their homes,
1.1.633: For lo! with hissing serpents in her hair,
1.1.634: Waving in downward whirl a blazing pine,
1.1.635: A fiend patrols the town, like that which erst
1.1.636: At Thebes urged on Agave, or which hurled
1.1.637: Lycurgus' bolts, or that which as he came
1.1.638: From Hades seen, at haughty Juno's word,
1.1.639: Brought terror to the soul of Hercules.
1.1.640: Trumpets like those that summon armies forth
1.1.641: Were heard re-echoing in the silent night:
1.1.642: And from the earth arising Sulla's ghost
1.1.643: Sang gloomy oracles, and by Anio's wave
1.1.644: All fled the homesteads, frighted by the shade
1.1.645: Of Marius waking from his broken tomb.
1.1.646: In such dismay they summon, as of yore,
1.1.647: The Tuscan sages to the nation's aid.
1.1.648: Aruns, the eldest, leaving his abode
1.1.649: In desolate Luca, came, well versed in all
1.1.650: The lore of omens; knowing what may mean
1.1.651: The flight of hovering bird, the pulse that beats
1.1.652: In offered victims, and the levin bolt.
1.1.653: All monsters first, by most unnatural birth
1.1.654: Brought into being, in accursed flames
1.1.655: He bids consume. Then round the walls of Rome
1.1.656: Each trembling citizen in turn proceeds.
1.1.657: The priests, chief guardians of the public faith,
1.1.658: With holy sprinkling purge the open space
1.1.659: That borders on the wall; in sacred garb
1.1.660: Follows the lesser crowd: the Vestals come
1.1.661: By priestess led with laurel crown bedecked,
1.1.662: To whom alone is given the right to see
1.1.663: Minerva's effigy that came from Troy.
1.1.664: Next come the keepers of the sacred books
1.1.665: And fate's predictions; who from Almo's brook
1.1.666: Bring back Cybebe laved; the augur too
1.1.667: Taught to observe sinister flight of birds;
1.1.668: And those who serve the banquets to the gods;
1.1.669: And Titian brethren; and the priest of Mars,
1.1.670: Proud of the buckler that adorns his neck;
1.1.671: By him the Flamen, on his noble head
1.1.672: The cap of office. While they tread the path
1.1.673: That winds around the walls, the aged seer
1.1.674: Collects the thunderbolts that fell from heaven,
1.1.675: And lays them deep in earth, with muttered words
1.1.676: Naming the spot accursed. Next a steer,
1.1.677: Picked for his swelling neck and beauteous form,
1.1.678: He leads to the altar, and with slanting knife
1.1.679: Spreads on his brow the meal, and pours the wine.
1.1.680: The victim's struggles prove the gods averse;
1.1.681: But when the servers press upon his horns
1.1.682: He bends the knee and yields him to the blow.
1.1.683: No crimson torrent issues at the stroke,
1.1.684: But from the wound a dark empoisoned stream
1.1.685: Ebbs slowly downward. Aruns at the sight
1.1.686: Aghast, upon the entrails of the beast
1.1.687: Essayed to read the anger of the gods.
1.1.688: Their very colour terrified the seer;
1.1.689: Spotted they were and pale, with sable streaks
1.1.690: Of lukewarm gore bespread; the liver damp
1.1.691: With foul disease, and on the hostile part
1.1.692: The angry veins defiant; of the lungs
1.1.693: The fibre hid, and through the vital parts
1.1.694: The membrane small; the heart has ceased to throb;
1.1.695: Blood oozes through the ducts; the caul is split:
1.1.696: And, fatal omen of impending ill,
1.1.697: One lobe o'ergrows the other; of the twain
1.1.698: The one lies flat and sick, the other beats
1.1.699: And keeps the pulse in rapid strokes astir.
1.1.700: Disaster's near approach thus learned, he cries-
1.1.701: ' Whatever may be the purpose of the gods,
1.1.702: ' Tis not for me to tell; this offered beast
1.1.703: ' Not Jove possesses, but the gods below.
1.1.704: ' We dare not speak our fears, yet fear doth make
1.1.705: ' The future worse than fact. May all the gods
1.1.706: ' Prosper the tokens, and the sacrifice
1.1.707: ' Be void of truth, and Tages (famous seer)
1.1.708: ' Have vainly taught these mysteries.' Such his words
1.1.711: For knowledge of the secret depths of space
1.1.712: And laws harmonious that guide the stars
1.1.713: Memphis could find no peer, then spake at large:
1.1.714: ' Either,' he said, ' the world and countless orbs
1.1.715: ' Throughout the ages wander at their will;
1.1.716: ' Or, if the fates control them, ruin huge
1.1.717: ' Hangs o'er this city and o'er all mankind.
1.1.718: ' Shall Earth yawn open and engulph the towns?
1.1.719: ' Shall scorching heat usurp the temperate air
1.1.720: ' And fields refuse their timely fruit? The streams
1.1.721: ' Flow mixed with poison? In what plague, ye gods,
1.1.722: 'In what destruction shall ye wreak your ire?
1.1.723: 'Whate'er the truth, the days in which we live
1.1.724: ' Shall find a doom for many. Had the star
1.1.725: ' Of baleful Saturn, frigid in the height,
1.1.726: ' Kindled his lurid fires, the sky had poured
1.1.727: 'Its torrents forth as in Deucalion's time,
1.1.728: ' And whelmed the world in waters. Or if thou,
1.1.729: ' Phoebus, beside the Nemean lion fierce
1.1.730: ' Wert driving now thy chariot, flames should seize
1.1.731: 'The universe and set the air ablaze.
1.1.732: ' These are at peace; but, Mars, why art thou bent
1.1.733: ' On kindling thus the Scorpion, his tail
1.1.734: ' Portending evil and his claws aflame?
1.1.735: ' Deep sunk is kindly Jupiter, and dull
1.1.736: ' Sweet Venus' star, and rapid Mercury
1.1.737: ' Stays on his course: Mars only holds the sky.
1.1.738: 'Why does Orion's sword too brightly shine?
1.1.739: ' Why planets leave their paths and through the void
1.1.740: 'Thus journey on obscure? Tis war that comes,
1.1.741: ' Fierce rabid war: the sword shall bear the rule
1.1.743: ' The name of virtue; and the havoc spread
1.1.744: ' Through many a year. But why entreat the gods?
1.1.745: ' The end Rome longs for and the final peace
1.1.746: 'Comes with a despot. Draw thou out thy chain
1.1.747: 'Of lengthening slaughter, and (for such thy fate)
1.1.748: ' Make good thy liberty through civil war.'
1.1.749: The frightened people heard, and as they heard
1.1.750: His words prophetic made them fear the more.
1.1.751: But worse remained; for as on Pindus' slopes
1.1.752: Possessed with fury from the Theban god
1.1.753: Speeds some Bacchante, thus in Roman streets
1.1.754: Behold a matron run, who, in her trance,
1.1.755: Relieves her bosom of the god within.
1.1.756: ' Where dost thou snatch me, Paean, to what shore
1.1.757: 'Through airy regions borne? I see the snows
1.1.759: 'Lie broad beneath. But why these battle lines,
1.1.760: 'No foe to vanquish-Rome on either hand?
1.1.762: 'That paint thine eastern skies, where regal Nile
1.1.763: 'Meets with his flowing wave the rising tide.
1.1.764: 'Known to mine eyes that mutilated trunk
1.1.765: ' That lies upon the sand! Across the seas
1.1.766: 'By changing whirlpools to the burning climes
1.1.767: 'Of Libya borne, again I see the hosts
1.1.768: 'From Thracia brought by fate's command. And now
1.1.769: 'Thou bear'st me o'er the cloud-compelling Alps
1.1.771: 'There in mid-Senate see the closing scene
1.1.772: 'Of this foul war in foulest murder done.
1.1.773: 'Again the factions rise; through all the world
1.1.774: Once more I pass; but give me some new land,
1.1.776: 'Washed by the Pontic billows! for these eyes
1.1.778: The frenzy left her and she speechless fell.

2.1.1: THUS was made plain the anger of the gods;
2.1.2: The world gave signs of war: Nature reversed
2.1.3: In monstrous tumult fraught with prodigies
2.1.4: Her laws, and prescient spake the coming guilt.
2.1.5: How seemed it just to thee, Olympus' king,
2.1.6: That suffering mortals at thy doom should know
2.1.7: By dreadful omens massacres to come?
2.1.8: Or did the primal parent of the world
2.1.9: When first the flames gave way and yielding left
2.1.10: Matter unformed to his subduing hand,
2.1.11: And realms unbalanced, fix by stern decree
2.1.12: Unalterable laws to bind the whole
2.1.13: (Himself, too, bound by law), so that for aye
2.1.14: All Nature moves within its fated bounds?
2.1.15: Or, is Chance sovereign over all, and we
2.1.16: The sport of Fortune and her turning wheel?
2.1.17: Whate'er be truth, keep thou the future veiled
2.1.18: From mortal vision, and amid their fears
2.1.20: Thus known how great the woes
2.1.21: The world should suffer, from the truth divine,
2.1.22: A solemn fast was called, the courts were closed,
2.1.23: All men in private garb; no purple hem
2.1.24: Adorned the togas of the chiefs of Rome;
2.1.25: No plaints were uttered, and a voiceless grief
2.1.26: Lay deep in every bosom: as when death
2.1.27: Knocks at some door but enters not as yet,
2.1.28: Before the mother calls the name aloud
2.1.29: Or bids her grieving maidens beat the breast,
2.1.30: While still she marks the glazing eye, and soothes
2.1.31: The stiffening limbs and gazes on the face,
2.1.32: In dread, not sorrow yet, in wondering awe
2.1.33: Of death approaching: and with mind distraught
2.1.34: Clings to the dying in a last embrace.
2.1.35: The matrons laid aside their wonted garb:
2.1.36: Crowds filled the temples-on the unpitying stones
2.1.37: Some dashed their bosoms; others bathed with tears
2.1.38: The statues of the gods; some tore their hair
2.1.39: Upon the holy threshold, and with shrieks
2.1.40: And vows unceasing called upon the names
2.1.41: Of those whom mortals supplicate. Nor all
2.1.42: Lay in the Thunderer's fane: at every shrine
2.1.43: Some prayers were offered which refused would bring
2.1.44: Reproach on heaven. One whose livid arms
2.1.45: Were dark with blows, whose cheeks with tears bedewed,
2.1.46: Cried, 'Now, unhappy mothers, rend the lock,
2.1.47: Nor keep your sorrows till the battle day:
2.1.48: Now ye may weep: when either chieftain wins
2.1.49: Rejoice ye must.' Thus sorrow stirs itself.
2.1.50: Meanwhile the men in seeking either camp
2.1.51: And marching onward in the path to war,
2.1.52: Address the cruel gods in just complaint.
2.1.53: Happy the youths who born in Punic days
2.1.54: On Cannae's uplands or by Trebia's stream
2.1.55: Fought and were slain! What wretched lot is ours!
2.1.56: No peace we ask for: let the nations rage;
2.1.57: Rouse fiercest cities! may the world find arms
2.1.58: To wage a war with Rome: let Parthian hosts
2.1.59: Rush forth from Susa; Scythian Ister curb
2.1.60: ' No more the Massagete: unconquered Rhine
2.1.61: ' Let loose from furthest North her fair-haired tribes:
2.1.62: ' Elbe, pour thy Suevians forth! Let us be foes
2.1.63: ' Of all the peoples. May the Getan press
2.1.64: ' Here, and the Dacian there; Pompeius meet
2.1.65: 'The Eastern archers, Caesar in the West
2.1.66: ' Confront th' Iberian. Leave to Rome no hand
2.1.67: ' To raise against herself in civil strife.
2.1.68: ' Or, if Italia by the gods be doomed,
2.1.69: ' Let all the sky, fierce Parent, be dissolved
2.1.70: 'And falling on the earth in flaming bolts,
2.1.71: ' Their hands still bloodless, strike both leaders down,
2.1.72: ' With both their hosts! Why plunge in novel crime
2.1.73: ' To settle which of them shall rule in Rome?
2.1.74: ' Scarce were it worth the price of civil war
2.1.75: ' To hinder either.' Thus the patriot voice
2.1.76: Still found an utterance, soon to speak no more.
2.1.77: Meantime, the aged fathers o'er their fates
2.1.78: In anguish grieved, detesting life prolonged
2.1.79: That brought with it another civil war.
2.1.80: And thus spake one, to justify his fears:
2.1.81: ' No other deeds the fates laid up in store
2.1.82: ' When Marius, victor over Teuton hosts,
2.1.83: ' Afric's high conqueror, cast out from Rome,
2.1.84: 'Lay hid in marshy ooze, at thy behest,
2.1.85: ' O Fortune! by the yielding soil concealed
2.1.86: ' And waving rushes; but ere long the chains
2.1.87: ' Of prison wore his weak and aged frame,
2.1.88: ' And lengthened squalor: thus he paid for crime
2.1.89: ' His punishment beforehand; doomed to die
2.1.90: ' Consul in triumph over wasted Rome.
2.1.91: 'Death oft refused him; and the very foe,
2.1.92: ' In act of slaughter, shuddered in the stroke
2.1.93: ' And dropped the weapon from his nerveless hand.
2.1.94: ' For through the prison gloom a flame of light
2.1.95: ' He saw; the deities of crime abhorred;
2.1.96: ' The Marius to come. A voice proclaimed
2.1.97: ' Mysterious, " Hold! the fates permit thee not
2.1.98: ' " That neck to sever. Many a death he owes
2.1.99: ' " To time's predestined laws ere his shall come;
2.1.100: ' " Cease from thy madness. If ye seek revenge
2.1.101: ' " For that he blotted out your Cimbrian tribes,
2.1.102: ' " Let this man live, live out his fated days."
2.1.103: ' Not as their darling did the gods protect

2.1.262: Thus, mindful of his youth, the aged man
2.1.263: Wept for the past, but feared the coming days.

2.1.265: No home. When others sat them down to fear
2.1.266: He did not so, but in the dewy night
2.1.267: When the great wain was turning round the pole
2.1.268: He sought his kinsman Cato's humble home.
2.1.269: Him sleepless did he find, not for himself
2.1.270: Fearing, but pondering the fates of Rome,
2.1.271: And deep in public cares. And thus he spake:
2.1.272: 'O thou in whom that virtue, which of yore
2.1.273: Took flight from earth, now finds its only home,
2.1.274: Outcast to all besides, but safe with thee:
2.1.275: Vouchsafe thy counsel to my wavering soul
2.1.276: And make my weakness strength. While Caesar some,
2.1.277: Pompeius others, follow in the fight,
2.1.278: Cato is Brutus' guide. Art thou for peace,
2.1.279: Holding thy footsteps in a tottering world
2.1.280: Unshaken? Or wilt thou with the leaders' crimes
2.1.281: And with the people's fury take thy part,
2.1.282: And by thy presence purge the war of guilt?
2.1.283: In impious battles men unsheath the sword;
2.1.284: But each by cause impelled: the household crime;
2.1.285: Laws feared in peace; want by the sword removed;
2.1.286: And credit, in the ruin of a world
2.1.287: Blending its ruin. Drawn by hope of gain,
2.1.288: And not by thirst for blood, they seek the camp.
2.1.289: Shall Cato for war's sake make war alone?
2.1.290: What profits it through all these wicked years
2.1.291: That thou hast lived untainted? This were all
2.1.292: Thy meed of virtue, that the wars which find
2.1.293: Guilt in all else, shall make thee guilty too.
2.1.294: ' Ye gods, permit not that this fatal strife
2.1.295: Should stir those hands to action! When the clouds
2.1.296: Of flying javelins hiss upon the air,
2.1.297: Let not a dart be thine; nor spent in vain
2.1.298: Such virtue! All the fury of the war
2.1.299: ' Shall launch itself on thee, for who, when faint
2.1.300: ' And wounded, would not rush upon thy sword,
2.1.301: 'Take thence his death, and make the murder thine?
2.1.302: 'Do thou live on thy peaceful life apart
2.1.303: 'As on their paths the stars unshaken roll.
2.1.304: 'The lower air that verges on the earth
2.1.305: ' Gives flame and fury to the levin bolt;
2.1.306: ' The deeps below the world engulph the winds
2.1.307: ' And tracts of flaming fire. By Jove's decree
2.1.308: 'Olympus rears his summit o'er the clouds:
2.1.309: 'In lowlier valleys storms and winds contend,
2.1.310: ' But peace eternal reigns upon the heights.
2.1.311: 'What joy for Caesar, if the tidings come
2.1.312: 'That such a citizen has joined the war?
2.1.313: ' Glad would he see thee e'en in Magnus' tents;
2.1.314: 'For Cato's conduct shall approve his own.
2.1.315: 'Pompeius, with the Consul in his ranks,
2.1.316: ' And half the Senate and the other chiefs,
2.1.317: ' Vexes my spirit; and should Cato too
2.1.318: ' Bend to a master's yoke, in all the world
2.1.319: 'The one man free is Caesar. But if thou
2.1.320: ' For freedom and thy country's laws alone
2.1.321: 'Be pleased to raise the sword, nor Magnus then
2.1.322: ' Nor Caesar shall in Brutus find a foe.
2.1.323: ' Not till the fight is fought shall Brutus strike,
2.1.326: Cato from inmost breast these sacred words:
2.1.327: 'Chief in all wickedness is civil war,
2.1.328: ' Yet virtue in the paths marked out by fate
2.1.329: 'Treads on securely. Heaven's will be the crime
2.1.330: 'To have made even Cato guilty. Who has strength
2.1.331: ' To gaze unawed upon a toppling world?
2.1.332: 'When stars and sky fall headlong, and when earth
2.1.333: 'Slips from her base, who sits with folded hands?
2.1.334: 'Shall unknown nations, touched by western strife,
2.1.335: ' And monarchs born beneath another clime
2.1.336: ' Brave the dividing seas to join the war?
2.1.337: ' Shall Scythian tribes desert their distant north,
2.1.338: ' And Getae haste to view the fall of Rome,
2.1.339: 'And I look idly on? As some fond sire,
2.1.340: ' Reft of his sons, compelled by grief, himself
2.1.341: ' Marshals the long procession to the tomb,
2.1.342: ' Thrusts his own hand within the funeral flames,
2.1.343: ' Soothing his heart, and, as the lofty pyre
2.1.344: 'Rises on high, applies the kindled torch:
2.1.345: ' Nought, Rome, shall tear thee from me, till I hold
2.1.346: ' Thy form in death embraced; and Freedom's name,
2.1.347: ' Shade though it be, I'll follow to the grave.
2.1.348: ' Yea! let the cruel gods exact in full
2.1.349: ' Rome's expiation: of no drop of blood
2.1.350: ' The war be robbed. I would that, to the gods
2.1.351: ' Of heaven and hell devoted, this my life
2.1.352: ' Might satisfy their vengeance. Decius fell,
2.1.353: ' Crushed by the hostile ranks. When Cato falls
2.1.354: ' Let Rhine's fierce barbarous hordes and both the hosts
2.1.355: 'Thrust through my frame their darts! May I alone
2.1.356: ' Receive in death the wounds of all the war!
2.1.357: 'Thus may the people be redeemed, and thus
2.1.358: ' Rome for her guilt pay the atonement due.
2.1.359: ' Why should men die who wish to bear the yoke
2.1.360: ' And shrink not from the tyranny to come?
2.1.361: 'Strike me, and me alone, of laws and rights
2.1.362: 'In vain the guardian: this vicarious life
2.1.363: ' Shall give Hesperia peace and end her toils.
2.1.364: ' Who then will reign shall find no need for war.
2.1.365: ' You ask, Why follow Magnus? If he wins
2.1.366: ' He too will claim the Empire of the world.
2.1.367: ' Then let him, conquering with my service, learn
2.1.368: ' Not for himself to conquer.' Thus he spoke
2.1.369: And stirred the blood that ran in Brutus' veins
2.1.370: Moving the youth to action in the war.
2.1.371: Soon as the sun dispelled the chilly night,
2.1.372: The sounding doors flew wide, and from the tomb
2.1.373: Of dead Hortensius grieving Marcia came.

2.1.375: Three children did she bear to grace his home:
2.1.376: Then Cato to Hortensius gave the dame
2.1.377: To be a fruitful mother of his sons
2.1.378: And join their houses in a closer tie.
2.1.379: And now the last sad offices were done
2.1.380: She came with hair dishevelled, beaten breast,
2.1.381: And ashes on her brow, and features worn
2.1.382: With grief; thus only pleasing to the man.
2.1.383: ' When youth was in me and maternal power
2.1.384: ' I did thy bidding, Cato, and received
2.1.385: ' A second husband: now in years grown old
2.1.386: ' Ne'er to be parted I return to thee.
2.1.388: ' Give back the name of wife: upon my tomb

2.1.390: ' Nor let men question in the time to come,

2.1.392: ' My first espousals. Not in happy times,
2.1.393: ' Partner of joys, I come; but days of care

2.1.396: ' Thy fond companion: why should Magnus' wife

2.1.398: Although the times were warlike and the fates

2.1.400: Yet must they plight their faith in simple form
2.1.401: Of law; their witnesses the gods alone.

2.1.634: ' He deems me slothful. Caesar, thou shalt learn

2.1.677: No loud acclaim received his words, nor shout

2.1.679: Drew back the standards, for the soldier's fears

2.1.687: And proves himself for battle, till his neck
2.1.688: Is ribbed afresh with muscle: then returns,
2.1.689: Defiant of the hind, and victor now
2.1.690: Leads wheresoever he will his lowing bands:
2.1.691: Thus Magnus, yielding to a stronger foe,
2.1.692: Gave up Italia, and sought in flight
2.1.693: Brundusium's sheltering battlements. Here of old

2.1.696: Here, where Hesperia, curving as a bow,
