3.1.140: The victor's road to rapine, and with voice
3.1.141: Clear ringing spake: ' Save o'er Metellus dead
3.1.142: 'This temple opens not; my sacred blood
3.1.143: ' Shall flow, thou robber, ere the gold be thine.
3.1.144: 'And surely shall the Tribune's power defied
3.1.145: 'Find an avenging god; this Crassus knew,
3.1.146: ' Who, followed by our curses, sought the war
3.1.147: 'And met disaster on the Parthian plains.
3.1.148: ' All Rome is empty; draw thy falchion then,
3.1.149: 'Nor fear a crowd to gaze upon the crime.
3.1.150: 'Not from our treasury reward for guilt
3.1.151: 'Thy hosts shall ravish: other towns are left,
3.1.152: 'And other nations; seek thy gifts from them;
3.1.153: 'Nor drain Rome's peace for spoil: war still is thine.'
3.1.154: Aroused to anger then the victor spake:
3.1.155: ' Vain is thy hope to fall in noble death;
3.1.156: 'Dost reckon Freedom safe with thee for guard?
3.1.157: ' With all thine honours, thou of Caesar's rage
3.1.158: 'Art little worthy: never shall thy blood
3.1.159: ' Defile his hand. Time lowest things with high
3.1.160: ' Confounds not yet so much that, if thy voice
3.1.161: ' Could save the laws, it were not better far
3.1.162: 'They fell by Caesar.' Such his lofty words.
3.1.163: But as the Tribune yielded not, his rage
3.1.164: Rose yet the more, and at his soldiers' swords
3.1.165: One look he cast, forgetting for the time
3.1.166: What robe he wore; but soon Metellus heard
3.1.167: These words from Cotta: ' When men bow to power
3.1.168: ' Freedom of speech is only Freedom's bane,
3.1.169: ' Whose shade at least survives, if with free will
3.1.170: ' Thou dost whate'er is bidden thee. For us
3.1.171: ' Some pardon may be found: a host of ills
3.1.172: ' Compelled submission, and the shame is less
3.1.173: 'That to have done which could not be refused.
3.1.174: ' Yield, then, this wealth, the seeds of direful war.
3.1.175: ' A nation's anger is by losses stirred,
3.1.176: ' When laws protect it; but the hungry slave
3.1.177: ' Brings danger to his master, not himself.'
3.1.178: At this Metellus yielded from the path;
3.1.179: And as the gates rolled backward, echoed loud
3.1.180: The rock Tarpeian, and the temple's depths
3.1.181: Gave up the treasure which for centuries
3.1.182: No hand had touched: all that the Punic foe
3.1.183: And Perses and Philippus conquered gave,
3.1.184: And all the gold which Pyrrhus panic-struck
3.1.185: Left when he fled: that gold, the price of Rome,
3.1.186: Which yet Fabricius sold not, and the hoard
3.1.187: Laid up by saving sires; the tribute sent
3.1.188: By Asia's richest nations; and the wealth
3.1.189: Which conquering Metellus brought from Crete,
3.1.190: And Cato bore from distant Cyprus home;
3.1.191: And last, the riches torn from captive kings
3.1.192: And borne before Pompeius when he came
3.1.193: In frequent triumph. Thus was robbed the shrine,
3.1.194: And Caesar first brought poverty to Rome.
3.1.195: Meanwhile all nations of the earth were moved
3.1.196: To share in Magnus' fortunes and the war,
3.1.197: And in his fated ruin. Graecia sent,
3.1.198: Nearest of all, her succours to the host.
3.1.199: From Cirrha and Parnassus' double peak
3.1.200: And from Amphissa, Phocis sent her youth:
3.1.202: And Theban Dirce, chiefs Boeotian came:
3.1.203: All Pisa mustered and Alpheus' youths,
3.1.204: Alpheus who in far Sicilian lands
3.1.205: Beyond the billows seeks the day again:
3.1.207: By Hercules, and old Dodona's oaks
3.1.208: Are left to silence; for the sacred train
3.1.209: With all Epirus rushes to the war.
3.1.210: Athens, deserted at the call to arms,
3.1.211: Yet found three vessels in Apollo's port
3.1.212: To prove her triumph o'er the Persian king.
3.1.213: Next seek the battle Creta's hundred tribes
3.1.214: Beloved of Jove and rivalling the east
3.1.215: In skill to wing the arrow from the bow.
3.1.216: The walls of Dardan Oricum, the woods
3.1.217: Where Athamanians wander, and the banks
3.1.218: Of swift Absyrtus foaming to the main
3.1.220: Whose king was Cadmus, and whose name records
3.1.221: His transformation, join the host; and those
3.1.222: Who till Penean fields and turn the share
3.1.224: There first men steeled their hearts to dare the waves
3.1.225: And 'gainst the rage of ocean and the storm
3.1.226: To match their strength, when the rude Argo sailed
3.1.227: Upon that distant quest, and spurned the shore,
3.1.228: Joining remotest nations in her flight,
3.1.229: And gave the fates another form of death.
3.1.230: Left too was Pholoe; pretended home
3.1.231: Where dwelt the fabled race of double form;
3.1.233: Named Hemus; Strymon, whence, as autumn falls,
3.1.234: Winged squadrons seek the banks of warmer Nile;
3.1.235: And all those isles the mouths of Ister bathe
3.1.236: Mixed with the tidal wave; the land through which
3.1.237: The cooling eddies of Caicus flow
3.1.238: Idalian; and Arisbe bare of glebe.
3.1.239: The hinds of Pitane, and those who till
3.1.240: Celaenae's fields which mourned of yore the gift
3.1.241: Of Pallas, and the vengeance of the god,
3.1.242: All draw the sword; and those from Marsyas' flood
3.1.243: First swift, then doubling backwards with the stream
3.1.244: Of sinuous Meander: and from where
3.1.245: Earth gives Pactolus and his golden store
3.1.246: Free passage forth; and where with rival wealth
3.1.247: Rich Hermus parts the meads. Nor stayed the bands
3.1.248: Of Troy, but (doomed as in old time) they joined
3.1.249: Pompeius' fated camp: nor held them back
3.1.250: The fabled past, nor Caesar's claimed descent
3.1.251: From their Iulus. Syrian peoples came
3.1.252: From palmy Idumea and the walls
3.1.253: Of Ninus great of yore; from windy plains
3.1.254: Of far Damascus and from Gaza's hold,
3.1.255: From Sidon's courts enriched with purple dye,
3.1.256: And Tyre oft trembling with the shaken earth.
3.1.257: All these led on by Cynosura's light
3.1.258: Furrow their certain path to reach the war.
3.1.260: Dared to record in characters; for yet
3.1.261: Papyrus was not fashioned, and the priests
3.1.262: Of Memphis, carving symbols upon walls
3.1.263: Of mystic sense (in shape of beast or fowl)
3.1.264: Preserved the secrets of their magic art.
3.1.265: Next Persean Tarsus and high Taurus' groves
3.1.266: Are left deserted, and Corycium's cave;
3.1.267: And all Cilicia's ports, pirate no more,
3.1.268: Resound with preparation. Nor the East
3.1.269: Refused the call, where furthest Ganges dares,
3.1.270: Alone of rivers, to discharge his stream
3.1.271: Against the sun opposing; on this shore
3.1.272: The Macedonian conqueror stayed his foot
3.1.273: And found the world his victor; Indus rolls
3.1.274: Here his vast torrent, by Hydaspes joined
3.1.275: Yet scarce augmented; here from luscious reed
3.1.276: Men draw sweet liquor; here they dye their locks
3.1.277: With tints of saffron, and with coloured gems
3.1.278: Bind down their flowing garments; here are they,
3.1.279: Who satiate of life and proud to die,
3.1.280: Ascend the blazing pyre, and conquering fate,
3.1.281: Scorn to live longer; but triumphant give
3.1.282: The remnant of their days in flame to heaven.
3.1.283: Nor failed to join the host a hardy band
3.1.284: Of Cappadocians, tilling now the soil,
3.1.285: Once pirates of the main: nor those who dwell
3.1.286: Where steep Niphates hurls the avalanche,
3.1.287: And where on Median Coatra's sides
3.1.288: The giant forest rises to the sky.
3.1.289: And you, Arabians, from your distant home
3.1.290: Came to a world unknown, and wondering saw
3.1.291: The shadows fall no longer to the left.
3.1.292: Then fired with ardour for the Roman war
3.1.293: Oretas came, and far Carmania's chiefs,
3.1.294: Whose clime lies southward, yet men thence descry
3.1.295: Low down the Pole star, and Bootes runs
3.1.296: Hasting to set, part seen, his nightly course;
3.1.297: And Ethiopians from that southern land
3.1.298: Which lies without the circuit of the stars,
3.1.299: Did not the Bull with curving hoof advanced
3.1.300: O'erstep the limit. From that mountain zone
3.1.301: They came, where rising from a common fount
3.1.302: Euphrates flows and Tigris, and did earth
3.1.303: Permit, were joined with either name; but now
3.1.304: While like th' Egyptian flood Euphrates spreads
3.1.306: Drawn down by earth in covered depths is plunged
3.1.307: And holds a secret course; then born again
3.1.308: Flows on unhindered to the Persian sea.
3.1.309: But warlike Parthia wavered 'twixt the chiefs,
3.1.310: Content to have made them two; while Scythia's hordes
3.1.311: Dipped fresh their darts in poison, whom the stream
3.1.312: Of Bactros bounds and vast Hyrcanian woods.
3.1.313: Hence springs that rugged nation swift and fierce,
3.1.314: Descended from the Twins' great charioteer.
3.1.315: Nor failed Sarmatia, nor the tribes that dwell
3.1.316: By richest Phasis, and on Halys' banks,
3.1.317: Which sealed the doom of Croesus king; nor where
3.1.318: From far Rhipaean ranges Tanais flows,
3.1.319: On either hand a quarter of the world,
3.1.320: Asia and Europe, and in winding course
3.1.321: Carves out a continent; nor where the strait
3.1.322: In boiling surge pours to the Pontic deep
3.1.324: Of those Herculean pillar-gates that guard
3.1.325: The entrance to an ocean. Thence with hair
3.1.327: And fierce Massagetae, who quaff the blood
3.1.328: Of the brave steed on which they fight and flee.
3.1.329: Not when great Cyrus on Memnonian realms
3.1.330: His warriors poured; nor when, their weapons piled,
3.1.331: The Persian told the number of his host;
3.1.332: Nor when th' avenger of a brother's shame
3.1.333: Loaded the billows with his mighty fleet,
3.1.334: Beneath one chief so many kings made war;
3.1.335: Nor e'er met nations varied thus in garb
3.1.336: And thus in language. To Pompeius' death
3.1.337: Thus Fortune called them: and a world in arms
3.1.338: Witnessed his ruin. From where Afric's god,
3.1.339: Two-horned Ammon, rears his temple, came
3.1.340: All Libya ceaseless, from the wastes that touch
3.1.341: The bounds of Egypt to the shore that meets
3.1.342: The Western Ocean. Thus, to award the prize
3.1.343: Of Empire at one blow, Pharsalia brought
3.1.344: 'Neath Caesar's conquering hand the banded world.
3.1.345: Now Caesar left the walls of trembling Rome
3.1.346: And swift across the cloudy Alpine tops
3.1.347: He winged his march; but while all others fled
3.1.348: Far from his path, in terror of his name,
3.1.350: Held to their pledged obedience, and dared
3.1.351: To follow right, not fate; but first of all
3.1.352: With olive boughs of truce before them borne
3.1.353: The chieftain they approach, with peaceful words
3.1.354: In hope to alter his unbending will
3.1.355: And tame his fury. 'Search the ancient books
3.1.356: Which chronicle the deeds of Latian fame;
3.1.357: Thou'lt ever find, when foreign foes pressed hard,
3.1.358: Massilia's prowess on the side of Rome.
3.1.359: And now, if triumphs in an unknown world
3.1.360: Thou seekest, Caesar, here our arms and swords
3.1.361: Accept in aid: but if, in impious strife
3.1.362: Of civil discord, with a Roman foe
3.1.363: Thou arm'st for battle, tears we give thee then
3.1.364: And hold aloof: no stranger hand may touch
3.1.365: Celestial wounds. Should all Olympus' hosts
3.1.366: Have rushed to war, or should the giant brood
3.1.367: Assault the stars, yet men would not presume
3.1.368: Or by their prayers or arms to help the gods:
3.1.369: And, ignorant of the fortunes of the sky,
3.1.370: Taught by the thunderbolts alone, would know
3.1.371: That Jupiter supreme still held the throne.
3.1.372: Add that unnumbered nations join the fray:
3.1.373: Nor shrinks the world so much from taint of crime
3.1.374: That civil wars reluctant swords require.
3.1.375: But grant that strangers shun thy destinies
3.1.376: And only Romans fight-shall not the son
3.1.377: Shrink ere he strike his father? on both sides
3.1.378: Brothers forbid the weapon to be hurled?
3.1.379: The world's end comes when other hands are armed
3.1.380: ' Than those which custom and the gods allow.
3.1.381: ' For us, this is our prayer: Leave, Caesar, here
3.1.382: ' Thy dreadful eagles, keep thy hostile signs
3.1.383: ' Back from our gates, but enter thou in peace
3.1.384: ' Massilia's ramparts; let our city rest
3.1.385: ' Withdrawn from crime, to Magnus and to thee
3.1.386: ' Safe: and should favouring fate preserve our walls
3.1.387: ' Inviolate, when both shall wish for peace
3.1.388: ' Here meet unarmed. Why hither dost thou turn
3.1.389: ' Thy rapid march, when to Iberian fights
3.1.390: 'The war commands thee? Weight nor power have we
3.1.391: ' To sway the mighty conflicts of the world.
3.1.392: ' We boast no victories since our fatherland
3.1.393: 'We left in exile: when Phocaea's fort
3.1.394: ' Perished in flames, we sought another here;
3.1.395: 'And here on foreign shores, in narrow bounds
3.1.396: ' Confined and safe, our boast is sturdy faith;
3.1.397: ' Nought else. But if our city to blockade
3.1.398: ' Is now thy mind-to force the gates, and hurl
3.1.399: ' Javelin and blazing torch upon our homes-
3.1.400: ' Do what thou wilt: cut off the source that fills
3.1.401: ' Our foaming river, force us, prone in thirst,
3.1.402: ' To dig the earth and lap the scanty pool;
3.1.403: ' Seize on our corn and leave us food abhorred:
3.1.404: ' This people shall not shun, for freedom's sake,
3.1.405: ' The ills Saguntum bore in Punic siege;
3.1.406: ' Torn, vainly clinging, from the shrunken breast
3.1.407: ' The starving babe shall perish in the flames.
3.1.408: ' Wives at their husbands' hands shall pray their fate,
3.1.409: ' And brothers' weapons deal a mutual death.
3.1.410: ' Such be our civil war; not, Caesar, thine.'
3.1.411: But Caesar's visage stern betrayed his ire
3.1.412: Which thus broke forth in words: ' Vain is the hope
3.1.413: Ye rest upon my march: speed though I may
3.1.414: Towards my western goal, time still remains
3.1.415: To blot Massilia out. Rejoice, my troops!
3.1.416: ' Unsought the war ye longed for meets you now:
3.1.417: The fates concede it. As the tempests lose
3.1.418: Their strength by sturdy forests unopposed,
3.1.419: And as the fire that finds no fuel dies,
3.1.420: Even so to find no foe is Caesar's ill.
3.1.421: When those who may be conquered will not fight,
3.1.423: Their gates admit me! Not content, forsooth,
3.1.424: With shutting Caesar out they shut him in!
3.1.425: They shun the taint of war! Such prayer for peace
3.1.426: Brings with it chastisement. In Caesar's age
3.1.427: Learn that not peace, but war within his ranks
3.1.430: Upon the fearless city, and beholds
3.1.431: Fast barred the gate-ways, while in arms the youths
3.1.432: Stand on the battlements. Hard by the walls
3.1.433: A hillock rose, upon the further side
3.1.434: Expanding in a plain of gentle slope,
3.1.435: Fit (as he deemed it) for a camp with ditch
3.1.436: And mound encircling. To a lofty height
3.1.437: The nearest portion of the city rose,
3.1.439: These summits with a mighty trench to bind
3.1.440: The chief resolves, gigantic though the toil.
3.1.441: But first, from furthest boundaries of his camp,
3.1.442: Enclosing streams and meadows, to the sea
3.1.443: To draw a rampart, upon either hand
3.1.444: Heaved up with earthy sod; with lofty towers
3.1.445: Crowned; and to shut Massilia from the land.
3.1.446: Then did the Grecian city win renown
3.1.448: Nor fearing for herself, but free to act
3.1.449: She made the conqueror pause: and he who seized
3.1.450: All in resistless course found here delay:
3.1.451: And Fortune, hastening to lay the world
3.1.452: Low at her favourite's feet, was forced to stay
3.1.453: For these few moments her impatient hand.
3.1.454: Now fell the forests far and wide, despoiled
3.1.455: Of all their giant trunks: for as the mound
3.1.456: On earth and brushwood stood, a timber frame
3.1.457: Held firm the soil, lest pressed beneath its towers
3.1.460: Which from the earliest time no hand of man
3.1.461: Had dared to violate; hidden from the sun
3.1.462: Its chill recesses; matted boughs entwined
3.1.463: Prisoned the air within. No sylvan nymphs
3.1.464: Here found a home, nor Pan, but savage rites
3.1.466: On massive stones upreared; sacred with blood
3.1.467: Of men was every tree. If faith be given
3.1.468: To ancient myth, no fowl has ever dared
3.1.469: To rest upon those branches, and no beast
3.1.470: Has made his lair beneath: no tempest falls,
3.1.471: Nor lightnings flash upon it from the cloud.
3.1.472: Stagnant the air, unmoving, yet the leaves
3.1.473: Filled with mysterious trembling; dripped the streams
3.1.474: From coal-black fountains; effigies of gods
3.1.475: Rude, scarcely fashioned from some fallen trunk
3.1.476: Held the mid space: and, pallid with decay,
3.1.477: Their rotting shapes struck terror. Thus do men
3.1.478: Dread most the god unknown. 'Twas said that caves
3.1.479: Rumbled with earthquakes, that the prostrate yew
3.1.480: Rose up again; that fiery tongues of flame
3.1.481: Gleamed in the forest depths, yet were the trees
3.1.482: Unkindled; and that snakes in frequent folds
3.1.483: Were coiled around the trunks. Men flee the spot
3.1.484: Nor dare to worship near: and e'en the priest
3.1.485: Or when bright Phoebus holds the height, or when
3.1.486: Dark night controls the heavens, in anxious dread
3.1.487: Draws near the grove and fears to find its lord.
3.1.488: Spared in the former war, still dense it rose
3.1.489: Where all the hills were bare, and Caesar now
3.1.490: Its fall commanded. But the brawny arms
3.1.491: Which swayed the axes trembled, and the men,
3.1.492: Awed by the sacred grove's dark majesty,
3.1.493: Held back the blow they thought would be returned.
3.1.494: This Caesar saw, and swift within his grasp
3.1.495: Uprose a ponderous axe, which downward fell
3.1.496: Cleaving a mighty oak that towered to heaven,
3.1.497: While thus he spake: ' Henceforth let no man dread
3.1.498: 'To fell this forest: all the crime is mine.
3.1.499: 'This be your creed.' He spake, and all obeyed,
3.1.500: For Caesar's ire weighed down the wrath of Heaven.
3.1.501: Yet ceased they not to fear. Then first the oak,
3.1.502: Dodona's ancient boast; the knotty holm;
3.1.503: The cypress, witness of patrician grief,
3.1.504: The buoyant alder, laid their foliage low
3.1.505: Admitting day; though scarcely through the stems
3.1.506: Their fall found passage. At the sight the Gauls
3.1.507: Grieved; but the garrison within the walls
3.1.508: Rejoiced: for thus shall men insult the gods
3.1.509: And find no punishment? Yet fortune oft
3.1.510: Protects the guilty; on the poor alone
3.1.511: The gods can vent their ire. Enough hewn down,
3.1.512: They seize the country wagons; and the hind,
3.1.513: His oxen gone which else had drawn the plough,
3.1.516: Impatient of the combat by the walls
3.1.517: Carries the warfare to the furthest west.
3.1.518: Meanwhile a giant mound, on star-shaped wheels
3.1.519: Concealed, they fashion, crowned with double towers
3.1.520: High as the battlements, by cause unseen
3.1.521: Slow creeping onwards; while amazed the foe
3.1.522: Beheld, and thought some subterranean gust
3.1.523: Had burst the caverns of the earth and forced
3.1.524: The nodding pile aloft, and wondered sore
3.1.525: Their walls should stand unshaken. From its height
3.1.526: Hissed down the weapons; but the Grecian bolts
3.1.527: WVith greater force were on the Romans hurled;
3.1.528: Nor by the arm unaided, for the lance
3.1.529: Urged by the catapult resistless rushed
3.1.530: Through arms and shield and flesh, and left a death
3.1.531: Behind, nor stayed its course: and massive stones
3.1.532: Cast by the beams of mighty engines fell;
3.1.533: As from the mountain top some time-worn rock
3.1.534: At length by winds dislodged, in all its track
3.1.535: Spreads ruin vast: nor crushed the life alone
3.1.536: Forth from the body, but dispersed the limbs
3.1.537: In fragments undistinguished and in blood.
3.1.538: But as protected by the armour shield
3.1.539: The might of Rome drew nigh beneath the wall
3.1.540: (The front rank with their bucklers interlaced
3.1.541: And held above their helms), the missiles fell
3.1.542: Behind their backs, nor could the toiling Greeks
3.1.543: Deflect their engines, throwing still the bolts
3.1.544: Far into space; but from the rampart top
3.1.545: Flung ponderous masses down. Long as the shields
3.1.546: Held firm together, like to hail that falls
3.1.547: Harmless upon a roof, so long the stones
3.1.548: Crushed down innocuous; but as the blows
3.1.549: Rained fierce and ceaseless and the Romans tired,
3.1.550: Some here and there sank fainting. Next the roof
3.1.551: Moves on with earth besprinkled: underneath
3.1.552: The ram conceals his head, which, poised and swung,
3.1.553: They dash with mighty force upon the wall,
3.1.554: Covered themselves with mantlets. Though the head
3.1.555: Light on the lower stones, yet as the shock
3.1.556: Falls and refalls, from battlement to base
3.1.557: The rampart soon shall topple. But by balks
3.1.558: And rocky fragments overwhelmed, and flames,
3.1.559: The roof at length gives way; and worn with toil
3.1.560: All spent in vain, the wearied troops withdraw
3.1.561: And seek the shelter of their tents again.
3.1.562: Thus far to hold their battlements was all
3.1.563: The Greeks had hoped; now, venturing attack,
3.1.564: With glittering torches for their arms, by night
3.1.565: Fearless they sallied forth: nor lance they bear
3.1.566: Nor deadly bow, nor shaft; for fire alone
3.1.567: Is now their weapon. Through the Roman works
3.1.568: Driven by the wind the conflagration spread:
3.1.569: Nor did the newness of the wood make pause
3.1.570: The fury of the flames, which, fed afresh
3.1.571: By living torches, 'neath a smoky pall
3.1.572: Leaped on in fiery tongues. Not wood alone
3.1.573: But stones gigantic crumbling into dust
3.1.574: Dissolved beneath the heat; the mighty mound
3.1.575: Lay prone, yet in its ruin larger seemed.
3.1.576: Next, conquered on the land, upon the main
3.1.577: They try their fortunes. On their simple craft
3.1.578: No painted figure-head adorned the bows
3.1.579: Nor claimed protection from the gods; but rude,
3.1.580: Just as they fell upon their mountain homes,
3.1.581: The trees were knit together, and the deck
3.1.582: Gave steady foot-hold for an ocean fight.
3.1.583: Meanwhile had Caesar's squadron left the Rhone
3.1.584: And reached with Brutus' turret ship the strait
3.1.585: By Stoechas' isles. Nor less the Grecian host-
3.1.586: Boys not yet grown to war, and aged men,
3.1.587: Armed for the conflict, with their all at stake.
3.1.588: Nor only did they marshal for the fight
3.1.589: Ships meet for service; but their ancient keels
3.1.590: Brought from the dockyards. When the morning rays
3.1.591: Broke from the waters, and the sky was clear,
3.1.592: And all the winds were still upon the deep,
3.1.593: Smoothed for the battle, swift on either part
3.1.594: The fleets essay the open; and the ships
3.1.595: Tremble beneath the oars that urge them on,
3.1.596: By sinewy arms impelled. Upon the wings
3.1.597: That bound the Roman fleet, the larger craft
3.1.598: With triple and quadruple banks of oars
3.1.599: Gird in the lesser: so they front the sea;
3.1.600: While in their rear, shaped as a crescent moon,
3.1.602: Towers Brutus' deck praetorian. Oars on oars
3.1.603: Propel the bulky vessel through the main,
3.1.604: Six ranks; the topmost strike the waves afar.
3.1.605: When such a space remained between the fleets
3.1.606: As could be covered by a single stroke,
3.1.608: Drowning with resonant din the beat of oars
3.1.609: And note of trumpet summoning: and all
3.1.610: Sit on the benches and with mighty stroke
3.1.611: Sweep o'er the sea and gain the space between.
3.1.612: Then crashed the prows together, and the keels
3.1.614: Or darkened all the sky or, in their fall,
3.1.615: The vacant ocean. As the wings grew wide,
3.1.616: Less densely packed the fleet, some Grecian ships
3.1.617: Pressed in between; as when with west and east
3.1.618: The tide contends, this way the waves are driven
3.1.619: And that the sea; so as they plough the deep
3.1.620: In various lines converging, what the prow
3.1.621: Throws up advancing, from the foemen's oars
3.1.622: Falls back repelled. But soon the Grecian fleet
3.1.623: Was handier found in battle, and in flight
3.1.624: Pretended, and in shorter curves could round;
3.1.625: More deftly governed by the guiding helm:
3.1.626: While on the Roman side their steadier keels
3.1.627: Gave vantage, as to men who fight on land.
3.1.628: Then Brutus to the pilot of his ship:
3.1.629: ' Dost suffer them to range the wider deep,
3.1.630: 'Contending with the foe in naval skill?
3.1.631: ' Draw close the war and drive us on the prows
3.1.632: 'Of these Phocaeans.' Him the pilot heard;
3.1.633: And turned his vessel slantwise to the foe.
3.1.634: Then was the sea all covered with the war:
3.1.635: Then Grecian ships attacking Brutus found
3.1.636: Their ruin in the stroke, and vanquished lay
3.1.637: Beside his bulwarks; with curved hooks and chains
3.1.638: The foe they grapple, by entangled oars
3.1.639: Themselves held back. And now no outstretched arm
3.1.640: Hurls forth the javelin, but sword in hand
3.1.641: They wage a naval fight: each from his ship
3.1.642: Leans forward to the stroke, and falls when slain
3.1.643: Upon a foeman's deck. Deep flows the stream
3.1.644: Of purple slaughter to the foamy main:
3.1.645: By piles of floating corpses are the sides,
3.1.646: Though grappled, kept asunder. Some, half dead,
3.1.647: Plunge in the ocean, gulping down the brine
3.1.648: Encrimsoned with their blood; some lingering still
3.1.649: Draw their last struggling breath amid the wreck
3.1.650: Of broken navies: weapons which have missed
3.1.651: Find yet their victims, and the falling steel
3.1.652: Fails not in middle deep to deal the wound.
3.1.653: One vessel circled by Phocaean keels
3.1.654: Divides her strength, and on the right and left
3.1.655: On either side with equal war contends;
3.1.656: On whose high poop while Tagus fighting gripped
3.1.657: The stern Phocaean, pierced his back and breast
3.1.658: Two fatal weapons; in the midst the steel
3.1.659: Met, and the blood, uncertain whence to flow,
3.1.660: Stood still, arrested, till with double course
3.1.661: Forth by a sudden gush it drove each dart,
3.1.662: And sent the life abroad through either wound.
3.1.663: Here fated Telon also steered his ship:
3.1.664: No pilot's hand upon an angry sea
3.1.665: More deftly ruled a vessel. Well he knew,
3.1.666: Or by the sun or crescent moon, how best
3.1.667: To set his canvas fitted for the breeze
3.1.668: The coming hours would bring. His rushing stem
3.1.669: Shattered a Roman vessel: but a dart
3.1.670: Hurled at the moment quivered in his breast.
3.1.671: He falls, and in the fall his dying hand
3.1.672: Diverts the prow. Then Gyareus, in act
3.1.673: To climb the friendly deck, by javelin pierced,
3.1.674: Still as he hung, by the retaining steel
3.1.675: Fast to the side was nailed.
3.1.677: A fruitful mother's pride; with different fates,
3.1.678: But ne'er distinguished till death's savage hand
3.1.679: Struck once, and ended error: he that lived,
3.1.680: Cause of fresh anguish to their sorrowing souls,
3.1.681: Called ever to the weeping parents back
3.1.682: The image of the lost: who, as the oars
3.1.683: Grecian and Roman mixed their teeth oblique,
3.1.684: Grasped with his dexter hand the Roman ship;
3.1.685: When fell a blow that shore his arm away.
3.1.686: So died, upon the side it held, the hand,
3.1.687: Nor loosed its grasp in death. Yet with the wound
3.1.688: His noble courage rose, and maimed he dared
3.1.689: Renew the fray, and stretched across the sea
3.1.690: To grasp the lost-in vain! another blow
3.1.691: Lopped arm and hand alike. Nor shield nor sword
3.1.692: Henceforth are his. Yet even now he seeks
3.1.693: No sheltering hold, but with his chest advanced
3.1.694: Before his brother armed, he claims the fight,
3.1.695: And holding in his breast the darts which else
3.1.696: Had slain his comrades, pierced with countless spears,
3.1.697: He falls in death well earned; yet ere his end
3.1.698: Collects his parting life, and all his strength
3.1.699: Strains to the utmost and with failing limbs
3.1.700: Leaps on the foeman's deck; by weight alone
3.1.701: Injurious; for streaming down with gore
3.1.702: And piled on high with corpses, while her sides
3.1.703: Sounded to ceaseless blows, the fated ship
3.1.704: Let in the greedy brine until her ways
3.1.705: Were level with the waters-then she plunged
3.1.706: In whirling eddies downwards-and the main
3.1.707: First parted, then closed in upon its prey.
3.1.708: Full many wondrous deaths, with fates diverse,
3.1.709: Upon the sea in that day's fight befell.
3.1.710: Caught by a grappling-hook that missed the side,
3.1.711: Had Lycidas been whelmed in middle deep;
3.1.712: But by his feet his comrades dragged him back,
3.1.713: And rent in twain he hung; nor slowly flowed
3.1.714: As from a wound the blood; but all his veins
3.1.715: Were torn asunder and the stream of life
3.1.716: Gushed o'er his limbs till lost amid the waves.
3.1.717: From no man dying has the vital breath
3.1.718: Rushed by so wide a path; the lower trunk
3.1.719: Succumbed to death, but with the lungs and heart
3.1.720: Long strove the fates, and hardly won the whole.
3.1.721: While, bent upon the fight, an eager crew
3.1.722: Were gathered to the margin of their deck
3.1.723: (Leaving the upper side as bare of foes),
3.1.724: Their ship was overset. Beneath the keel
3.1.725: Which floated upwards, prisoned in the sea,
3.1.726: And powerless by spread of arms to float
3.1.727: The main, they perished. One who haply swam
3.1.728: Amid the battle, chanced upon a death
3.1.729: Strange and unheard of; for two meeting prows
3.1.730: Transfixed his body. At the double stroke
3.1.731: Wide yawns his chest; blood issues from his mouth
3.1.732: With flesh commingled; and the brazen beaks
3.1.733: Resounding clash together, by the bones
3.1.734: Unhindered: now they part and through the gap
3.1.735: Swift pours the sea and drags the corse below.
3.1.736: Next, of a shipwrecked crew, the larger part
3.1.737: Struggling with death upon the waters, reached
3.1.738: A comrade bark; but when with elbows raised
3.1.739: They seized upon the bulwarks and the ship
3.1.740: Rolled, nor could bear their weight, the ruthless crew
3.1.741: Hacked off their straining arms; then maimed they sank
3.1.742: Below the seething waves, to rise no more.
3.1.743: Now every dart was hurled and every spear,
3.1.744: The soldier weaponless; yet their rage found arms:
3.1.745: One hurls an oar; another's brawny arm
3.1.746: Tugs at the twisted stern; or from the seats
3.1.747: The oarsmen driving, swings a bench in air.
3.1.748: The ships are broken for the fight. They seize
3.1.749: The fallen dead and snatch the sword that slew.
3.1.750: Nay, many from their wounds, frenzied for arms,
3.1.751: Pluck forth the deadly steel, and pressing still
3.1.752: Upon their yawning sides, hurl forth the spear
3.1.753: Back to the hostile ranks from which it came;
3.1.754: Then ebbs their life blood forth.
3.1.756: Was that fell force most hostile to the sea;
3.1.757: For, thrown in torches and in sulphurous bolts
3.1.758: Fire all-consuming ran among the ships,
3.1.759: Whose oily timbers soaked in pitch and wax
3.1.760: Inflammable, gave welcome to the flames.
3.1.761: Nor could the waves prevail against the blaze
3.1.762: Which claimed as for its own the fragments borne
3.1.763: Upon the waters. Lo! on burning plank
3.1.764: One hardly 'scapes destruction; one to save
3.1.765: His flaming ship, gives entrance to the main.
3.1.766: Of all the forms of death each fears the one
3.1.767: That brings immediate dying: yet quail not
3.1.768: Their hearts in shipwreck: from the waves they pluck
3.1.769: The fallen darts and furnishing the ships
3.1.770: Essay the feeble stroke; and should that hope
3.1.771: Still fail their hand, they call the sea to aid
3.1.772: And seizing in their grasp some floating foe
3.1.773: Drag him to mutual death. But on that day
3.1.774: Phoceus above all others proved his skill.
3.1.775: Well trained was he to dive beneath the main
3.1.776: And search the waters with unfailing eye;
3.1.777: And should an anchor 'gainst the straining rope
3.1.778: Too firmly bite the sands, to wrench it free.
3.1.779: Oft in his fatal grasp he seized a foe
3.1.780: Nor loosed his grip until the life was gone.
3.1.781: Such was his frequent deed; but this his fate:
3.1.782: For rising, victor (as he thought), to air,
3.1.783: Full on a keel he struck and found his death.
3.1.784: Some, drowning, seized a hostile oar and checked
3.1.785: The flying vessel; not to die in vain,
3.1.786: Their single care; some on their vessel's side
3.1.787: Hanging, in death, with wounded frame essayed
3.1.788: To check the charging prow. Tyrrhenus high
3.1.789: Upon the bulwarks of his ship was struck
3.1.790: By leaden bolt from Balearic sling
3.1.791: Of Lygdamus; straight through his temples passed
3.1.792: The fated missile; and in streams of blood
3.1.793: Forced from their seats his trembling eyeballs fell.
3.1.794: Plunged in a darkness as of night, he thought
3.1.795: That life had left him; yet ere long he knew
3.1.796: The living vigour of his limbs; and cried,
3.1.797: 'Place me, O friends, as some machine of war
3.1.798: Straight facing towards the foe; then shall my darts
3.1.799: Strike as of old; and thou, Tyrrhenus, spend
3.1.800: Thy latest breath, still left, upon the fight:
3.1.801: So shalt thou play, not wholly dead, the part
3.1.802: That fits a soldier, and the spear that strikes
3.1.803: Thy frame, shall miss the living.' Thus he spake,
3.1.804: And hurled his javelin, blind, but not in vain;
3.1.805: For Argus, generous youth of noble blood,
3.1.806: Below the middle waist received the spear
3.1.807: And falling drave it home. His aged sire
3.1.808: From furthest portion of the conquered ship
3.1.809: Beheld; than whom in pride of manhood none
3.1.810: More brave in battle: now no more he fought,
3.1.811: Yet did the memory of his prowess stir
3.1.812: Phocaean youths to emulate his fame.
3.1.813: Oft stumbling o'er the benches the old man hastes
3.1.814: To reach his boy, and finds him breathing still.
3.1.815: No tear bedewed his cheek; upon his breast
3.1.816: No blow he struck; but all his frame was stiff,
3.1.817: His hands outspread: and o'er his eyes there fell
3.1.818: A dark impenetrable veil of mist
3.1.819: That blotted out the day; nor could he more
3.1.820: Discern his luckless Argus. He, who saw
3.1.821: His parent, raising up his drooping head
3.1.822: With parted lips and silent features asks
3.1.823: A father's latest kiss, a father's hand
3.1.824: To close his dying eyes. But soon his sire,
3.1.825: Recovering from his swoon, when ruthless grief
3.1.826: Possessed his spirit, 'This short space,' he cried,
3.1.827: ' I lose not, which the cruel gods have given,
3.1.828: ' But die before thee. Grant thy sorrowing sire
3.1.829: ' Forgiveness that he fled thy last embrace.
3.1.830: Not yet has passed thy life blood from the wound
3.1.831: Nor yet is death upon thee-still thou may'st
3.1.832: Outlive thy parent.' Thus he spake, and seized
3.1.833: The reeking sword and drave it to the hilt,
3.1.834: Then plunged into the deep, with headlong bound,
3.1.835: To anticipate his son: for this he feared
3.1.836: A single form of death should not suffice.
3.1.837: Now gave the fates their judgment, and in doubt
3.1.838: No longer was the war: the Grecian fleet
3.1.839: In most part sunk; -some ships by Romans oared
3.1.840: Conveyed the victors home: in headlong flight
3.1.841: Some sought the yards for shelter. On the strand
3.1.842: What tears of parents for their offspring slain,
3.1.843: How wept the mothers! 'Mid the pile confused
3.1.844: Ofttimes the wife sought madly for her spouse
3.1.845: And chose for her last kiss some Roman slain;
3.1.846: While wretched fathers by the blazing pyres
3.1.847: Fought for the dead. But Brutus thus at sea
3.1.848: First gained a triumph for great Caesar's arms.

4.1.1: BUT in the distant regions of the earth
4.1.2: Fierce Caesar warring, though in fight he dealt
4.1.3: No baneful slaughter, hastened on the doom
4.1.4: To swift fulfilment. There on Magnus' side
4.1.6: Who ruled alternate, and the rampart guard
4.1.7: Obeyed the standard of each chief in turn.
4.1.8: There with the Romans in the camp were joined
4.1.9: Asturians swift, and Vettons lightly armed,
4.1.10: And Celts who, exiled from their ancient home,
4.1.11: Had joined 'Iberus' to their former name.
4.1.12: Where the rich soil in gentle slope ascends
4.1.13: And forms a modest hill, Ilerda stands,
4.1.14: Founded in ancient days; beside her glides
4.1.15: Not least of western rivers, Sicoris
4.1.16: Of placid current, by a mighty arch
4.1.17: Of stone o'erspanned, which not the winter floods
4.1.18: Shall overwhelm. Upon a rock hard by
4.1.19: Was Magnus' camp; but Caesar's on a hill,
4.1.20: Rivalling the first; and in the midst a stream.
4.1.21: Here boundless plains are spread beyond the range
4.1.22: Of human vision; Cinga girds them in
4.1.23: With greedy waves; forbidden to contend
4.1.24: With tides of ocean; for that larger flood
4.1.25: Who names the land, Iberus, sweeps along
4.1.26: The lesser stream commingled with his own.
4.1.27: Guiltless of war, the first day saw the hosts
4.1.28: In long array confronted; standard rose
4.1.30: Attacked, through shame of strife; one bloodless day
4.1.31: They gave their country and her broken laws.
4.1.32: But Caesar, when from heaven fell the night,
4.1.33: Drew round a hasty trench; his foremost rank
4.1.34: With close array concealing those who wrought.
4.1.35: Then with the morn he bids them seize the hill
4.1.36: Which parted from the camp Ilerda's walls,
4.1.37: And gave them safety. But in fear and shame
4.1.38: On rushed the foe and seized the vantage ground,
4.1.39: First in the onset. From the height they held
4.1.40: Their hopes of conquest; but to Caesar's men
4.1.41: Their hearts by courage stirred, and their good swords
4.1.42: Promised the victory. Burdened up the ridge
4.1.43: The soldier climbed, and from the opposing steep
4.1.44: But for his comrade's shield had fallen back;
4.1.45: None had the space to hurl the quivering lance
4.1.46: Upon the foeman: spear and pike made sure
4.1.47: The failing foothold, and the falchion's edge
4.1.48: Hewed out their upward path. But Caesar saw
4.1.49: Ruin impending, and he bade his horse
4.1.50: By circuit to the left, with shielded flank,
4.1.51: Hold back the foe. Thus gained his troops retreat,
4.1.52: For none pressed on them; and the victor chiefs,
4.1.53: Forced to withdrawal, gained the day in vain.
4.1.54: Henceforth the fitful changes of the year
4.1.55: Governed the fates and fashioned out the war.
4.1.56: For stubborn frost still lay upon the land,
4.1.57: And northern winds, controlling all the sky,
4.1.58: Prisoned the rain in clouds; the hills were nipped
4.1.59: With snow unmelted, and the lower plains
4.1.60: By frosts that fled before the rising sun;
4.1.61: And all the land, there nearer to the sky
4.1.62: That whelms the stars, was hard and arid grown
4.1.63: By suns of winter. But when Titan neared
4.1.64: The Ram, who, backward gazing on the stars,
4.1.65: Bore perished Helle, and the hours were held
4.1.66: In balance, and the days again prevailed,
4.1.67: The earliest faded moon which in the vault
4.1.68: Hung with uncertain horn, from eastern wind
4.1.69: Received a fiery radiance; whose blast
4.1.70: Forced Boreas back: and breaking on the mists
4.1.71: Within his regions, to the Occident
4.1.72: Drave all that shroud Arabia and the land
4.1.73: Of Ganges; all that or by Caurus borne
4.1.74: Bedim the Orient sky, or rising suns
4.1.75: Permit to gather; pitiless flamed the day
4.1.76: Behind them, while in front the wide expanse
4.1.77: Was driven; nor on mid earth sank the clouds
4.1.78: Though weighed with vapour. North and south alike
4.1.79: Were showerless, for on Calpe's rock alone
4.1.80: All moisture gathered; here at last, forbidden
4.1.81: To pass that sea by Zephyr's bounds contained,
4.1.82: And by the furthest belt of heaven, they pause,
4.1.83: In masses huge convolved; the widest breadth
4.1.84: Of murky air scarce holds them, which divides
4.1.85: Earth from the heavens; till pressed by weight of sky
4.1.86: In densest volume to the earth they pour
4.1.87: Their cataracts; no lightning could endure
4.1.88: Such storm unquenched: though oft athwart the gloom
4.1.89: Gleamed its pale fire. Meanwhile a watery arch
4.1.90: Scarce touched with colour, in imperfect shape
4.1.91: Embraced the sky and drank the ocean waves,
4.1.92: So rendering to the clouds their flood outpoured.
4.1.93: And now the snows which Titan never yet
4.1.94: Could melt were thawed: the Pyrenaean rocks
4.1.95: Are wet with flowing ice; accustomed springs
4.1.96: Find not discharge; and from the very banks
4.1.97: Each stream receives a torrent. Caesar's arms
4.1.98: Are shipwrecked on the field, his tottering camp
4.1.99: Swims on the rising flood; the trench is filled
4.1.100: With whirling waters; and the plain no more
4.1.101: Yields corn or kine; for those who forage seek,
4.1.102: Err from the hidden furrow. Famine knocks
4.1.103: (First herald of o'erwhelming ills to come)
4.1.104: Fierce at the door; and while no foe blockades
4.1.105: The soldier hungers; fortunes buy not now
4.1.106: The meanest measure; yet, alas! is found
4.1.107: The fasting peasant, who, in gain of gold,
4.1.108: Will sell his little all! And now the hills
4.1.109: Are seen no more; rivers in one vast sea
4.1.110: Of whirlpools overwhelmed; beasts borne away
4.1.111: And sucked beneath the stream; their rocky dens
4.1.112: Sweep onwards; and the torrent's raging force
4.1.113: Bears back the inflowing ocean. Nor does night
4.1.114: Acknowledge Phoebus' rise, for all the sky
4.1.115: Feels her dominion and obscures its face,
4.1.116: And darkness joins with darkness. Thus doth lie
4.1.117: The lowest earth beneath the snowy zone
4.1.118: And never-ending winters, where the sky
4.1.119: Is starless ever, and no growth of herb
4.1.120: Sprouts from the frozen earth; but standing ice
4.1.121: Tempers the stars which in the middle zone
4.1.122: Kindle their flames. Thus, Father of the world,
4.1.123: And thou, O trident-god who rul'st the sea
4.1.124: Second in place, Neptunus, load the air
4.1.125: With clouds continual; forbid the tide,
4.1.126: Once risen, to return: forced by thy waves
4.1.127: Let rivers backward run in different course,
4.1.128: Thy shores no longer reaching; and the earth,
4.1.129: Shaken, make way for floods. Let Rhine o'erflow
4.1.130: And Rhone their banks; let torrents spread afield
4.1.132: Spread lakes upon the land, and seas profound,
4.1.133: And snatch the groaning world from civil war.
4.1.134: Thus for a little moment Fortune tried
4.1.135: Her darling son; then smiling to his part
4.1.136: Returned; and gained her pardon for the past
4.1.137: By greater gifts to come. For now the air
4.1.138: Had grown more clear, and Phoebus' warmer rays
4.1.139: Coped with the flood and scattered all the clouds
4.1.140: In fleecy masses; and the reddening east
4.1.141: Proclaimed the coming day; the land resumed
4.1.142: Its ancient marks; no more in middle air
4.1.143: The moisture hung, but from about the stars
4.1.144: Sank to the depths; the forest glad upreared
4.1.145: Its foliage; hills again emerged to view
4.1.146: And 'neath the warmth of day the plains grew firm.
4.1.147: When Sicoris kept his banks, the shallop light
4.1.148: Of hoary willow bark they build, which bent
4.1.149: On hides of oxen, bears the weight of man
4.1.150: And swims the torrent. Thus on sluggish Po
4.1.151: Venetians float; and on th' encircling sea
4.1.152: Are borne Britannia's nations; and when Nile
4.1.153: Fills all the land, are Memphis' thirsty reeds
4.1.154: Shaped into fragile boats that swim his waves.
4.1.155: The further bank thus gained, they haste to curve
4.1.156: The fallen forest, and to form the arch
4.1.157: By which imperious Sicoris shall be spanned.
4.1.158: Yet fearing he might rise in wrath anew,
4.1.159: Not on the nearest marge they place the beams,
4.1.160: But in mid-field. Thus the presumptuous stream
4.1.161: They tame with chastisement, parting his flood
4.1.162: In devious channels out; and curb his pride.
4.1.163: Petreius, seeing that all things gave way
4.1.164: To Caesar's destiny, leaves Ilerda's steep,
4.1.165: His trust no longer in the Roman world;
4.1.166: And seeks for strength amid those distant tribes,
4.1.167: Who, loving death, rush in upon the foe,
4.1.168: And win their conquests at the point of sword.
4.1.169: But in the dawn, when Caesar saw the camp
4.1.170: Stand empty on the hill, ' To arms! ' he cries:
4.1.171: ' No bridge nor ford; but stem with brawny arms
4.1.172: ' The foaming river.' Rushing to the fray
4.1.173: They dare the torrent they had feared in flight.
4.1.174: Their arms regained, they race until the blood
4.1.175: Throbs in their veins anew, and their wet limbs
4.1.176: Are warm again. At length the shadows fall
4.1.177: Short on the sward, and day is at the height.
4.1.178: Then dash the horsemen on, and hold the foe
4.1.179: 'Twixt flight and battle. In the plain arose
4.1.180: Two rocky heights: from each a loftier ridge
4.1.181: Of hills ranged onwards, sheltering in their midst
4.1.182: A hollow vale, whose deep and winding paths
4.1.183: Were safe from warfare; which, when Caesar saw
4.1.184: That if Petreius held, the war must pass
4.1.185: To lands remote by savage tribes possessed;
4.1.186: 'Speed on,' he cries, ' and meet their flight in front;
4.1.187: 'Fierce be your frown and battle in your glance:
4.1.188: ' No coward's death be theirs; but as they flee
4.1.189: 'Plunge in their breasts the sword.' They seize the pass
4.1.190: And place their camp. Short was the span between
4.1.191: Th' opposing sentinels; with eager eyes
4.1.192: Undimmed by space, they gazed on brothers, sons,
4.1.193: Or friends and fathers; and within their souls
4.1.194: They grasped the impious horror of the war.
4.1.195: Yet for a little while no voice was heard,
4.1.196: For fear restrained; by waving blade alone
4.1.197: Or gesture, spake they; but their passion grew,
4.1.198: And broke all discipline; and soon they leap
4.1.199: The hostile rampart; every hand outstretched
4.1.200: Embraces hand of foeman, palm in palm;
4.1.201: One calls by name his neighbour, one his host,
4.1.202: Another with his schoolmate talks again
4.1.203: Of olden studies: he who in the camp
4.1.204: Found not a comrade, was no son of Rome.
4.1.205: Wet are their arms with tears, and sobs break in
4.1.206: Upon their kisses; each, unstained by blood,
4.1.207: Dreads what he might have done. Why beat thy breast?
4.1.208: Why, madman, weep? The guilt is thine alone
4.1.209: To do or to abstain. Dost fear the man
4.1.210: Who takes his title to be feared from thee?
4.1.211: When Caesar's trumpets sound the call to arms
4.1.212: Heed not the summons; when thou seest advance
4.1.213: His standards, halt. The civil Fury thus
4.1.214: Shall fold her wings; and in a private robe
4.1.217: Who sway'st the universe, whose firm embrace
4.1.218: Binds the compacted fabric of the world;
4.1.219: Come, gentle Concord! these our times do now
4.1.220: For good or evil destiny control
4.1.221: The coming centuries! Ah, cruel fate!
4.1.222: Now have the people lost their cloak for crime:
4.1.223: Their hope of pardon. They have known their kin.
4.1.224: Woe for the respite given by the gods
4.1.225: Making more black the hideous guilt to come!
4.1.226: Now all was peaceful, and in either camp
4.1.227: Sweet converse held the soldiers; on the grass
4.1.228: They place the meal, and pour the mingled cup;
4.1.229: Bright glows the turf upon the friendly fire;
4.1.230: On mutual couch with stories of their fights,
4.1.231: They while the sleepless hours in talk away;
4.1.232: 'Where stood the ranks arrayed, from whose right hand
4.1.233: The quivering lance was sped:' and while they boast,
4.1.234: Or challenge, deeds of prowess in the war,
4.1.235: Faith is renewed and trust. Thus envious fate
4.1.236: Made worse their doom, and all the crimes to be
4.1.237: Grew with their love. For when Petreius knew
4.1.238: The treaties made, himself and all his camp
4.1.239: Sold to the foe, he stirred his guard to work
4.1.240: An impious slaughter: the defenceless foe
4.1.241: Flung headlong forth: and parted fond embrace
4.1.242: By stroke of weapon and in streams of blood.
4.1.243: And thus in words of wrath, to stir the war:
4.1.244: 'Of Rome forgetful, to your faith forsworn!
4.1.245: 'And could ye not with victory gained return,
4.1.247: 'Lose then! but losing call not Caesar lord.
4.1.248: 'While still your swords are yours, with blood to shed
4.1.249: 'In doubtful battle, while the fates are hid,
4.1.250: 'Will you like cravens to your master bear
4.1.251: 'Doomed eagles? Will you ask upon your knees
4.1.252: 'That Caesar deign to treat his slaves alike,
4.1.253: 'And spare, forsooth, like yours, your leaders' lives?
4.1.254: 'Nay! never shall our safety be the price
4.1.255: 'Of base betrayal! Not for boon of life
4.1.256: 'We wage a civil war. This name of peace
4.1.257: 'Drags us to slavery. Ne'er from depths of earth,
4.1.258: 'Fain to withdraw her wealth, should toiling men
4.1.259: 'Draw store of iron; ne'er entrench a town;
4.1.260: 'Ne'er should the war-horse dash into the fray
4.1.261: 'Nor fleet with turret bulwarks breast the main,
4.1.262: If freedom ever could for peace be sold,
4.1.263: And fame unsoiled: 'tis true our foes are sworn
4.1.264: To cursed crime; should you whose cause is just,
4.1.265: And who may hope for pardon in defeat,
4.1.266: Hold cheap your honour? Shame upon your peace!
4.1.267: Thou callest, Magnus, ignorant of fate,
4.1.268: From all the world thy powers, and dost entreat
4.1.269: Monarchs of distant realms, while haply here
4.1.270: We in our treaties bargain for thy-life! '
4.1.271: Thus did he stir their minds and rouse anew
4.1.272: The love of impious battle. So when beasts
4.1.273: Grown strange to forests, long confined in dens,
4.1.274: Their fierceness lose, and learn to bear with man;
4.1.275: Once should they taste of blood, their thirsty jaws
4.1.276: Swell at the touch, and all the ancient rage
4.1.277: Comes back upon them till they hardly spare
4.1.278: Their keeper. Thus they rush on every crime:
4.1.279: And blows which dealt in blindness of affray
4.1.280: Might seem the crimes of chance, or of the gods
4.1.281: Wreaking their hate, such recent vows of love
4.1.282: Made monstrous, horrid. Where they lately spread
4.1.283: The mutual couch and banquet, and embraced
4.1.284: Some new-found friend, now falls the fatal blow
4.1.285: Upon the self-same breast; and though at first
4.1.286: Groaning at the fell chance, they drew the sword;
4.1.287: Hate rises as they strike, the murderous arm
4.1.288: Confirms the doubtful will: in dreadful joy
4.1.289: Through the wild camp they smote their kinsmen down;
4.1.290: And carnage raged unchecked; and each man strove,
4.1.291: Proud of his crime, before his leader's face
4.1.292: To prove his shamelessness of guilt.
4.1.294: Caesar, though losing of thy best, dost know
4.1.295: The gods do favour thee. Thessalian fields
4.1.296: Gave thee no better fortune, nor the waves
4.1.297: That lave Massilia; nor on Pharos' main
4.1.298: Didst thou so triumph. By this crime alone
4.1.299: Thou from this moment of the better cause
4.1.302: With foulest slaughter thus, their leaders shunned
4.1.303: All camps with Caesar's joined, and sought again
4.1.304: Ilerda's lofty walls; but Caesar's horse
4.1.305: Seized on the plain and forced them to the hills
4.1.306: Reluctant. There by steepest trench shut in,
4.1.307: He cuts them from the river, nor permits
4.1.308: Their circling ramparts to enclose a spring.
4.1.309: By this dread path Death trapped his captive prey.
4.1.310: Which when they knew, fierce anger filled their souls,
4.1.311: And took the place of fear. They slew the steeds
4.1.312: Now useless grown, and rushed upon their fate;
4.1.313: Hopeless of life and flight. But Caesar cried:
4.1.314: Hold back your weapons, soldiers, from the foe,
4.1.315: Strike not the breast advancing; let the war
4.1.316: ' Cost me no blood; he falls not without price
4.1.317: ' Who with his life-blood challenges the fray.
4.1.318: Scorning their own base lives and hating light,
4.1.319: To Caesar's loss they rush upon their death,
4.1.320: Nor heed our blows. But let this frenzy pass,
4.1.321: This madman onset; let the wish for death
4.1.322: Die in their souls.' Thus to its embers shrank
4.1.323: The fire within, when battle was denied,
4.1.324: And fainter grew their rage until the night
4.1.325: Drew down her starry veil and sank the sun.
4.1.326: Thus keener fights the gladiator whose wound
4.1.327: Is recent, while the blood within the veins
4.1.328: Still gives the sinews motion, ere the skin
4.1.329: Shrinks on the bones: but as the victor stands
4.1.330: His fatal thrust achieved, and points the blade
4.1.331: Unfaltering, watching for the end, there creeps
4.1.332: Torpor upon the limbs, the blood congeals
4.1.333: About the gash, more faintly throbs the heart,
4.1.334: And slowly fading, ebbs the life away.
4.1.335: Raving for water now they dig the plain
4.1.336: Seeking for hidden fountains, not with spade
4.1.337: And mattock only searching out the depths,
4.1.338: But with the sword; they hack the stony heights,
4.1.339: In shafts that reach the level of the plain.
4.1.340: No further flees from light the pallid wretch
4.1.341: Who tears the bowels of the earth for gold.
4.1.342: Yet neither riven stones revealed a spring,
4.1.343: Nor streamlet whispered from its hidden source;
4.1.344: No water trickled on the gravel bed,
4.1.345: Nor dripped within the cavern. Worn at length
4.1.346: With labour huge, they crawl to light again,
4.1.347: After such toil to fall to thirst and heat
4.1.348: The readier victims: this was all they won.
4.1.349: All food they loathe; and 'gainst their deadly thirst
4.1.350: Call famine to their aid. Damp clods of earth
4.1.351: They squeeze upon their mouths with straining hands.
4.1.352: Wherever on foulest mud some stagnant slime
4.1.353: Or moisture lies, each dying soldier strives
4.1.354: With dying comrade first to lap the draught,
4.1.355: Loathsome had life been his. Like beasts they drain
4.1.356: The swollen udder, and where milk was not,
4.1.357: They suck the life-blood forth. From herbs and boughs
4.1.358: Dripping with dew, from tender shoots they press,
4.1.359: Nay, from the pith of trees, the juice within.
4.1.360: Happy the host that onward marching finds
4.1.361: Its savage enemy has fouled the wells
4.1.362: With murderous venom; hadst thou, Caesar, cast
4.1.363: The reeking filth of shambles in the stream,
4.1.364: And henbane dire and all the poisonous herbs
4.1.365: That lurk on Cretan slopes, still had they drunk
4.1.366: The fatal waters, rather than endure
4.1.367: Such lingering agony. Their bowels racked
4.1.368: With torments as of flame; the swollen tongue
4.1.369: And jaws now parched and rigid, and the veins;
4.1.370: Each laboured breath with anguish from the lungs
4.1.372: And scarce again returned; and yet agape,
4.1.373: Their panting mouths suck in the nightly dew;
4.1.374: They watch for showers from heaven, and in despair
4.1.375: Gaze on the clouds, whence lately poured a flood.
4.1.376: Nor were their tortures less that Meroe
4.1.377: Saw not their sufferings, nor Cancer's zone,
4.1.378: Nor where the Garamantian turns the soil;
4.1.379: But Sicoris and Iberus at their feet,
4.1.380: Two mighty floods, but far beyond their reach,
4.1.381: Rolled down in measureless volume to the main.
4.1.382: But now their leaders yield; Afranius,
4.1.383: Vanquished, throws down his arms, and leads his troops,
4.1.384: Now hardly living, to the hostile camp
4.1.385: Before the victor's feet, and sues for peace.
4.1.386: Proud is his bearing, and despite of ills,
4.1.387: His mien majestic, of his triumphs past
4.1.388: Still mindful in disaster thus he stands,
4.1.389: Though suppliant for grace, a leader yet;
4.1.390: From fearless heart thus speaking: 'Had the fates
4.1.391: Thrown me before some base ignoble foe,
4.1.392: Not, Caesar, thee; still had this arm fought on
4.1.393: And snatched my death. Now if I suppliant ask,
4.1.394: 'Tis that I value still the boon of life
4.1.395: Given by a worthy hand. No party ties
4.1.396: 'Roused us to arms against thee; when the war,
4.1.397: 'This civil war, broke out, it found us chiefs;
4.1.398: And with our former cause we kept the faith,
4.1.399: So long as brave men should. The fates' decree
4.1.400: 'No longer we withstand. Unto thy will
4.1.401: We yield the western tribes: the east is thine
4.1.402: 'And all the world lies open to thy march.
4.1.403: 'Be generous! blood nor sword nor wearied arm
4.1.404: 'Thy conquests bought. Thou hast not to forgive
4.1.405: Aught but thy victory won. Nor ask we much.
4.1.406: 'Give us repose; to lead in peace the life
4.1.407: 'Thou shalt bestow; suppose these armed lines
4.1.408: 'Are corpses prostrate on the field of war,
4.1.409: 'Ne'er were it meet that thy victorious ranks
4.1.410: Should mix with ours, the vanquished. Destiny
4.1.411: 'Has run for us its course: one boon I beg;
4.1.412: 'Bid not the conquered conquer in thy train.'
4.1.413: Such were his words, and Caesar's gracious smile
4.1.414: Granted his prayer, remitting rights that war
4.1.415: Gives to the victor. To th' unguarded stream
4.1.416: The soldiers speed: prone on the bank they lie
4.1.417: And lap the flood or foul the crowded waves.
4.1.418: In many a burning throat the sudden draught
4.1.419: Poured in too copious, filled the empty veins
4.1.420: And choked the breath within: yet left unquenched
4.1.421: The burning pest which, though their frames were full,
4.1.422: Craved water for itself. Then, nerved once more,
4.1.423: Their strength returned. Oh, lavish luxury,
4.1.424: Contented never with the frugal meal!
4.1.425: Oh, greed that searchest over land and sea
4.1.426: To furnish forth the banquet! Pride that joy'st
4.1.427: In sumptuous tables! learn what life requires,
4.1.428: How little nature needs! No ruddy juice
4.1.429: Pressed from the vintage in some famous year,
4.1.430: Whose consuls are forgotten, served in cups
4.1.431: With gold and jewels wrought, restores the spark,
4.1.432: The failing spark, of life; but water pure
4.1.433: And simplest fruits of earth. The flood, the field
4.1.434: Suffice for nature. Ah! the weary lot
4.1.435: Of those who war! But these, their armour laid
4.1.436: Low at the victor's feet, with lightened breast,
4.1.437: Secure themselves, no longer dealing death,
4.1.438: Beset by care no more, seek out their homes.
4.1.439: What priceless gift in peace had they secured!
4.1.440: How grieved it now their souls to have poised the dart
4.1.441: With arm outstretched; to have felt their raving thirst;
4.1.442: And prayed the gods for victory in vain!
4.1.443: Nay, hard they think the victor's lot, for whom
4.1.444: A thousand risks and battles still remain;
4.1.445: If fortune never is to leave his side,
4.1.446: How often must he triumph! and how oft
4.1.447: Pour out his blood where'er great Caesar leads!
4.1.448: Happy, thrice happy, he who, when the world
4.1.449: Is nodding to its ruin, knows the spot
4.1.450: Where he himself shall, though in ruin, lie!
4.1.451: No trumpet call shall break his sleep again:
4.1.452: But in his humble home, with faithful spouse
4.1.453: And sons unlettered, Fortune leaves him free
4.1.454: From rage of party; for if life he owes
4.1.455: To Caesar, Magnus sometime was his lord.
4.1.456: Thus happy they alone live on apart,
4.1.457: Nor hope nor dread the event of civil war.
4.1.458: Not thus did Fortune upon Caesar smile
4.1.459: In all the parts of earth; but 'gainst his arms
4.1.460: Dared somewhat, where Salona's lengthy waste
4.1.461: Is laved by Hadria, and Iadar warm
4.1.462: Meets with his waves the breezes of the west.
4.1.463: There brave Curectae dwell, whose island home
4.1.464: Is girded by the main; on whom relied
4.1.465: Antonius, and, beleaguered by the foe,
4.1.466: Upon the furthest margin of the shore
4.1.467: (Safe from all ills but famine) placed his camp.
4.1.468: But for his steeds the earth no forage gave,
4.1.469: Nor golden Ceres harvest; and his troops
4.1.470: Gnawed the dry herbage of the scanty turf
4.1.471: Within their rampart lines. But when they knew
4.1.472: That Basilus was on th' opposing shore
4.1.473: With friendly force, by novel mode of flight
4.1.474: They aim to reach him. Not the accustomed keel
4.1.475: They lay, nor build the ship, but shapeless rafts
4.1.476: Of timbers knit together, strong to bear
4.1.477: All ponderous weight; on empty casks beneath
4.1.478: By tightened chains made firm, in double rows
4.1.479: Supported; nor upon the deck were placed
4.1.480: The oarsmen, to the hostile dart exposed,
4.1.481: But in a hidden space, by beams concealed.
4.1.482: And thus the eye amazed beheld the mass
4.1.483: Move silent on its path across the sea,
4.1.484: By neither sail nor stalwart arm propelled.
4.1.485: They watch the main until the refluent waves
4.1.486: Ebb from the growing sands; then, on the tide
4.1.487: Receding, launch their vessel; thus she floats
4.1.488: With comrades twin: and rises over each
4.1.489: With quivering battlements a lofty tower.
4.1.491: Restrained his swifter keels, and left the rafts
4.1.492: Free from attack, in hope of larger spoil
4.1.493: From fresh adventures; for the peaceful sea
4.1.494: Might tempt them, and their goal in safety reached,
4.1.495: To dare a second voyage. Round the stag
4.1.496: Thus will the cunning hunter draw a line
4.1.497: Of tainted feathers poisoning the air;
4.1.498: Or spread the mesh, and muzzle in his grasp
4.1.499: The straining jaws of the Molossian hound,
4.1.500: And leash the Spartan pack; nor is the brake
4.1.501: Trusted to any dog but such as tracks
4.1.502: The scent with lowered nostrils, and refrains
4.1.503: From giving tongue the while; content to mark
4.1.504: By shaking cord the covert of the prey.
4.1.505: Ere long they manned the rafts in eager wish
4.1.506: To quit the island, when the latest glow
4.1.507: Still parted day from night. But Magnus' troops,
4.1.508: Cilician once, taught by their ancient art,
4.1.509: In fraudulent deceit had left the sea
4.1.510: To view unguarded; but with chains unseen
4.1.511: Fast to Illyrian shores, and hanging loose,
4.1.512: They blocked the outlet in the waves beneath.
4.1.513: The leading rafts passed safely, but the third,
4.1.514: Caught by the rope, was drawn beneath the rocks.
4.1.515: These, hollowed by the sea, in ponderous mass
4.1.516: O'erhanging, seemed upon the point to fall;
4.1.517: And trees made dark the wave. Here oft the main
4.1.518: Within the deep recess sweeps broken wrecks
4.1.519: And bodies of the drowned, till ebbing tides
4.1.520: Return the spoil. Then from the cavernous arch
4.1.521: Is belched the ocean forth in such turmoil
4.1.522: Of swirling billows, as excels the rage
4.1.523: Of that famed whirlpool on Sicilian shores.
4.1.524: Here, with Venetian settlers for its load,
4.1.525: Stood motionless the raft. Octavius' ships
4.1.526: Gathered around, while foemen on the land
4.1.527: Filled all the shore. But well the captain knew,
4.1.528: Volteius, how the secret fraud was planned,
4.1.529: And tried in vain with sword and steel to burst
4.1.530: The chains that held them; without hope he fights,
4.1.531: Uncertain where to avoid or front the foe.
4.1.532: Caught in the strait they strove as brave men should
4.1.533: Against opposing hosts; nor long the fight,
4.1.534: For fallen darkness brought a truce to arms.
4.1.535: Then to his men disheartened and in fear
4.1.536: Of coming fate Volteius, great of soul,
4.1.537: Thus spake in tones commanding: ' Free no more,
4.1.538: 'Save for this little night, consult ye now
4.1.539: 'In this last moment, soldiers, how to face
4.1.540: 'Your final fortunes. No man's life is short
4.1.541: ' Who can take thought for death, nor is your fame
4.1.542: ' Less than a conqueror's, if with breast advanced
4.1.543: 'Ye meet your destined doom. None know how long
4.1.544: 'The life that waits them. Summon your own fate,
4.1.545: 'And equal is your praise, whether the hand
4.1.546: 'Quench the last flicker of departing light,
4.1.547: ' Or shear the hope of years. But choice to die
4.1.548: 'Is thrust not on the mind-we cannot flee;
4.1.549: 'See at our throats, e'en now, our kinsmen's swords.
4.1.550: ' Then choose for death; desire what fate decrees.
4.1.551: 'At least in war's blind cloud we shall not fall;
4.1.552: ' Nor when the flying weapons hide the day,
4.1.553: 'And slaughtered heaps of foemen load the field,
4.1.554: 'And death is common, and the brave man sinks
4.1.556: 'Seen of both friends and foes, the gods have placed;
4.1.557: 'Both land and sea and island cliffs shall bear,
4.1.558: 'From either shore, their witness to our death,
4.1.559: 'In which some great and memorable fame
4.1.560: 'Thou, Fortune, dost prepare. What glorious deeds
4.1.561: ' Of warlike heroism, of noble faith,
4.1.562: 'Time's annals show! All these shall we surpass.
4.1.563: 'True, Caesar, that to fall upon our swords
4.1.564: 'For thee is little; yet beleaguered thus,
4.1.565: 'With neither sons nor parents at our sides,
4.1.566: 'Shorn of the glory that we might have earned,
4.1.567: 'We give thee here the only pledge we may.
4.1.568: 'Yet let these hostile thousands fear the souls
4.1.569: 'That rage for battle and that welcome death,
4.1.570: 'And know us for invincible, and joy
4.1.571: 'That no more rafts were stayed. They'll offer terms,
4.1.572: 'And tempt us with a base unhonoured life.
4.1.573: 'Would that, to give that death which shall be ours
4.1.574: 'The greater glory, they may bid us hope
4.1.575: 'For pardon and for life! lest when our swords
4.1.576: 'Are reeking with our hearts'-blood, they may say
4.1.577: 'This was despair of living. Great must be
4.1.578: 'The prowess of our end, if in the hosts
4.1.579: 'That fight his battles, Caesar is to mourn
4.1.580: 'This little handful lost. For me, should fate
4.1.581: 'Grant us retreat-myself would scorn to shun
4.1.582: 'The coming onset. Life I cast away,
4.1.583: 'The frenzy of the death that comes apace
4.1.584: 'Controls my being. Those whose end is near
4.1.585: 'Alone may know the happiness of death;
4.1.586: 'Which pitying heaven from all else conceals
4.1.587: 'That men may bear to live.' His stirring words
4.1.588: Warmed his brave comrades' hearts-they who with fear
4.1.589: And tearful eyes had looked upon the Wain,
4.1.590: Turning his nightly course, now hoped for day,
4.1.591: Such precepts deep within them. Nor delayed
4.1.592: The sky to dip the stars below the main;
4.1.593: For Phoebus in the Twins his chariot drave
4.1.594: At noon near Cancer; and the hours of night
4.1.597: Lo! on the rocks the Istrians; while the sea
4.1.598: Swarmed with the galleys and their Grecian fleet
4.1.599: All armed for fight: but first the war was stayed
4.1.600: And terms proposed: life to the foe they thought
4.1.601: Would seem the sweeter, by delay of death
4.1.602: Thus granted. But the band devoted stood,
4.1.603: Proud of their promised end, life all forsworn,
4.1.604: And careless of the fight: no jarring note
4.1.605: Opposed their high resolve. In numbers few
4.1.606: 'Gainst foemen numberless by land and sea,
4.1.607: They wage the desperate war; then satiate
4.1.608: Turn from the foe. And first demanding death
4.1.609: Volteius bared his throat. ' What youth,' he cries,
4.1.610: ' Dares strike me down, and through his captain's wounds
4.1.611: 'Attest his love for death? ' Then through his side
4.1.612: Plunge blades uncounted on the moment drawn.
4.1.613: He praises all: but him who struck the first
4.1.614: Grateful, with dying strength, he does to death.
4.1.615: They rush together, and without a foe
4.1.616: Work all the guilt of battle. Thus of yore,
4.1.617: Rose up the glittering Dircaean band
4.1.618: From seed by Cadmus sown, and fought and died,
4.1.619: Dire omen for the brother kings of Thebes.
4.1.620: And so in Phasis' fields the sons of earth,
4.1.621: Born of the sleepless dragon, all inflamed
4.1.622: By magic incantations, with their blood
4.1.623: Deluged the monstrous furrow, while the Queen
4.1.624: Feared at the spells she wrought. Devoted thus
4.1.625: To death, they fall, yet in their death itself
4.1.626: Less valour show than in the fatal wounds
4.1.627: They take and give; for e'en the dying hand
4.1.628: Missed not a blow nor did the stroke alone
4.1.629: Inflict the wound, but rushing on the sword
4.1.630: Their throat or breast received it to the hilt;
