5.1.132: To speak the future, fearing for their fates.
5.1.133: Nor does the priestess sorrow that the voice
5.1.134: Is heard no longer; and the silent fane
5.1.135: To her is happiness; for whatever breast
5.1.136: Contains the deity, its shattered frame
5.1.137: Surges with frenzy, and the soul divine
5.1.138: Shakes the frail breath that with the god receives,
5.1.139: As prize or punishment, untimely death.
5.1.140: These tripods Appius seeks, unmoved for years,
5.1.141: These soundless caverned rocks, in quest to learn
5.1.143: To loose the sacred gateways and permit
5.1.144: The prophetess to enter to the god,
5.1.145: The keeper calls Phemonoe; whose steps
5.1.146: Round the Castalian fount and in the grove
5.1.147: Were wandering careless; her he bids to pass
5.1.148: The portals. But the priestess feared to tread
5.1.149: The awful threshold, and with vain deceits
5.1.150: Sought to dissuade the chieftain from his zeal
5.1.151: To learn the future. ' What this hope,' she cried,
5.1.152: Roman, that moves thy breast to know the fates?
5.1.153: 'Long has Parnassus and its silent cleft
5.1.154: 'Stifled the god; perhaps the breath divine
5.1.155: 'Has left its ancient gorge and through the world
5.1.156: 'Wanders in devious paths; or else the fane,
5.1.158: 'Closed up the deep recess and choked the path
5.1.159: 'Of Phoebus; or the ancient Sibyl's books
5.1.160: 'Disclosed enough of fate, and thus the gods
5.1.161: 'Decreed to close the oracle; or else
5.1.162: 'Since wicked steps are banished from the fane,
5.1.163: 'In this our impious age the god finds none
5.1.164: 'Whom he may answer.' But the maiden's guile
5.1.165: Was known, for though she would deny the gods
5.1.166: Her fears approved them. On her front she binds
5.1.167: A twisted fillet, while a shining wreath
5.1.168: Of Phocian laurels crowns the locks that flow
5.1.170: The priest compelled her, and she passed within.
5.1.171: But horror filled her of the holiest depths
5.1.172: From which the mystic oracle proceeds;
5.1.173: And resting near the doors, in breast unmoved
5.1.174: She dares invent the god in words confused,
5.1.175: Which proved no mind possessed with fire divine;
5.1.176: By such false chant less injuring the chief
5.1.177: Than faith in Phoebus and the sacred fane.
5.1.178: No burst of words with tremor in their tones,
5.1.179: No voice re-echoing through the spacious vault
5.1.180: Proclaimed the deity, no bristling locks
5.1.181: Shook off the laurel chaplet; but the grove
5.1.182: Unshaken, and the summits of the shrine,
5.1.183: Gave proof she shunned the god. The Roman knew
5.1.184: The tripods yet were idle, and in rage,
5.1.185: 'Wretch,' he exclaimed, 'to us and to the gods,
5.1.186: 'Whose presence thou pretendest, thou shalt pay
5.1.187: 'The punishment; unless thou enter the recess,
5.1.188: 'And cease to speak in phrases of thine own
5.1.189: Of this vast conflict, of a world by war
5.1.190: 'Convulsed and shaken.' Then by fear compelled,
5.1.191: At length the priestess sought the furthest depths,
5.1.192: And stayed beside the tripods; and there came
5.1.193: Into her unaccustomed breast the god,
5.1.194: Breathed from the living rock for centuries
5.1.195: Untouched; nor ever with a mightier power
5.1.196: Did Paean's inspiration seize the frame
5.1.197: Of Delphic priestess; his pervading touch
5.1.198: Expelled the mortal, and her former mind,
5.1.199: And made her wholly his. In maddened trance
5.1.200: She whirled throughout the cave, her locks erect
5.1.201: With horror, and the fillets of the god
5.1.202: Dashed to the ground; her steps unguided turned
5.1.203: To this side and to that; the tripods fell
5.1.204: O'erturned; within her seethed the mighty fire
5.1.205: Of angry Phoebus; nor with whip alone
5.1.206: He urged her onwards, but with curb restrained;
5.1.207: Nor was it given her by the god to speak
5.1.208: All that she knew; for into one vast mass
5.1.209: All time was gathered, and her panting chest
5.1.210: Groaned 'neath the centuries. In order long
5.1.211: All things lay bare: the future yet unveiled
5.1.212: Struggled for light; each fate required a voice;
5.1.213: The compass of the seas, Creation's birth,
5.1.214: Creation's death, the number of the sands,
5.1.215: All these she knew. Thus on a former day
5.1.216: The prophetess upon the Cuman shore,
5.1.217: Disdaining that her frenzy should be slave
5.1.218: To other nations, from the boundless threads
5.1.219: Chose out with pride of hand the fates of Rome.
5.1.220: E'en so Phemonoe, for a time oppressed
5.1.221: With fates unnumbered, laboured ere she found,
5.1.223: Thine, Appius, who alone hadst sought the god
5.1.224: In land Castalian; then from foaming lips
5.1.225: First rushed the madness forth, and murmurs loud
5.1.226: Uttered with panting breath and blent with groans;
5.1.227: Till through the spacious vault a voice at length
5.1.228: Broke from the virgin conquered by the god:
5.1.229: 'From this great struggle thou, O Roman, free
5.1.230: 'Escap'st the threats of war: alive, in peace,
5.1.231: 'Thou shalt possess the hollow in the coast
5.1.232: 'Of vast Euboea.' Thus she spake, no more.
5.1.233: Ye mystic tripods, guardians of the fates
5.1.234: And Paean, thou, from whom no day is hid
5.1.235: By heaven's high rulers, Master of the truth,
5.1.236: Why fear'st thou to reveal the deaths of kings,
5.1.237: Rome's murdered princes, and the latest doom
5.1.238: Of her great Empire tottering to its fall,
5.1.239: And all the bloodshed of that western land?
5.1.240: Were yet the stars in doubt on Magnus' fate
5.1.241: Not yet decreed, and did the gods yet shrink
5.1.242: From that, the greatest crime? Or wert thou dumb
5.1.243: That Fortune's sword for civil strife might wreak
5.1.244: Just vengeance, and a Brutus' arm once more
5.1.247: Rushed forth the prophetess in frenzy driven,
5.1.248: Not all her knowledge uttered; and her eyes,
5.1.249: Still troubled by the god who reigned within,
5.1.250: Or filled with wild affright, or fired with rage
5.1.251: Gaze on the wide expanse: still works her face
5.1.252: Convulsive; on her cheeks a crimson blush
5.1.253: With ghastly pallor blent, though not of fear.
5.1.254: Her weary heart throbs ever; and as seas
5.1.255: Boom swollen by northern winds, she finds in sighs,
5.1.257: She hastes from that dread light in which she saw
5.1.258: The fates, to common day, lo! on her path
5.1.259: The darkness fell. Then by a Stygian draught
5.1.260: Of the forgetful river, Phoebus snatched
5.1.261: Back from her soul his secrets; and she fell
5.1.262: Yet hardly living. Nor did Appius dread
5.1.263: Approaching death, but by dark oracles
5.1.264: Baffled, while yet the Empire of the world
5.1.265: Hung in the balance, sought his promised realm
5.1.266: In Chalcis of Euboea. Yet to escape
5.1.267: All ills of earth, the crash of war-what god
5.1.268: Can give thee such a boon, but death alone?
5.1.269: For on the solitary shore a grave
5.1.270: Awaits thee, where Carystos' marble crags
5.1.271: Draw in the passage of the sea, and where
5.1.272: The fane of Rhamnus rises to the gods
5.1.273: Who hate the proud, and where the ocean strait
5.1.274: Boils in swift whirlpools, and Euripus draws
5.1.275: Deceitful in his tides, a bane to ships,
5.1.276: Chalcidian vessels to bleak Aulis' shore.
5.1.277: But Caesar carried from the conquered west
5.1.278: His eagles to another world of war;
5.1.279: When envying his victorious course the gods
5.1.280: Almost turned back the prosperous tide of fate.
5.1.281: Not on the battle-field borne down by arms,
5.1.282: But in his tents, within the rampart lines,
5.1.283: The hoped-for prize of this unholy war
5.1.284: Seemed for a moment gone. That faithful host,
5.1.285: His comrades trusted in a hundred fields,
5.1.286: Almost forsook him. The sad trump perchance
5.1.287: Mute for a moment, and the blade in sheath
5.1.288: Grown cold, had tamed their frenzy for the war;
5.1.289: Or else in hope of greater gifts, their cause
5.1.290: And leader they betrayed, and sold the sword
5.1.291: Still soiled with murder. By no other risk
5.1.292: Caesar more surely learned how as he looked
5.1.293: O'er all things else, the height on which he stood
5.1.294: Trembled beneath him. But a moment since
5.1.295: His high behest drew nations to the war;
5.1.296: Now, maimed of all who smote, no weapon left
5.1.297: Saving his own, he knows that swords unsheathed
5.1.298: Are wielded by the soldier, not the chief.
5.1.299: No timorous voice was there; no silent wrath
5.1.300: Concealed; nor doubting mind, as though alone
5.1.301: Indignant at the wrong, and in distrust
5.1.302: Of those in turn distrusting. Fear in each
5.1.303: Had fled before the boldness of the host:
5.1.304: The crime is free where thousands bear the guilt.
5.1.305: They hurled their menace: 'Caesar, give us leave
5.1.306: 'To quit thy crimes; thou seek'st by land and sea
5.1.307: 'The sword to slay us; let the fields of Gaul
5.1.308: And far Iberia, and the world proclaim
5.1.309: 'How for thy victories our comrades fell.
5.1.310: 'What boots it us that by an army's blood
5.1.311: 'The Rhine and Rhone and all the northern lands
5.1.312: 'Thou hast subdued? Thou giv'st us civil war
5.1.313: 'For all these battles; such the prize. When fled
5.1.314: 'The Senate trembling, and when Rome was ours
5.1.315: 'What homes or temples did we spoil? Our hands
5.1.316: 'Reek with offence! Aye, but our poverty
5.1.317: 'Proclaims our innocence! What end shall be
5.1.318: Of arms and armies? What shall be enough
5.1.319: 'If Rome suffice not? and what lies beyond?
5.1.320: 'Behold these silvered locks, these nerveless hands
5.1.321: 'And shrunken arms, once stalwart! In thy wars
5.1.322: 'Gone is the strength of life, gone all its pride!
5.1.323: 'Dismiss thine aged soldiers to their deaths.
5.1.324: 'How shameless is our prayer! Not on hard turf
5.1.325: 'To stretch our dying limbs; nor seek in vain,
5.1.326: ' When parts the soul, a hand to close our eyes;
5.1.327: 'Not with the helm to strike the stony ground:
5.1.328: ' Rather to feel the dear one's last embrace,
5.1.329: ' And gain a humble but a separate tomb.
5.1.330: 'Let sickness end old age. If Caesar's slaves,
5.1.331: ' Let something more than battle be our doom.
5.1.332: ' Deem'st thou we are thy dupes? that we alone
5.1.333: ' In civil war are ignorant what crime
5.1.334: ' Will fetch the highest price? What thou canst dare
5.1.335: ' These years have proved, or nothing; law divine
5.1.336: ' Nor human ordinance shall hold thine hand.
5.1.337: 'He was our leader on the banks of Rhine;
5.1.338: ' Now is our equal; for the stain of crime
5.1.339: ' Makes all men like. And for a judge ingrate
5.1.340: ' We waste our valour; for as fortune's gift
5.1.341: ' He takes the victory which our arms have won:
5.1.342: 'But we his fortunes are, his fates are ours
5.1.343: 'To fashion as we will. Boast that the gods
5.1.344: ' Shall do thy bidding! Nay, thy soldiers' will
5.1.345: ' Shall close the war.' With threatening mien and speech
5.1.346: Thus through the camp the troops demand their chief.
5.1.347: When faith and loyalty are fled, and hope
5.1.348: For aught but evil, thus may civil war
5.1.349: In mutiny and discord find its end!
5.1.350: What general had not feared at such revolt?
5.1.351: But mighty Caesar trusting on the throw,
5.1.352: As was his wont, his fortune, and o'erjoyed
5.1.353: To front their anger raging at its height
5.1.354: Unflinching comes. No temples of the gods,
5.1.355: Not Jove's high fane on the Tarpeian rock,
5.1.356: Not Rome's high dames nor maidens had he grudged
5.1.357: To their most savage lust: that they should ask
5.1.358: The worst, his wish, and love the spoils of war.
5.1.359: Nor feared he aught save order at the hands
5.1.360: Of that unconquered host. Art thou not shamed
5.1.361: That strife should please thee only, now condemned
5.1.362: Even by thy minions? Shall they shrink from blood,
5.1.363: They from the sword recoil? and thou rush on
5.1.364: Heedless of guilt, through right and through unright,
5.1.365: Nor learn that men may lay their arms aside
5.1.366: Yet bear to live? This civil butchery
5.1.367: Escapes thy grasp. Stay thou thy crimes at length;
5.1.368: Nor force thy will on those who will no more.
5.1.369: Upon a turfy mound unmoved he stood
5.1.370: And, since he feared not, worthy to be feared;
5.1.371: And thus while anger stirred his soul began:
5.1.372: ' Thou that with voice and hand didst rage but now
5.1.373: ' Against thine absent chief, behold me here;
5.1.374: Plunge in this breast, all ready for the wound
5.1.375: And bare, thy sword; and end the war and flee.
5.1.376: This mutiny devoid of daring deed
5.1.377: Betrays your coward souls, betrays the youth
5.1.378: ' Who tires of victories which gild the arms
5.1.379: Of an unconquered chief, and yearns for flight.
5.1.380: Leave me to fate; with that I'll wage the war
5.1.381: You I cast forth. For every weapon left,
5.1.382: Fortune shall find a man, to wield it well.
5.1.383: Shall Magnus in his flight with such a fleet
5.1.384: Draw nations in his train; and not to me
5.1.385: ' My victories bring legions? They shall reap
5.1.386: ' For its mere close the prizes of the war
5.1.387: ' Won by your toil, and scatheless join the train
5.1.388: 'That leads my chariot to the sacred hill:
5.1.389: ' While you, despised in age and battle worn,
5.1.390: ' Gaze on our triumph from the civic crowd.
5.1.391: ' Think you your dastard flight shall give me pause?
5.1.392: ' If all the rivers that now seek the sea
5.1.393: ' Were to withdraw their waters, it would fail
5.1.394: ' By not one inch, no more than by their flow
5.1.395: 'It rises now. Have then your efforts given
5.1.396: ' Strength to my cause? Not so: the heavenly gods
5.1.397: ' Stoop not so low; fate has no time to judge
5.1.398: ' Your lives and deaths. The fortunes of the world
5.1.399: ' Follow heroic souls: for the fit few
5.1.400: 'The many live; and you who terrified
5.1.401: ' With me the northern and Iberian worlds,
5.1.402: ' Would flee when led by Magnus. Strong with me
5.1.404: ' A homeless exile with his chief preferred.
5.1.405: ' Nor were your faith more firm if, neither side
5.1.406: 'Espoused, you ceased from arms. Who leaves me once,
5.1.407: 'Though not to fight against me with the foe,
5.1.408: 'Joins not my ranks again. Surely the gods
5.1.409: 'Smile on these arms who for so great a war
5.1.410: 'Grant me fresh soldiers. From what heavy load
5.1.411: 'Fortune relieves me! for the hands which aimed
5.1.412: 'At all, to which the world did not suffice,
5.1.413: 'I now disarm, and for myself alone
5.1.414: 'Reserve the conflict. Quit ye, then, my camp,
5.1.415: 'And leave my standards to the grasp of men,
5.1.417: 'I keep, not as their captain, but their judge.
5.1.418: 'Lie, traitors, prone on earth, stretch out the neck
5.1.419: 'And take th' avenging blow. And thou whose strength
5.1.420: 'Shall now support me, young and yet untaught,
5.1.421: 'Behold the doom and learn to strike and die.'
5.1.422: Such were his words of ire, and all the host
5.1.423: Drew back and trembled at the voice of him
5.1.424: They would depose, as though their very swords
5.1.425: Would from their scabbards leap at his command
5.1.426: Themselves unwilling; but he only feared
5.1.427: Lest hand and blade to satisfy the doom
5.1.428: Might be denied; till they submitting pledged
5.1.429: Their lives and swords alike, beyond his hope.
5.1.430: To strike and suffer holds in surest thrall
5.1.431: The heart inured to guilt; and Caesar kept,
5.1.432: By dreadful compact ratified in blood,
5.1.433: Those whom he feared to lose.
5.1.435: In ten days' march Brundusium, and recall
5.1.436: From old Tarentum and from Hydrus lone
5.1.437: His navy, and from Leucas' point remote,
5.1.438: And the Salapian marsh where Sipus lies
5.1.439: By rich Garganus, jutting from the shore
5.1.440: In huge escarpment that divides the waves
5.1.441: Of Hadria; on each hand, his seaward slopes
5.1.442: Buffeted by the winds; or Auster borne
5.1.443: From sweet Apulia, or the sterner blast
5.1.444: Of Boreas rushing from Dalmatian strands.
5.1.445: But Caesar entered safe without a guard
5.1.446: Rome, trembling, taught to serve the garb of peace,
5.1.447: Dictator named, to grant their prayers, forsooth:
5.1.448: Consul, in honour of the roll of Rome.
5.1.449: Then first of all the names by which we now
5.1.450: Lie to our masters, men found out the use:
5.1.451: For to preserve his right to wield the sword
5.1.452: He mixed the civil axes with his brands;
5.1.453: With eagles, fasces; with an empty word
5.1.454: Clothing his power; and stamped upon the time
5.1.455: A worthy designation; for what name
5.1.456: Could better mark the dread Pharsalian year
5.1.457: Than 'Caesar, Consul'? Now the famous field
5.1.459: The tribes in order and divides the votes
5.1.460: In vain solemnity of empty urns.
5.1.461: Nor did they heed the portents of the sky:
5.1.462: Deaf were the augurs to the thunder roll;
5.1.463: The owl flew on the left; yet were the birds
5.1.464: Propitious sworn. Then was the ancient name
5.1.465: Degraded first; and monthly Consuls, now
5.1.466: Shorn of their rank, were chosen to mark the years.
5.1.467: And Trojan Alba's god (since Latium's fall
5.1.468: Deserving not) beheld the wonted fires
5.1.469: Blaze from his altars on the festal night.
5.1.470: Then through Apulia's fallows, which her hinds
5.1.471: Left all untilled, to sluggish weeds a prey
5.1.472: Passed Caesar onward, swifter than the fire
5.1.473: Of heaven, or tigress dam: until he reached
5.1.474: Brundusium's winding ramparts, built of old
5.1.475: By Cretan colonists. There icy winds
5.1.476: Constrained the billows, and his trembling fleet
5.1.477: Feared for the winter storms nor dared the main.
5.1.478: But Caesar's soul burned at the moments lost
5.1.479: For speedy battle, nor could brook delay
5.1.480: Within the port, indignant that the sea
5.1.481: Should give safe passage to his routed foe:
5.1.482: And thus he stirred his troops, in seas unskilled,
5.1.483: With words of courage: 'When the winter wind
5.1.484: 'Has seized on sky and ocean, firm its hold;
5.1.485: But the inconstancy of cloudy spring
5.1.487: 'Upon the billows. Straight shall be our course.
5.1.488: 'No winding nooks of coast, but open seas
5.1.489: Struck by the northern wind alone we plough,
5.1.490: 'And may he bend the spars, and bear us swift
5.1.492: 'From coasts Phaeacian, with their swifter oars
5.1.493: May catch our flagging sails. Cast loose the ropes
5.1.494: 'From our victorious prows. Too long we waste
5.1.495: 'Tempests that blow to bear us to our goal.'
5.1.496: Now sank the sun to rest; the evening star
5.1.497: Shone on the darkening heaven, and the moon
5.1.498: Reigned with her paler light, when all the fleet
5.1.499: Freed from retaining cables seized the main.
5.1.500: With slackened sheet the canvas wooed the breeze,
5.1.501: Which rose and fell and fitful died away,
5.1.502: Till motionless the sails, and all the waves
5.1.503: Were still as deepest pool, where never wind
5.1.504: Ripples the surface. Thus in Scythian climes
5.1.506: Bound fast in frosty fetters; Ister's streams
5.1.507: No more impel the main, and ships constrained
5.1.508: Stand fast in ice; and while in depths below
5.1.509: The waves still murmur, loud the charger's hoof
5.1.510: Sounds on the surface, and the travelling wheel
5.1.511: Furrows a track upon the frozen marsh.
5.1.512: Cruel as tempest was the calm that lay
5.1.513: In stagnant pools upon the mournful deep:
5.1.514: Against the course of nature lay outstretched
5.1.515: A rigid ocean: 'twas as if the sea
5.1.516: Forgat its ancient ways and knew no more
5.1.517: The ceaseless tides, nor any breeze of heaven,
5.1.518: Nor quivered at the image of the sun,
5.1.519: Mirrored upon its wave. For while the fleet
5.1.520: Hung in mid passage motionless, the foe
5.1.521: Might hurry to attack, with sturdy stroke
5.1.522: Churning the deep; or famine's deadly grip
5.1.523: Might seize the ships becalmed. For dangers new
5.1.524: New vows they found: for tempests was their prayer,
5.1.525: To rouse the billows till the watery plain
5.1.526: Freed from its torpor should be sea once more.
5.1.527: But cloudless was the sky and calm the deep,
5.1.528: All hope of shipwreck gone, till night was fled,
5.1.529: And marred by gathering mist the day arose
5.1.530: And stirred the depths, and moved the fleet along
5.1.531: Towards the Ceraunian headland; and the waves
5.1.532: And favouring breezes followed on the ships,
5.1.533: Now speeding faster, till (their goal attained)
5.1.534: They cast their anchors on Palaeste's shore.
5.1.535: This land first saw the chiefs in neighbouring camps
5.1.536: Confronted, which the streams of Apsus bound
5.1.537: And swifter Genusus; a lengthy course
5.1.538: Is run by neither, but on Apsus' waves
5.1.539: Scarce flowing from a marsh, the frequent boat
5.1.540: Finds room to swim; while on the foamy bed
5.1.541: Of Genusus by sun or shower compelled
5.1.542: The melted snows pour seawards. Here were met
5.1.543: (So Fortune ordered it) the mighty pair;
5.1.544: And in its woes the world yet vainly hoped
5.1.545: That, brought to nearer touch, their crime itself
5.1.546: Might breed abhorrence: for from either camp
5.1.547: Voices were clearly heard and features seen.
5.1.548: Nor e'er, Pompeius, since that distant day
5.1.549: When Caesar's daughter and thy spouse was reft
5.1.550: By pitiless fate away, nor left a pledge,
5.1.551: Did thy loved kinsman (save on sands of Nile)
5.1.552: So nearly look upon thy face again.
5.1.553: But Caesar's mind though frenzied for the fight
5.1.554: Was forced to pause until Antonius brought
5.1.555: The rearward troops; Antonius even now
5.1.556: Rehearsing Leucas' fight. With prayers and threats
5.1.557: Caesar exhorts him. ' Why delay the fates,
5.1.558: Thou cause of evil to the suffering world?
5.1.559: My speed hath won the major part: from thee
5.1.560: Fortune demands the final stroke alone.
5.1.561: Do Libyan whirlpools with deceitful tides
5.1.562: Uncertain separate us? Is the deep
5.1.563: Untried to which I call? To unknown risks
5.1.564: Art thou commanded? Caesar bids thee come,
5.1.565: Thou sluggard, not to leave him. Long ago
5.1.566: I ran my ships midway through sands and shoals
5.1.567: To harbours held by foes; and dost thou fear
5.1.568: My friendly camp? I mourn the waste of days
5.1.569: 'Which fate allotted us. Upon the waves
5.1.570: And winds I call unceasing: hold not back
5.1.571: Thy willing troops, but let them dare the sea;
5.1.572: Here gladly shall they come to join my camp,
5.1.573: Though risking shipwreck: with indignant voice
5.1.574: I call upon thee. Not in equal shares
5.1.575: 'The world has fallen between us: thou alone
5.1.576: Dost hold Italia, but Epirus I
5.1.577: And all the lords of Rome.' Twice called and thrice
5.1.578: Antonius lingered still: but Caesar's mind
5.1.579: Was that he failed the gods, not they his cause.
5.1.580: By night he braved the strait which others feared
5.1.581: Though bidden: for he knew that daring deeds
5.1.582: Are safely wrought beneath the smile of heaven:
5.1.583: And thus he hoped in fragile boat to cross
5.1.584: The stormy billows fearful to a fleet.
5.1.585: Now gentle night had brought repose from arms;
5.1.586: And sleep, blest guardian of the poor man's couch,
5.1.587: Restored the weary; and the camp was still.
5.1.588: The hour was come that called the second watch
5.1.589: When mighty Caesar, in the silence vast
5.1.590: With cautious tread advanced to such a deed
5.1.591: As slaves should dare not. Fortune for his guide,
5.1.592: Alone he passes on, and o'er the guard
5.1.593: Stretched in repose he leaps, in secret wrath
5.1.594: At such a sleep. Pacing the winding beach,
5.1.595: Fast to a sea-worn rock he finds a boat
5.1.596: On ocean's marge afloat. Hard by on shore
5.1.597: Its master dwelt within his humble home.
5.1.598: No solid front it reared, for sterile rush
5.1.599: And marshy reed enwoven formed the walls,
5.1.600: Propped by a shallop with its bending sides
5.1.601: Turned upwards. Caesar's hand upon the door
5.1.602: Knocks twice and thrice until the fabric shakes.
5.1.603: Amyclas from his couch of soft seaweed
5.1.604: Arising, calls: ' What shipwrecked sailor seeks
5.1.605: 'My humble home? Who hopes for aid from me,
5.1.606: ' By fates adverse compelled? ' He stirs the heap
5.1.607: Upon the hearth, until a tiny spark
5.1.608: Glows in the darkness, and throws wide the door.
5.1.609: Careless of war, he knew that civil strife
5.1.610: Stoops not to cottages. O! happy life
5.1.611: That poverty affords! great gift of heaven
5.1.612: Too little understood! what mansion wall,
5.1.613: What temple of the gods, would feel no fear
5.1.614: When Caesar called for entrance? Then the chief:
5.1.615: ' Enlarge thine hopes and look for better things.
5.1.616: ' Do but my bidding, and on yonder shore
5.1.617: ' Place me, and thou shalt cease from one poor boat
5.1.618: ' To earn thy living; and in years to come
5.1.619: ' Look for a rich old age: and trust thy fates
5.1.620: ' To those high gods whose wont it is to bless
5.1.621: ' The poor with sudden plenty.' So he spake
5.1.622: E'en at such time in accents of command,
5.1.623: For how could Caesar else? Amyclas said,
5.1.624: ''Twere dangerous to brave the deep to-night.
5.1.625: ' The sun descended not in ruddy clouds
5.1.626: ' Or peaceful rays to rest; part of his beams
5.1.627: ' Presaged a southern gale, the rest proclaimed
5.1.628: ' A northern tempest; and his middle orb,
5.1.629: ' Shorn of its strength, permitted human eyes
5.1.630: ' To gaze upon his grandeur; and the moon
5.1.631: ' Rose not with silver horns upon the night
5.1.632: ' Nor pure in middle space; her slender points
5.1.633: 'Not drawn aright, but blushing with the track
5.1.634: ' Of raging tempests, till her lurid light
5.1.635: 'Was sadly veiled within the clouds. Again
5.1.636: ' The forest sounds; the surf upon the shore;
5.1.637: ' The dolphin's mood, uncertain where to play;
5.1.638: ' The sea-mew on the land; the heron used
5.1.639: ' To wade among the shallows, borne aloft
5.1.640: ' And soaring on his wings-all these alarm;
5.1.641: ' The raven, too, who plunged his head in spray,
5.1.642: ' As if to anticipate the coming rain,
5.1.643: And trod the margin with unsteady gait.
5.1.644: But if the cause demands, behold me thine.
5.1.645: 'Either we reach the bidden shore, or else
5.1.646: 'Storm and the deep forbid-we can no more.'
5.1.647: Thus said he loosed the boat and raised the sail.
5.1.648: No sooner done than stars were seen to fall
5.1.649: In flaming furrows from the sky: nay, more;
5.1.650: The pole star trembled in its place on high:
5.1.651: Black horror marked the surging of the sea;
5.1.652: The main was boiling in long tracts of foam,
5.1.653: Uncertain of the wind, yet seized with storm.
5.1.654: Then spake the captain of the trembling bark:
5.1.655: See what remorseless ocean has in store!
5.1.656: Whether from east or west the storm may come
5.1.657: Is still uncertain, for as yet confused
5.1.658: 'The billows tumble. Judged by clouds and sky
5.1.659: 'A western tempest: by the murmuring deep
5.1.660: 'A wild south-eastern gale shall sweep the sea.
5.1.661: 'Nor bark nor man shall reach Hesperia's shore
5.1.662: In this wild rage of waters. To return
5.1.663: 'Back on our course forbidden by the gods,
5.1.664: 'Is our one refuge, and with labouring boat
5.1.665: 'To reach the shore ere yet the nearest land
5.1.668: Was in himself, to make all dangers yield.
5.1.669: And thus he answered: ' Scorn the threatening sea,
5.1.670: Spread out thy canvas to the raging wind;
5.1.671: If for thy pilot thou refusest heaven,
5.1.672: 'Me in its stead receive. Alone in thee
5.1.673: One cause of terror just-thou dost not know
5.1.674: 'Thy comrade, ne'er deserted by the gods,
5.1.675: 'Whom fortune blesses e'en without a prayer.
5.1.676: 'Break through the middle storm and trust in me.
5.1.677: 'The burden of this fight falls not on us
5.1.678: But on the sky and ocean; and our bark
5.1.679: Shall swim the billows safe in him it bears.
5.1.680: Nor shall the wind rage long: the boat itself
5.1.681: Shall calm the waters. Flee the nearest shore,
5.1.682: Steer for the ocean with unswerving hand:
5.1.683: Then in the deep, when to our ship and us
5.1.684: No other port is given, believe thou hast
5.1.685: 'Calabria's harbours. And dost thou not know
5.1.686: 'The purpose of such havoc? Fortune seeks
5.1.687: 'In all this tumult of the sea and sky
5.1.690: Swooped on the boat and tore away the sheet:
5.1.691: The fluttering sail fell on the fragile mast:
5.1.692: And groaned the joints. From all the universe
5.1.693: Commingled perils rushed. In Atlas' seas
5.1.694: First Corus raised his head, and stirred the depths
5.1.695: To fury, and had forced upon the rocks
5.1.696: Whole seas and oceans; but the chilly north
5.1.697: Drove back the deep that doubted which was lord.
5.1.698: But Scythian Aquilo prevailed, whose blast
5.1.699: Tossed up the main and showed as shallow pools
5.1.700: Each deep abyss; and yet was not the sea
5.1.701: Heaped on the crags, for Corus' billows met
5.1.702: The waves of Boreas: such seas had clashed
5.1.703: Even were the winds withdrawn; Eurus enraged
5.1.704: Burst from the cave, and Notus black with rain,
5.1.705: And all the winds from every part of heaven
5.1.706: Strove for their own; and thus the ocean stayed
5.1.707: Within his boundaries. No petty seas
5.1.708: Rapt in the storm are whirled. The Tuscan deep
5.1.709: Invades th' AEgean; in Ionian gulfs
5.1.710: Sounds wandering Hadria. How long the crags
5.1.711: Which that day fell, the Ocean's blows had braved!
5.1.712: What lofty peaks did vanquished earth resign!
5.1.713: And yet on yonder coast such mighty waves
5.1.714: Took not their rise; from distant regions came
5.1.715: Those monster billows, driven on their course
5.1.716: By that great current which surrounds the world.
5.1.717: Thus did the King of Heaven, when length of years
5.1.718: Wore out the forces of his thunder, call
5.1.719: His brother's trident to his help, what time
5.1.720: The earth and sea one second kingdom formed
5.1.721: And ocean knew no limit but the sky.
5.1.722: Now, too, the sea had risen to the stars
5.1.723: In mighty mass, had not Olympus' chief
5.1.724: Pressed down its waves with clouds: that night from heaven
5.1.725: Came not, as others; but the murky air
5.1.726: Was dim with pallor of the realms below;
5.1.727: The sky lay on the deep; within the clouds
5.1.728: The waves received the rain: the lightning flash
5.1.729: Clove through the parted air a path obscured
5.1.730: By mist and darkness: and the heavenly vaults
5.1.731: Re-echoed to the tumult, and the frame
5.1.732: That holds the sky was shaken. Nature feared
5.1.733: Chaos returned, as though the elements
5.1.734: Had burst their bonds, and night had come to mix
5.1.737: Not to have perished was their only hope.
5.1.738: Far as from Leucas point the placid main
5.1.739: Spreads to the horizon, from the billow's crest
5.1.740: They viewed the dashing of th' infuriate sea;
5.1.741: Thence sinking to the middle trough, their mast
5.1.742: Scarce topped the watery height on either hand,
5.1.743: Their sails in clouds, their keel upon the ground.
5.1.744: For all the sea was piled into the waves,
5.1.745: And drawn from depths between laid bare the sand.
5.1.746: The master of the boat forgot his art,
5.1.747: For fear o'ercame; he knew not where to yield
5.1.748: Or where to meet the wave: but safety came
5.1.749: From ocean's self at war: one billow forced
5.1.750: The vessel under, but a huger wave
5.1.751: Repelled it upwards, and she rode the storm
5.1.752: Through every blast triumphant. Not the shore
5.1.753: Of humble Sason, nor Thessalia's coast
5.1.755: Dismayed the mariners, but the giddy tops
5.1.758: Thinking the peril worthy of his fates:
5.1.759: Are such the labours of the gods? ' exclaimed,
5.1.760: Bent on my downfall have they sought me thus,
5.1.761: Here in this puny skiff in such a sea?
5.1.762: If to the deep the glory of my fall
5.1.763: Is due, and not to war, intrepid still
5.1.764: Whatever death they send shall strike me down.
5.1.765: Let fate cut short the deeds that I would do
5.1.766: And hasten on the end: the past is mine.
5.1.767: The northern nations fell beneath my sword;
5.1.768: 'My dreaded name compels the foe to flee.
5.1.769: 'Pompeius yields me place; the people's voice
5.1.770: Gave at my order what the wars denied.
5.1.771: And all the titles which denote the powers
5.1.772: Known to the Roman state my name shall bear.
5.1.773: Let none know this but thou who hear'st my prayers,
5.1.774: Fortune! that Caesar summoned to the shades,
5.1.775: Dictator, Consul, full of honours, died
5.1.776: Ere his last prize was won. I ask no pyre
5.1.777: Or tomb, ye gods! wherein my dust may rest:
5.1.778: Nay! plunge in middle deep this battered frame!
5.1.779: All earth shall look for me, nor shall men cease
5.1.780: At Caesar's name to fear.' Such words he spake,
5.1.781: When lo! a tenth gigantic billow raised
5.1.782: The feeble keel, and where between the rocks
5.1.783: A cleft gave safety, placed it on the shore.
5.1.784: Thus in a moment fortune, kingdoms, lands,
5.1.787: When daylight came, he entered not the camp
5.1.788: Silent as when he parted; for his friends
5.1.789: Soon pressed around him, and with weeping eyes
5.1.790: In accents welcome to his ears began:
5.1.791: 'Whither in reckless daring hast thou gone,
5.1.792: Unpitying Caesar? Were these humble lives
5.1.793: Left here unguarded while thy limbs were given,
5.1.794: Unsought for, to be scattered by the storm?
5.1.795: 'When on thy breath so many nations hang
5.1.796: For life and safety, and so great a world
5.1.797: Calls thee its master, to have courted death
5.1.798: Proves want of heart. Were none of all thy friends
5.1.799: Deserving held to join their fate with thine?
5.1.800: 'When thou wast tossed upon the stormy main
5.1.801: We lay in slumber! Shame upon such sleep!
5.1.802: 'And why thyself didst seek Italia's shores?
5.1.803: '"Twere cruel (such thy thought) to speak the word
5.1.804: That bade another dare the furious sea.
5.1.805: All men must bear what chance or fate may bring,
5.1.806: The sudden peril and the stroke of death;
5.1.807: But shall the ruler of the world attempt
5.1.809: Why weary heaven? is it indeed enough
5.1.810: To crown the war, that Fortune and the deep
5.1.811: 'Have cast thee on our shores? And wouldst thou use
5.1.812: 'The grace of favouring deities, to gain
5.1.813: Not lordship, not the empire of the world,
5.1.814: 'But lucky shipwreck! ' Night dispersed, and soon
5.1.815: The sun beamed on them, and the wearied deep,
5.1.816: The winds permitting, lulled its waves to rest.
5.1.817: And when Antonius saw a breeze arise
5.1.818: Fresh from a cloudless heaven, to break the sea,
5.1.819: He loosed his ships which, by the pilots' hands
5.1.820: And by the wind in equal order held,
5.1.821: Swept as a marching host across the main.
5.1.822: But night unfriendly from the seamen snatched
5.1.823: All governance of sail, parting the ships
5.1.824: In divers paths asunder. Like as cranes
5.1.825: Deserting frozen Strymon for the streams
5.1.826: Of Nile, when winter falls, in casual lines
5.1.827: Of wedge-like figures first ascend the sky;
5.1.828: But when in loftier heaven the southern breeze
5.1.829: Strikes on their pinions tense, in loose array
5.1.830: Dispersed at large, in flight irregular,
5.1.831: They wing their journey onwards. Stronger winds
5.1.832: With day returning blew the navy on,
5.1.833: Past Lissus' shelter which they vainly sought,
5.1.834: Till bare to northern blasts, Nymphaeum's port,
5.1.835: But safe in southern, gave the fleet repose.
5.1.836: When Caesar's troops were gathered in their strength
5.1.837: And Magnus saw the battle day was near
5.1.838: Before his camp, Cornelia he resolved
5.1.839: To send to Lesbos' shore, from rage of fight
5.1.840: Safe and apart: so lifting from his soul
5.1.841: The weight that burdened it. Thus, lawful Love,
5.1.842: Thus art thou tyrant o'er the mightiest mind!
5.1.843: His spouse was the one cause why Magnus stayed
5.1.844: Nor met his fortunes, though he staked the world
5.1.845: And all the destinies of Rome. The word
5.1.846: He speaks not though resolved; so sweet it seemed,
5.1.847: When on the future pondering, to gain
5.1.848: A pause from Fate! But at the close of night,
5.1.849: When drowsy sleep had fled, Cornelia sought
5.1.850: To soothe the anxious bosom of her lord
5.1.851: And win his kisses; when amazed she saw
5.1.852: His cheek was tearful, and with boding soul
5.1.853: Shrank from the hidden wound, nor dared surprise
5.1.854: Magnus in tears. But sighing thus he spake:
5.1.855: ' Dearer to me than life itself, when life
5.1.856: 'Is happy (not at moments such as these);
5.1.857: 'The day of sorrow comes, too long delayed,
5.1.858: 'Nor long enough! With Caesar at our gates
5.1.859: ' With all his forces, a secure retreat
5.1.860: 'Shall Lesbos give thee. Try me not with prayers.
5.1.861: 'This fatal boon I have denied myself.
5.1.862: 'Thou wilt not long be absent from thy spouse.
5.1.864: With speediest ruin. 'Tis enough for thee
5.1.865: ' To hear of Magnus' peril; and thy love
5.1.866: 'Deceives thee with the thought that thou canst gaze
5.1.867: 'Unmoved on civil strife. It shames my soul
5.1.868: 'On the eve of war to slumber at thy side,
5.1.869: 'And rise from thy dear breast when trumpets call
5.1.870: 'A woeful world to misery and arms.
5.1.871: 'I dread lest Magnus in this war endure
5.1.872: 'Nor loss nor sorrow. But do thou lie hid
5.1.873: 'Safer than kings or peoples, far removed;
5.1.874: 'That so the grievous fortunes of thy lord
5.1.875: ' May lighter fall on thee. If unkind heaven
5.1.876: ' Our armies rout, still let my choicest part
5.1.877: ' Survive in thee; if fated is my flight,
5.1.878: ' Still leave me that whereto I fain would flee.'
5.1.879: Hardly at first her senses grasped the words
5.1.880: In their full misery; then her mind amazed
5.1.881: Could scarce find utterance for the grief that pressed.
5.1.882: Nought, Magnus, now is left wherewith to upbraid
5.1.883: 'The gods and fates of marriage; 'tis not death
5.1.884: 'That parts our love, nor yet the funeral pyre,
5.1.885: Nor that dread torch which marks the end of all.
5.1.886: I share the ignoble lot of vulgar lives:
5.1.887: 'My spouse rejects me. Yes, the foe is come!
5.1.888: 'Break we our bonds and Julia's sire appease! -
5.1.889: Is this thy consort, Magnus, this thy faith
5.1.890: 'In her fond loving heart? Can danger fright
5.1.891: 'Her and not thee? Long since our mutual fates
5.1.892: 'Hang by one chain; and dost thou bid me now
5.1.894: Without thee? Is it well that I should die
5.1.895: 'Even while you pray for fortune? And suppose
5.1.896: ' I flee from evil and with death self-sought
5.1.897: ' Follow thy footsteps to the realms below—
5.1.898: ' Am I to live till to that distant isle
5.1.899: ' Some tardy rumour of thy fall may come?
5.1.900: ' And then thou say'st, unfeeling! that by use
5.1.901: ' Strength shall be mine to bear such load of ills
5.1.902: ' As fate reserves for us: but at such a strength
5.1.903: ' My spirit trembles. Ah! forgive the truth.
5.1.904: ' And if the favouring gods shall hear my prayers,
5.1.905: ' I shall be last to hear the victory
5.1.906: ' In that lone isle of rocks. When all are glad,
5.1.907: ' My heart shall throb with anguish, and the sail
5.1.908: ' Which brings the message I shall see with fear,
5.1.909: ' Not safe e'en then: for Caesar in his flight
5.1.910: ' Might seize me there, abandoned and alone
5.1.911: To be his hostage. If thou place me there,
5.1.912: The spouse of Magnus, shall not all the world
5.1.914: This my last prayer: if all is lost but flight,
5.1.915: 'And thou shalt seek the ocean, to my shores
5.1.916: 'Turn not thy keel, ill-fated one: for there,
5.1.917: 'There will they seek thee.' Thus she spoke distraught,
5.1.918: Leaped from the couch and rushed upon her fate;
5.1.919: No stop nor stay: she clung not to his neck
5.1.920: Nor threw her arms about him; both forego

5.1.929: And grasped the sands, embracing, till at last
5.1.930: Her maidens placed her senseless in the ship.
5.1.931: Not in such grief she left her country's shores

5.1.936: Its cold, its solitude. When slumber found
5.1.937: Her eyelids, and forgetfulness her soul,
5.1.938: Seeking with outstretched arms the form beloved,
5.1.939: She grasps but air. Though tossed by restless love,
5.1.940: She leaves a place beside her as for him
5.1.941: Returning. Yet she feared Pompeius lost
