6.1.1: Now that the chiefs with minds intent on fight
6.1.2: Had drawn their armies near upon the hills
6.1.3: And all the gods beheld their chosen pair,
6.1.4: Caesar, the Grecian towns despising, scorned
6.1.5: To reap the glory of successful war
6.1.6: Save at his kinsman's cost. In all his prayers
6.1.7: He seeks that moment, fatal to the world,
6.1.8: When shall be cast the die, to win or lose,
6.1.9: And all their fortunes hang upon the throw.
6.1.10: Thrice he drew out his troops, his eagles thrice,
6.1.11: Demanding battle; to the ruin of Rome
6.1.12: Thus prompt as ever: but his kinsman foe,
6.1.13: Proof against every art, refused to leave
6.1.14: The rampart of his camp. Then marching swift
6.1.15: By hidden path between the wooded fields
6.1.16: He seeks, and hopes to seize, Dyrrhachium's fort;
6.1.17: But Magnus, swifter speeding by the sea,
6.1.18: First camped on Petra's slopes, a rocky hill
6.1.19: Thus by the natives named. From thence he keeps
6.1.20: Watch o'er the fortress of Corinthian birth
6.1.21: Which by its towers alone without a guard
6.1.22: Was safe against a siege. No hand of man
6.1.23: In ancient days built up her lofty wall,
6.1.24: No hammer rang upon her massive stones:
6.1.25: Not all the works of war, nor Time himself
6.1.26: Shall undermine her. Nature's hand has raised
6.1.27: Her adamantine rocks and hedged her in
6.1.28: With bulwarks girded by the foamy main:
6.1.29: And but for one short bridge of narrow earth
6.1.30: Dyrrhachium were an island. Steep and fierce,
6.1.31: Dreaded of sailors, are the cliffs that bear
6.1.32: Her walls; and tempests, howling from the south,
6.1.33: Toss up the foaming main upon the roofs;
6.1.34: And homes and temples tremble at the shock.
6.1.35: Thirsting for battle and with hopes inflamed
6.1.36: Here Caesar hastes, with distant rampart lines
6.1.37: Seeking unseen to coop his foe within,
6.1.38: Though spread in spacious camp upon the hills.
6.1.39: With eagle eye he measures out the land
6.1.40: Meet to be compassed, nor content with turf
6.1.41: Fit for a hasty mound, he bids his troops
6.1.42: Tear from the quarries many a giant rock:
6.1.43: And spoils the dwellings of the Greeks, and drags
6.1.44: Their walls asunder for his own. Thus rose
6.1.45: A mighty barrier which no ram could burst
6.1.46: Nor any ponderous machine of war.
6.1.47: Mountains are cleft, and level through the hills
6.1.48: The work of Caesar strides: wide yawns the moat,
6.1.49: Forts show their towers rising on the heights,
6.1.50: And in vast circle forests are enclosed
6.1.51: And groves and spacious lands, and beasts of prey,
6.1.52: As in a line of toils. Pompeius lacked
6.1.53: Nor field nor forage in th' encircled span
6.1.54: Nor room to move his camp; nay, rivers rose
6.1.55: Within, and ran their course and reached the sea;
6.1.56: And Caesar wearied ere he saw the whole,
6.1.57: And daylight failed him. Let the ancient tale
6.1.58: Attribute to the labours of the gods
6.1.59: The walls of Ilium: let the fragile bricks
6.1.60: Which compass in great Babylon, amaze
6.1.61: The fleeting Parthian. Here a larger space
6.1.62: Than those great cities which Orontes swift
6.1.63: And Tigris' stream enclose, or that which boasts
6.1.64: In Eastern climes, the lordly palaces
6.1.65: Fit for Assyria's kings, is closed by walls
6.1.66: Amid the haste and tumult of a war
6.1.67: Forced to completion. Yet this labour huge
6.1.68: Was spent in vain. So many hands had joined
6.1.69: Or Sestos with Abydos, or had tamed
6.1.70: With mighty mole the Hellespontine wave,
6.1.71: Or Corinth from the realm of Pelops king
6.1.72: Had rent asunder, or had spared each ship
6.1.73: Her voyage round the long Malean cape,
6.1.74: Or had done anything most hard, to mould
6.1.75: The world's created surface. Here the war
6.1.76: Was prisoned: blood predestinate to flow
6.1.77: In all the parts of earth; the host foredoomed
6.1.78: To fall in Libya or in Thessaly
6.1.79: Was here: in such small amphitheatre
6.1.80: The tide of civil passion rose and fell.
6.1.81: At first Pompeius knew not: so the hind
6.1.82: Who peaceful tills the mid-Sicilian fields
6.1.83: Hears not Pelorus sounding to the storm;
6.1.84: So billows thunder on Rutupian shores,
6.1.86: But when he saw the mighty barrier stretch
6.1.87: O'er hill and valley, and enclose the land,
6.1.88: He bade his columns leave their rocky hold
6.1.89: And seize on posts of vantage in the plain;
6.1.90: Thus forcing Caesar to extend his troops
6.1.91: On wider lines; and holding for his own
6.1.92: Such space encompassed as divides from Rome
6.1.93: Aricia, sacred to that goddess chaste
6.1.94: Of old Mycenae; or as Tiber holds
6.1.95: From Rome's high ramparts to the Tuscan sea,
6.1.96: Unless he deviate. No trumpet call
6.1.97: Commands an onset, and the darts that fly
6.1.98: Fly though forbidden; but the arm that flings
6.1.99: For proof the lance, at random, here and there
6.1.100: Deals impious slaughter. Weighty care compelled
6.1.101: Each leader to withhold his troops from fight;
6.1.102: For there the weary earth of produce failed
6.1.103: Pressed by Pompeius' steeds, whose horny hoofs
6.1.104: Rang in their gallop on the grassy fields
6.1.105: And killed the succulence. They strengthless lay
6.1.106: Upon the mown expanse, nor pile of straw,
6.1.107: Brought from full barns in place of living grass,
6.1.108: Relieved their craving; shook their panting flanks,
6.1.109: And as they wheeled Death struck his victim down.
6.1.110: Then foul contagion filled the murky air
6.1.111: Whose poisonous weight pressed on them in a cloud
6.1.112: Pestiferous; as in Nesis' isle the breath
6.1.113: Of Styx rolls upwards from the mist-clad rocks;
6.1.114: Or that fell vapour which the caves exhale
6.1.115: From Typhon raging in the depths below.
6.1.116: Then died the soldiers, for the streams they drank
6.1.117: Held yet more poison than the air: the skin
6.1.118: Was dark and rigid, and the fiery plague
6.1.119: Made hard their vitals, and with pitiless tooth
6.1.120: Gnawed at their wasted features, while their eyes
6.1.121: Started from out their sockets, and the head
6.1.122: Drooped from sheer weariness. So the disease
6.1.123: Grew swifter in its strides till scarce was room,
6.1.124: 'Twixt life and death, for sickness, and the pest
6.1.125: Slew as it struck its victim, and the dead
6.1.126: Thrust from the tents (such all their burial) lay
6.1.127: Blent with the living. Yet their camp was pitched
6.1.128: Hard by the breezy sea by which might come
6.1.129: All nations' harvests, and the northern wind
6.1.130: Not seldom rolled the murky air away.
6.1.131: Their foe, not vexed with pestilential air
6.1.132: Nor stagnant waters, ample range enjoyed
6.1.133: Upon the spacious uplands: yet as though
6.1.134: In leaguer, famine seized them for its prey.
6.1.135: Scarce were the crops half grown when Caesar saw
6.1.136: How prone they seized upon the food of beasts,
6.1.137: And stripped of leaves the bushes and the groves,
6.1.138: And dragged from roots unknown the doubtful herb,
6.1.139: Which might be death: all things they ate that fire
6.1.140: May soften, or teeth may bite, or arid throat
6.1.141: May swallow; things that never heretofore
6.1.142: Were placed on tables-thus the host at large-
6.1.143: Yet was there plenty with the leaguered foe.
6.1.144: When Magnus first was pleased to break his bonds,
6.1.145: No nightly dash he makes, by craft to seize
6.1.146: His sleeping foe unarmed: his soul had scorned
6.1.147: Such path obscure to victory. Twas his aim,
6.1.148: To lay the turrets low; to mark his track,
6.1.149: By ruin spread afar; and with the sword
6.1.150: To hew a path between his slaughtered foes.
6.1.151: Minucius' turret was the chosen spot
6.1.152: Where groves of trees and thickets gave approach
6.1.153: Safe, unbetrayed by dust. Up from the fields
6.1.154: Flashed all at once his eagles into sight
6.1.155: And all his trumpets blared. But ere the sword
6.1.156: Could win the battle, on the hostile ranks
6.1.157: Dread panic fell; prone as in death they lay
6.1.158: Where else upright they should withstand the foe;
6.1.159: Nor more availed their valour, and in vain
6.1.160: The cloud of weapons flew, with none to slay.
6.1.161: Then blazing torches rolling pitchy flame
6.1.162: Are hurled, and shaken nod the lofty towers
6.1.163: And threaten ruin, and the bastions groan
6.1.164: Struck by the frequent engine, and the troops
6.1.165: Of Magnus by triumphant eagles led
6.1.166: Stride o'er the rampart, in their front the world.
6.1.167: Yet now that passage which not Caesar's self
6.1.168: Nor thousand valiant squadrons had availed
6.1.169: To rescue from their grasp, one man in arms
6.1.170: Steadfast till death refused them; Scaeva named
6.1.171: This hero soldier: long he served in fight
6.1.172: Waged 'gainst the savage on the banks of Rhone;
6.1.173: And now centurion made, through deeds of blood,
6.1.174: He bore the staff before the marshalled line.
6.1.175: Prone to all wickedness, he little recked
6.1.176: How valourous deeds in civil war may be
6.1.177: Greatest of crimes; and when he saw how turned
6.1.178: His comrades fron the war and sought in flight
6.1.179: A refuge, ' Whence,' he cried, 'this impious fear
6.1.180: Unknown to Caesar's armies? Do ye turn
6.1.181: 'Your backs on death, and are ye not ashamed
6.1.182: Not to be found where slaughtered heroes lie?
6.1.183: 'Is loyalty too weak? Yet love of fight
6.1.184: 'Might bid you stand. We are the chosen few
6.1.185: 'Through whom the foe would break. Unbought by blood
6.1.186: 'This day shall not be theirs. 'Neath Caesar's eye,
6.1.187: 'True, death would be more happy; but this boon
6.1.188: 'Fortune denies: at least my fall shall be
6.1.189: 'Praised by Pompeius. Shatter with your breasts
6.1.190: ' Their weapons; blunt the edges of their swords
6.1.191: ' With throats unyielding. In the distant lines
6.1.192: ' The dust is seen already, and the sound
6.1.193: ' Of tumult and of ruin finds the ear
6.1.194: Of Caesar: strike; the victory is ours:
6.1.195: 'For he shall come who while his soldiers die
6.1.196: Shall make the fortress his.' His voice calls forth
6.1.197: The courage that the trumpets failed to rouse
6.1.198: When first they rang: his comrades mustering come
6.1.199: To watch his deeds; and, wondering at the man,
6.1.200: To test if valour thus by foes oppressed,
6.1.201: In narrow space, could hope for aught but death.
6.1.202: But Scaeva standing on the tottering bank
6.1.203: Heaves from the brimming turret on the foe
6.1.204: The corpses of the fallen; the ruined mass
6.1.205: Gives weapons to his hands; with beams and poles
6.1.206: And ponderous stones, with his own breast he threats
6.1.207: His enemies; and thrusts with mighty stakes
6.1.208: The host advancing; when they grasp the wall
6.1.209: He lops the arm: rocks crush the foeman's skull
6.1.210: And rive the scalp asunder: fiery bolts
6.1.211: Dashed at another set his hair aflame,
6.1.212: Till rolls the greedy blaze about his eyes
6.1.213: With hideous crackle. As the pile of slain
6.1.214: Rose to the summit of the wall he sprang,
6.1.215: Swift as across the nets a hunted pard,
6.1.216: Above the swords upraised, till in mid throng
6.1.217: Of foes he stood, hemmed in by densest ranks
6.1.218: And ramparted by war; in front and rear,
6.1.219: Where'er he struck, the victor. Now his sword
6.1.220: Blunted with gore congealed no more could wound,
6.1.221: But brake the stricken limb; while every hand
6.1.222: Flung every quivering dart at him alone;
6.1.223: Nor missed their aim, for rang against his shield
6.1.224: Dart after dart unerring, and his helm
6.1.225: In broken fragments pressed upon his brow;
6.1.226: His vital parts were safeguarded by spears
6.1.227: That bristled in his body. Fortune saw
6.1.228: Thus waged a novel combat, for there warred
6.1.229: Against one man an army. Why with darts,
6.1.230: Madmen, assail him and with slender shafts,
6.1.231: 'Gainst which his life is proof? Or ponderous stones
6.1.232: This warrior chief shall overwhelm, or bolts
6.1.233: Flung by the twisted thongs of mighty slings.
6.1.234: Let steel-shod ram or catapult remove
6.1.235: This champion of the gate. No fragile wall
6.1.236: Stands here for Caesar, blocking with its bulk
6.1.237: Pompeius' way to freedom. Now he trusts
6.1.238: His shield no more, lest his sinister hand,
6.1.239: Idle, give life by shame; and on his breast
6.1.240: Bearing a forest of spears, though spent with toil
6.1.241: And worn with onset, falls upon his foe
6.1.242: And braves alone the wounds of all the war.
6.1.243: Thus may an elephant in Afric wastes,
6.1.244: Oppressed by frequent darts, break those that fall
6.1.245: Rebounding from his horny hide, and shake
6.1.246: Those that find lodgment, while his life within
6.1.247: Lies safe, protected, nor does spear avail
6.1.248: To reach the fount of blood. Unnumbered wounds
6.1.249: By arrow dealt, or lance, thus fail to slay
6.1.250: This single warrior. But lo! from far
6.1.251: A Cretan archer's shaft, more sure of aim
6.1.252: Than vows could hope for, strikes on Scaeva's brow
6.1.253: To light within his eye: the hero tugs
6.1.254: Intrepid, bursts the nerves, and tears the shaft
6.1.255: Forth with the eyeball, and with dauntless heel
6.1.256: Treads them to dust. Not otherwise a bear
6.1.257: Pannonian, fiercer for the wound received,
6.1.258: Maddened by dart from Libyan thong propelled,
6.1.259: Turns circling on her wound, and still pursues
6.1.260: The weapon fleeing as she whirls around.
6.1.261: Thus, in his rage destroyed, his shapeless face
6.1.262: Stood foul with crimson flow. The victors' shout
6.1.263: Glad to the sky arose; no greater joy
6.1.264: A little blood could give them had they seen
6.1.265: That Caesar's self was wounded. Down he pressed
6.1.266: Deep in his soul the anguish, and, with mien
6.1.267: No longer bent on fight, submissive cried,
6.1.268: Spare me, ye citizens; remove the war
6.1.269: Far hence: no weapons now can haste my death;
6.1.270: Draw from my breast the darts, but add no more.
6.1.271: Yet raise me up to place me in the camp
6.1.272: Of Magnus, living: this your gift to him;
6.1.273: No brave man's death my title to renown,
6.1.274: But Caesar's flag deserted.' So he spake.
6.1.275: Unhappy Aulus thought his words were true,
6.1.276: Nor saw within his hand the ready sword;
6.1.277: And leaping forth in haste to make his own
6.1.278: The prisoner and his arms, in middle throat
6.1.279: Received the lightning blade. By this one death
6.1.280: Rose Scaeva's valour again; and thus he cried,
6.1.281: Such be the punishment of all who thought
6.1.282: Great Scaeva vanquished; if Pompeius seeks
6.1.283: Peace from this reeking sword, low let him lay
6.1.284: ' At Caesar's feet his standards. Me do ye think
6.1.285: ' Such as yourselves, and slow to meet the fates?
6.1.286: 'Your love for Magnus and the Senate's cause
6.1.287: 'Is less than mine for death.' These were his words;
6.1.288: And dust in columns proved that Caesar came.
6.1.289: Thus was Pompeius' glory spared the stain
6.1.290: Of flight compelled by Scava. He, when ceased
6.1.291: The battle, fell, no more by rage of fight,
6.1.292: Or sight of blood out-pouring from his wounds,
6.1.293: Roused to the combat. Fainting there he lay
6.1.294: Upon the shoulders of his comrades borne,
6.1.296: Dwelt in his bosom) for his matchless deeds,
6.1.297: Plucked forth the gory shafts and took his arms
6.1.298: To deck the gods and shield the breast of Mars.
6.1.299: Thrice happy thou with such a name achieved,
6.1.300: Had but the fierce Iberian from thy sword,
6.1.301: Or heavy shielded Teuton, or had fled
6.1.302: The light Cantabrian: now no spoils of thine
6.1.303: Shall deck the Thunderer's temple, nor upraise
6.1.304: The shout of triumph in the ways of Rome.
6.1.305: For all thy prowess, all thy deeds of pride
6.1.308: Repulsed, Pompeius idly ceased from war,
6.1.309: Content within his bars; but as the sea
6.1.310: Tireless, which tempests force upon the crag
6.1.311: That breaks it, or which gnaws a mountain side
6.1.312: Some day to fall in ruin on itself;
6.1.313: He sought the turrets nearest to the main,
6.1.314: On double onset bent; nor closely kept
6.1.315: His troops in hand, but on the spacious plain
6.1.316: Spread forth his camp. They joyful leave the tents
6.1.317: And wander at their will. Thus Padus flows
6.1.318: In brimming flood, and foaming at his bounds,
6.1.319: Making whole districts quake; and should the bank
6.1.320: Fail 'neath his swollen waters, all his stream
6.1.321: Breaks forth in swirling eddies over fields
6.1.322: Not his before; some lands are lost, the rest
6.1.325: Had Caesar seen the fire or known the fight:
6.1.326: And coming found the rampart overthrown,
6.1.327: The dust no longer stirred, the ruins cold
6.1.328: As from a battle done. The peace that reigned
6.1.329: There and on Magnus' side, as though men slept,
6.1.330: Their victory won, aroused his angry soul.
6.1.331: Quick he prepares, so that he end their joy
6.1.332: Careless of slaughter or defeat, to rush
6.1.333: With threatening columns on Torquatus' post.
6.1.334: But swift as sailor, by his trembling mast
6.1.335: Warned of Circeian tempest, furls his sails,
6.1.336: So swift Torquatus saw, and prompt to wage
6.1.337: The war more closely, he withdrew his men
6.1.340: Were Caesar's companies, when from the hills
6.1.341: Pompeius hurled his host upon their ranks
6.1.342: Shut in, and hampered. Not so much o'erwhelmed
6.1.343: As Caesar's soldiers is the hind who dwells
6.1.344: On Etna's slopes, when blows the southern wind,
6.1.345: And all the mountain pours its cauldrons forth
6.1.346: Upon the vale; and huge Enceladus
6.1.347: Writhing beneath his load spouts o'er the plains
6.1.348: A blazing torrent. Blinded by the dust,
6.1.349: Encircled, vanquished, ere the fight, they fled
6.1.350: In cloud of terror on their rearward foe,
6.1.351: So rushing on their fates. Thus had the war
6.1.352: Shed its last drop of blood and peace ensued,
6.1.353: But Magnus suffered not, and held his troops
6.1.356: Free, happy, mistress of thy laws and rights
6.1.357: Were Sulla here. Now shalt thou ever grieve
6.1.358: That in his crowning crime, to have met in fight
6.1.359: A pious kinsman, Caesar's vantage lay.
6.1.360: Oh tragic destiny! Nor Munda's fight
6.1.361: Hispania had wept, nor Libya mourned
6.1.364: A nobler corse than her Egyptian kings:
6.1.365: Nor Juba lain unburied on the sands,
6.1.366: Nor Scipio with his blood outpoured appeased
6.1.367: The ghosts of Carthage; this had been thy last
6.1.368: Disaster, Rome; nor had the blameless life
6.1.369: Of Cato ended: and Pharsalia's name
6.1.370: Had so been blotted from the book of fate.
6.1.371: But Caesar left the region where his arms
6.1.372: Had found the deities adverse, and marched
6.1.373: His shattered columns to Thessalian lands.
6.1.374: Then to Pompeius came (whose mind was bent
6.1.375: To follow Caesar wheresoe'er he fled)
6.1.376: His captains, striving to persuade their chief
6.1.377: To seek Ausonia, his native land,
6.1.378: Now freed from foes. 'Ne'er will I pass,' he said,
6.1.379: ' My country's limit, nor revisit Rome
6.1.380: ' Like Caesar, at the head of banded hosts.
6.1.381: ' Hesperia when the war began was mine;
6.1.382: ' Mine, had I chosen in our country's shrines,
6.1.383: ' In midmost forum of her capital,
6.1.384: ' To join the battle. So that banished far
6.1.385: ' Be war from Rome, I'll cross the torrid zone
6.1.386: ' Or those for ever frozen Scythian shores.
6.1.387: What! shall my victory rob thee of the peace
6.1.388: I gave thee by my flight? Rather than thou
6.1.389: Shouldst feel the evils of this impious war,
6.1.390: 'Let Caesar deem thee his.' He turned his course
6.1.391: Towards the uprising sun, and sought by paths
6.1.392: Remote, and forests wide, the land by fate
6.1.393: Foredoomed to see the issue of the war.
6.1.394: Thessalia on that side where Titan first
6.1.395: Raises the wintry day, by Ossa's rocks
6.1.396: Is prisoned in: but in th' advancing year
6.1.397: When higher in the vault his chariot rides
6.1.398: 'Tis Pelion that meets the morning rays.
6.1.399: And when beside the Lion's flames he drives
6.1.400: The middle course, Othrys with woody top
6.1.401: Screens his chief ardour. On the hither side
6.1.402: Pindus receives the breezes of the west
6.1.403: And as the evening falls brings darkness in.
6.1.404: There too Olympus, at whose foot who dwells
6.1.405: Nor fears the north nor sees the shining bear.
6.1.406: Between these mountains hemmed, in ancient time
6.1.407: The fields were marsh, for Tempe's pass not yet
6.1.408: Was cleft, to give an exit to the streams
6.1.409: That filled the plain: but when Alcides' hand
6.1.410: Smote Ossa from Olympus at a blow,
6.1.411: And Nereus wondered at the sudden flood
6.1.412: Of waters to the main, then on the shore
6.1.413: (Would it had slept for ever 'neath the deep)
6.1.415: And Phylace whence sailed that ship of old
6.1.416: Whose keel first touched upon the beach of Troy;
6.1.417: And Dorion mournful for the Muses' ire
6.1.419: Strong in the shafts of Hercules, the price
6.1.420: Of that most awful torch; Larissa's hold
6.1.421: Potent of yore; and Argos, famous erst,
6.1.422: O'er which men pass the ploughshare: and the spot
6.1.423: Fabled as Echionian Thebes, where once
6.1.424: Agave bore in exile to the pyre
6.1.425: (Grieving 'twas all she had) the head and neck
6.1.426: Of Pentheus massacred. The lake set free
6.1.427: Flowed forth in many rivers: to the west
6.1.428: AEas, a gentle stream; nor stronger flows
6.1.429: The sire of Isis ravished from his arms;
6.1.430: And Achelous, rival for the hand
6.1.431: Of OEneus' daughter, rolls his earthy flood
6.1.432: To silt the shore beside the neighbouring isles.
6.1.433: Evenus purpled by the Centaur's blood
6.1.434: Wanders through Calydon: in the Malian Gulf
6.1.435: Thy rapids fall, Spercheius: pure the wave
6.1.436: With which Amphrysos irrigates the meads
6.1.437: Where once Apollo served: Anaurus flows
6.1.438: Breathing no vapour forth; no humid air
6.1.439: Ripples his surface: and whatever stream,
6.1.440: Nameless itself, to Ocean gives its waves
6.1.441: Through thee, Peneus: whirled in eddies foams
6.1.443: Swift only when fresh streams his volume swell:
6.1.444: And thus Asopus takes his ordered course,
6.1.445: Phoenix and Melas; but Eurotas keeps
6.1.446: His stream aloof from that with which he flows,
6.1.447: Peneus, gliding on his top as though
6.1.448: Upon the channel. Fable says that, sprung
6.1.449: From darkest pools of Styx, with common floods
6.1.450: He scorns to mingle, mindful of his source,
6.1.451: So that the gods above may fear him still.
6.1.452: Soon as were sped the rivers, Boebian ploughs
6.1.453: Dark with its riches broke the virgin soil;
6.1.454: Then came Lelegians to press the share,
6.1.455: And Dolopes and sons of AEolus
6.1.456: By whom the glebe was furrowed. Steed-renowned
6.1.457: Magnetians dwelt there, and the Minyan race
6.1.458: Who smote the sounding billows with the oar.
6.1.459: There in the cavern from the pregnant cloud
6.1.460: Ixion's sons found birth, the Centaur brood
6.1.461: Half beast, half human: Monychus who broke
6.1.462: The stubborn rocks of Pholoe, Rhoetus fierce
6.1.463: Hurling from OEta's top gigantic elms
6.1.464: Which northern storms could hardly overturn;
6.1.465: Pholus, Alcides' host: Nessus who bore
6.1.466: The Queen across Evenus' waves, to feel
6.1.467: The deadly arrow for his shameful deed;
6.1.468: And aged Chiron who with wintry star
6.1.469: Against the huger Scorpion draws his bow.
6.1.470: Here sparkled on the land the warrior seed;
6.1.471: Here leaped the charger from Thessalian rocks
6.1.472: Struck by the trident of the Ocean King,
6.1.473: Omen of dreadful war; here first he learned,
6.1.474: Champing the bit and foaming at the curb,
6.1.475: Yet to obey his lord. From yonder shore
6.1.476: The keel of pine first floated, and bore men
6.1.477: To dare the perilous chance of seas unknown:
6.1.478: And here Ionus ruler of the land
6.1.479: First from the furnace molten masses drew
6.1.480: Of iron and brass; here first the hammer fell
6.1.481: To weld them, shapeless; here in glowing stream
6.1.482: Ran silver forth and gold, soon to receive
6.1.483: The minting stamp. 'Twas thus that money came
6.1.484: Whereby men count their riches, cause accursed
6.1.485: Of warfare. Hence came down that Python huge
6.1.486: On Cirrha: hence the laurel wreath which crowns
6.1.487: The Pythian victor: here Aloeus' sons
6.1.488: Gigantic rose against the gods, what time
6.1.489: Pelion had almost touched the stars supreme,
6.1.490: And Ossa's loftier peak amid the sky
6.1.492: When in this fated land the chiefs had placed
6.1.493: Their several camps, foreboding of the end
6.1.494: Now fast approaching, all men's thoughts were turned
6.1.495: Upon the final issue of the war.
6.1.496: And as the end drew near, all coward minds
6.1.497: Trembling beneath the shadow of the fate
6.1.498: Now hanging o'er them, deemed disaster near:
6.1.499: While some took heart; yet doubted what might fall,
6.1.500: In hope and fear alternate. 'Mid the throng
6.1.501: Sextus, unworthy son of worthy sire
6.1.502: Who soon upon the waves that Scylla guards,
6.1.503: Sicilian pirate, exile from his home,
6.1.504: Stained by his deeds of shame the fights he won,
6.1.505: Could bear delay no more; his feeble soul,
6.1.506: Sick of uncertain fate, by fear compelled,
6.1.507: Forecast the future: yet consulted not
6.1.508: The shrine of Delos nor the Pythian caves;
6.1.509: Nor was he satisfied to learn the sound
6.1.510: Of Jove's brass cauldron, 'mid Dodona's oaks,
6.1.511: By her primaeval fruits the nurse of men:
6.1.512: Nor sought he sages who by flight of birds,
6.1.513: Or watching with Assyrian care the stars
6.1.514: And fires of heaven, or by victims slain,
6.1.515: May know the fates to come; nor any source
6.1.516: Lawful though secret. For to him was known
6.1.517: That which excites the hate of gods above;
6.1.518: Magicians' lore, the savage creed of Dis
6.1.519: And all the shades; and sad with gloomy rites
6.1.520: Mysterious altars. For his frenzied soul
6.1.521: Heaven knew too little. And the spot itself
6.1.522: Kindled his madness, for hard by there dwelt
6.1.523: The brood of Haemon whom no storied witch
6.1.524: Of fiction e'er transcended; all their art
6.1.525: In things most strange and most incredible;
6.1.526: There were Thessalian rocks with deadly herbs
6.1.527: Thick planted, sensible to magic chants,
6.1.528: Funereal, secret: and the land was full
6.1.529: Of violence to the gods: the Queenly guest
6.1.530: From Colchis gathered here the fatal roots
6.1.531: That were not in her store: hence vain to heaven
6.1.533: For deaf the ears divine: save for one voice
6.1.534: Which penetrates the furthest depths of air
6.1.536: To hearken to its accents. Not the care
6.1.537: Of the revolving sky or starry pole
6.1.538: Can call them from it ever. Once the sound
6.1.539: Of those dread tones unspeakable has reached
6.1.541: Nor secret Memphis, though they open wide
6.1.542: The shrines of ancient magic and entreat
6.1.543: The gods, could draw them from the fires that smoke
6.1.544: Upon the altars of far Thessaly.
6.1.545: To hearts of flint those incantations bring
6.1.546: Love, strange, unnatural; the old man's breast
6.1.547: Burns with illicit fire. Nor lies the power
6.1.548: In harmful cup nor in the juicy pledge
6.1.549: Of love maternal from the forehead drawn;
6.1.550: Charmed forth by spells alone the mind decays,
6.1.551: By poisonous drugs unharmed. With woven threads
6.1.552: Crossed in mysterious fashion do they bind
6.1.553: Those whom no passion born of beauteous form
6.1.554: Or loving couch unites. All things on earth
6.1.555: Change at their bidding; night usurps the day;
6.1.556: The heavens disobey their wonted laws;
6.1.557: At that dread hymn the Universe stands still;
6.1.558: And Jove while urging the revolving wheels
6.1.559: Wonders they move not. Torrents are outpoured
6.1.560: Beneath a burning sun; and thunder roars
6.1.561: Uncaused by Jupiter. From their flowing locks
6.1.562: Vapours immense shall issue at their call;
6.1.563: When falls the tempest seas shall rise and foam
6.1.564: Moved by their spell; though powerless the breeze
6.1.565: To raise the billows. Ships against the wind
6.1.566: With bellying sails move onward. From the rock
6.1.567: Hangs motionless the torrent: rivers run
6.1.568: Uphill; the summer heat no longer swells
6.1.569: Nile in his course; Maeander's stream is straight;
6.1.570: Slow Rhone is quickened by the rush of Saone;
6.1.571: Hills dip their heads and topple to the plain;
6.1.572: Olympus sees his clouds drift overhead;
6.1.574: Melt in mid-winter; the inflowing tides
6.1.575: Driven onward by the moon, at that dread chant
6.1.576: Ebb from their course; earth's axes, else unmoved,
6.1.577: Have trembled, and the force centripetal
6.1.578: Has tottered, and the earth's compacted frame
6.1.579: Struck by their voice has gaped, till through the void
6.1.580: Men saw the moving sky. All beasts most fierce
6.1.581: And savage fear them, yet with deadly aid
6.1.582: Furnish the witches' arts. Tigers athirst
6.1.583: For blood, and noble lions on them fawn
6.1.584: With bland caresses: serpents at their word
6.1.585: Uncoil their circles, and extended glide
6.1.586: Along the surface of the frosty field;
6.1.587: The viper's severed body joins anew;
6.1.588: And dies the snake by human venom slain.
6.1.589: Whence comes this labour on the gods, compelled
6.1.590: To hearken to the magic chant and spells,
6.1.591: Nor daring to despise them? Doth some bond
6.1.592: Control the deities? Is their pleasure so,
6.1.593: Or must they listen? and have silent threats
6.1.595: So great a guerdon? Against all the gods
6.1.596: Is this their influence, or on one alone
6.1.597: Who to his will constrains the universe,
6.1.598: Himself constrained? Stars most in yonder clime
6.1.599: Shoot headlong from the zenith; and the moon
6.1.600: Gliding serene upon her nightly course
6.1.601: Is shorn of lustre by their poisonous chant,
6.1.602: Dimmed by dark earthly fires, as though our orb
6.1.603: Shadowed her brother's radiance and barred
6.1.604: The light bestowed by heaven; nor freshly shines
6.1.605: Until descending nearer to the earth
6.1.606: She sheds her baneful drops upon the mead.
6.1.607: These sinful rites and these her sister's songs
6.1.608: Abhorred Erichtho, fiercest of the race,
6.1.609: Spurned for their piety, and yet viler art
6.1.610: Practised in novel form. To her no home
6.1.611: Beneath a sheltering roof-her direful head
6.1.612: Thus to lay down were crime: deserted tombs
6.1.613: Her dwelling-place, from which, darling of hell,
6.1.614: She dragged the dead. Nor life nor gods forbad
6.1.615: But that she knew the secret homes of Styx
6.1.616: And learned to hear the whispered voice of ghosts
6.1.617: At dread mysterious meetings. Never sun
6.1.618: Shed his pure light upon that haggard cheek
6.1.619: Pale with the pallor of the shades, nor looked
6.1.620: Upon those locks unkempt that crowned her brow.
6.1.621: In starless nights of tempest crept the hag
6.1.622: Out from her tomb to seize the levin bolt;
6.1.623: Treading the harvest with accursed foot
6.1.624: She burned the fruitful growth, and with her breath
6.1.625: Poisoned the air else pure. No prayer she breathed
6.1.626: Nor supplication to the gods, nor knew
6.1.627: The pulse of entrails: logs from flaming pyres
6.1.628: She loves to cast on altars of the gods,
6.1.629: And incense pilfered from the smoking tomb.
6.1.630: The gods at her first utterance grant her prayer
6.1.631: For things unlawful, lest they hear again
6.1.632: Its fearful accents: men whose limbs were quick
6.1.633: With vital power she thrust within the grave
6.1.634: Despite the fates who owed them years to come:
6.1.635: The funeral reversed brought from the tomb
6.1.636: Those who were dead no longer; and the pyre
6.1.637: Yields to her shameless clutch still smoking dust
6.1.638: And bones enkindled, torches which but now
6.1.639: Some grieving father held, and fragments mixed
6.1.640: In sable smoke and ceremental cloths
6.1.641: Singed with the redolent fire that burned the dead.
6.1.642: But those who lie within a stony cell
6.1.643: Untouched by fire, whose dried and mummied frames
6.1.644: No longer know corruption, limb by limb
6.1.645: Venting her rage she tears, the bloodless eyes
6.1.646: Drags from their cavities, and mauls the nail
6.1.647: Upon the withered hand: she gnaws the noose
6.1.648: By which some wretch has died, and from the tree
6.1.649: Drags down a pendent corpse, its members torn
6.1.650: Asunder to the winds: forth from the palms
6.1.651: Wrenches the iron, and from the unbending bond
6.1.652: Hangs by her teeth, and with her hands collects
6.1.653: The slimy gore which drips upon the limbs.
6.1.654: Where lay a corpse upon the naked earth
6.1.655: On ravening birds and beasts of prey the hag
6.1.656: Kept watch, nor marred by knife or hand her spoil,
6.1.657: Till on his victim seized some nightly wolf;
6.1.658: Then dragged the morsel from his thirsty fangs;
6.1.659: Nor fears she murder, if some banquet fell
6.1.660: Need blood fresh issued from the gaping throat,
6.1.661: Or panting entrail. By unnatural means
6.1.662: Wombs yield to her the infant to be placed
6.1.663: On glowing altars: and whene'er she needs
6.1.664: Some fierce undaunted ghost, he fails not her
6.1.665: Who has all deaths in use. Her hand has chased
6.1.666: From smiling cheeks the rosy bloom of life;
6.1.667: And with sinister hand from dying youth
6.1.668: Has shorn the fatal lock: and holding oft
6.1.669: In foul embraces some departed friend
6.1.670: Severed the head, and through the ghastly lips,
6.1.671: Held by her own apart, some impious tale
6.1.672: Dark with mysterious horror hath conveyed
6.1.673: Down to the darkness of the Stygian shades.
6.1.674: When Sextus first, through rumours of the place,
6.1.675: Heard of the hag, what time beneath the earth
6.1.676: Titan was wheeling at full height, and here
6.1.677: Night in mid course, in quest of her he trod
6.1.678: Through desert fields. Meanwhile a faithful band,
6.1.679: His ministers of guilt, mid tombs and vaults
6.1.680: All ruined wandering, beheld the witch
6.1.681: Seated afar upon a lofty crag
6.1.682: Where Haemus reaches out Pharsalian spurs.
6.1.683: There was she proving for her gods and priests
6.1.684: Of magic, words unknown, and framing chants
6.1.685: Of dire and novel purpose: for she feared
6.1.686: Lest Mars should stray into another world,
6.1.687: And spare Thessalian soil the blood ere long
6.1.688: To flow in torrents; and thus she forbade
6.1.689: Philippi's field, polluted with her song,
6.1.690: Thick with her poisonous distilments sown,
6.1.691: To let the war pass by. Such deaths, she hopes,
6.1.692: Soon shall be hers! the blood of all the world
6.1.693: Shed for her use! to her it shall be given
6.1.694: To sever from their trunks the heads of kings,
6.1.695: Plunder the ashes of the noble dead,
6.1.696: Italia's bravest, and in triumph add
6.1.697: The mightiest warriors to her host of shades.
6.1.698: This her sole toil, from Magnus' tombless corse
6.1.699: What she may snatch, on which of Caesar's limbs
6.1.703: Of Haemon's daughters, in whose power it lies
6.1.704: Or to reveal the fates, or from its course
6.1.705: 'To turn the future, be it mine to know
6.1.706: 'By thy sure utterance to what final end
6.1.707: 'Fortune now guides the issue. Not the least
6.1.708: 'Of all the Roman host on yonder plain
6.1.709: Am I, but Magnus' most illustrious son,
6.1.710: Lord of the world or heir to death and doom.
6.1.711: 'The unknown affrights me: I can firmly face
6.1.712: The certain terror. Bid my destiny
6.1.713: Yield to thy power the dark and hidden end,
6.1.714: And let me fall foreknowing. From the gods
6.1.715: Extort the truth, or, if thou spare the gods,
6.1.716: Force it from hell itself. Fling back the gates
6.1.717: That bar th' Elysian fields; let Death confess
6.1.718: 'Whom from our ranks he seeks. No humble task
6.1.719: I bring, but worthy of Erichtho's skill
6.1.720: Of such a struggle fought for such a prize
6.1.721: To search and tell the issue.'
6.1.723: Pleased that her impious fame was noised abroad
6.1.724: Thus made her answer: 'If some lesser fates
6.1.725: 'Thy wish had been to change, against their wish
6.1.726: 'It had been easy to compel the gods
6.1.727: 'To its accomplishment. My art has power
6.1.728: When of one man the constellations press
6.1.729: The speedy death, to compass a delay;.
6.1.730: And mine it is, though every star decrees
6.1.731: A ripe old age, by mystic herbs to shear
6.1.732: The life midway. But should some purpose set
6.1.733: From the beginning of the universe,
6.1.734: And all the labouring fortunes of mankind,
6.1.735: 'Be brought in question, then Thessalian art
6.1.736: 'Bows to the power supreme. But if thou be
6.1.737: Content to know the issue pre-ordained,
6.1.738: 'Simple the task and plain; for earth and air
6.1.739: And sea and space and Rhodopaean crags
6.1.740: 'Shall speak the future. Yet it easiest seems
6.1.741: Where death in these Thessalian fields abounds
6.1.742: 'To raise a single corpse. From dead men's lips
6.1.743: Scarce cold, in fuller accents falls the voice;
6.1.744: Not from some mummied frame in accents shrill
6.1.747: And through redoubled night, a squalid veil
6.1.748: Swathing her pallid features, stole among
6.1.749: Unburied carcases. Fast fled the wolves,
6.1.750: The carrion birds with maw unsatisfied
6.1.751: Relaxed their talons, as with creeping step
6.1.752: She sought her prophet. Firm must be the flesh
6.1.753: As yet, though cold in death, and firm the lungs
6.1.754: Untouched by wound. Now in the balance hung
6.1.755: The fates of slain unnumbered; had she striven
6.1.756: Armies to raise and order back to life
6.1.757: Whole ranks of warriors, the laws had failed
6.1.758: Of Erebus; and, summoned up from Styx,
6.1.759: Its ghostly tenants had obeyed her call,
6.1.760: And rising fought once more. At length the witch
6.1.761: Picks out her victim with pierced throat agape
6.1.762: Fit for her purpose. Gripped by pitiless hook
6.1.763: O'er rocks she drags him to the mountain cave
6.1.764: Accursed by her fell rites, that shall restore
6.1.765: The dead man's life. Close to the hidden brink
6.1.766: The land that girds the precipice of hell
6.1.767: Sinks towards the depths: with ever falling leaves
6.1.768: A wood o'ershadows, and a spreading yew
6.1.770: Fills all the space, and in the deep recess
6.1.771: Darkness unbroken, save by chanted spells,
6.1.772: Reigns ever. Not where gape the misty jaws
6.1.773: Of caverned Taenarus, the gloomy bound
6.1.774: Of either world, through which the nether kings
6.1.775: Permit the passage of the dead to earth,
6.1.776: So poisonous, mephitic, hangs the air.
6.1.777: Nay, though the witch had power to call the shades
6.1.778: Forth from the depths, 'twas doubtful if the cave
6.1.779: Were not a part of hell. Discordant hues
6.1.780: Flamed on her garb as by a fury worn;
6.1.781: Bare was her visage, and upon her brow
6.1.782: Dread vipers hissed, beneath her streaming locks
6.1.783: In sable coils entwined. But when she saw
6.1.784: The youth's companions trembling, and himself
6.1.785: With eyes cast down, with visage as of death,
6.1.786: Thus spake the witch: ' Forbid your craven souls
6.1.787: 'These fears to cherish: soon returning life
6.1.788: 'This frame shall quicken, and in tones which reach
6.1.789: Even the timorous ear shall speak the man.
6.1.790: 'If I have power the Stygian lakes to show,
6.1.791: The bank that sounds with fire, the fury band,
6.1.792: 'And giants fettered, and the hound that shakes
6.1.793: 'Bristling with heads of snakes his triple head,
6.1.794: What fear is this that cringes at the sight
6.1.797: First through his gaping bosom blood she pours
6.1.798: Still fervent, washing from his wounds the gore.
6.1.799: Then copious poisons from the moon distils
6.1.800: Mixed with all monstrous things which Nature's pangs
6.1.801: Bring to untimely birth; the froth from dogs
6.1.802: Stricken with madness, foaming at the stream;
6.1.803: A lynx's entrails: and the knot that grows
6.1.804: Upon the fell hyaena; flesh of stags
6.1.805: Fed upon serpents; and the sucking fish
6.1.806: Which holds the vessel back though eastern winds
6.1.807: Make bend the canvas; dragon's eyes; and stones
6.1.808: That sound beneath the brooding eagle's wings.
6.1.809: Nor Araby's viper, nor the ocean snake
6.1.810: Who in the Red Sea waters guards the shell,
6.1.811: Are wanting; nor the slough on Libyan sands
6.1.812: By horned reptile cast; nor ashes fail
6.1.813: Snatched from an altar where the Phoenix died.
6.1.814: And viler poisons many, which herself
6.1.815: Has made, she adds, whereto no name is given:
6.1.816: Pestiferous leaves pregnant with magic chants
6.1.817: And blades of grass which in their primal growth
6.1.818: Her cursed mouth had slimed. Last came her voice
6.1.819: More potent than all herbs to charm the gods
6.1.820: Who rule in Lethe. Dissonant murmurs first
6.1.821: And sounds discordant from the tongues of men
6.1.822: She utters, scarce articulate: the bay
6.1.823: Of wolves, and barking as of dogs, were mixed
6.1.824: With that fell chant; the screech of nightly owl
6.1.825: Raising her hoarse complaint; the howl of beast
6.1.826: And sibilant hiss of snake-all these were there;
6.1.827: And more-the wail of waters on the rock,
6.1.828: The sound of forests and the thunder peal.
6.1.829: Such was her voice; but soon in clearer tones
6.1.830: Reaching to Tartarus, she raised her song:
6.1.832: ' Of Hell upon the damned, and Chaos huge
6.1.833: ' Who striv'st to mix innumerable worlds,
6.1.834: ' And Pluto, king of earth, whose weary soul
6.1.835: ' Grieves at his godhead; Styx; and plains of bliss
6.1.836: ' We may not enter: and thou, Proserpine,
6.1.837: ' Hating thy mother and the skies above,
6.1.838: ' My patron goddess, last and lowest form
6.1.839: ' Of Hecate, through whom the shades and I
6.1.840: ' Hold silent converse; warder of the gate
6.1.841: ' Who castest human offal to the dog:
6.1.842: ' Ye sisters who shall spin the threads again;
6.1.843: ' And thou, O boatman of the burning wave,
6.1.844: ' Now wearied of the shades from hell to me
6.1.845: ' Returning, hear me if with voice I cry
6.1.846: ' Abhorred, polluted; if the flesh of man
6.1.847: ' Hath ne'er been absent from my proffered song,
6.1.848: Flesh washed with brains still quivering; if the child
6.1.849: Whose severed head I placed upon the dish
6.1.850: But for this hand had lived-a listening ear
6.1.851: Lend to my supplication! From the caves
6.1.852: 'Hid in the innermost recess of hell
6.1.853: ' I claim no soul long banished from the light.
6.1.854: ' For one but now departed, lingering still
6.1.855: ' Upon the brink of Orcus, is my prayer.
6.1.856: Grant (for ye may) that listening to the spell
6.1.857: 'Once more he seek his dust; and let the shade
6.1.858: Of this our soldier perished (if the war
6.1.859: Well at your hands has merited), proclaim
6.1.860: The destiny of Magnus to his son.'
6.1.861: Such prayers she uttered; then upraised her head
6.1.862: And foaming lips, and present saw the ghost.
6.1.863: Hard by he stood, beside the hated corpse
6.1.864: His ancient prison, and loathed to enter in.
6.1.865: There was the yawning chest where fell the blow
6.1.866: That was his death; and yet the gift supreme
6.1.867: Of death, his right, (Ah, wretch! ) was reft away.
6.1.868: Angered at Death the witch, and at the pause
6.1.869: Conceded by the fates, with living snake
6.1.870: Scourges the nerveless corse; and on the dead
6.1.871: She barks through fissures gaping to her song,
6.1.872: Breaking the silence of their gloomy home:
6.1.874: Flies not this wretched soul before your whips
6.1.875: ' The void of Erebus? By your very names,
6.1.876: ' She-dogs of hell, I'll call you to the day,
6.1.877: Not to return; through sepulchres and death
6.1.878: Your gaoler: from funereal urns and tombs
6.1.879: I'll chase you forth. And thou, too, Hecate,
6.1.880: Who to the gods in comely shape and mien,
6.1.881: Not that of Erebus, appear'st, henceforth
6.1.882: Wasted and pallid as thou art in hell
6.1.883: 'At my command shalt come. I'll noise abroad
6.1.884: The banquet that beneath the solid earth
6.1.885: Holds thee, thou maid of Enna; by what bond
6.1.886: 'Thou lov'st night's King, by what mysterious stain
6.1.887: Infected, so that Ceres fears from hell
6.1.888: 'To call her daughter. And for thee, base king,
6.1.889: 'Titan shall pierce thy caverns with his rays
6.1.890: And sudden day shall smite thee. Do ye hear?
6.1.891: 'Or shall I summon to mine aid that god
6.1.892: 'At whose dread name earth trembles; who can look
6.1.893: Unflinching on the Gorgon's head, and drive
6.1.894: 'The Furies with his scourge, who holds the depths
6.1.895: ' Ye cannot fathom, and above whose haunts
6.1.896: Ye dwell supernal; who by waves of Styx
6.1.899: Grew warm and liquid, and with softening touch
6.1.900: Cherished the stiffened wounds and filled the veins,
6.1.901: Till throbbed once more the slow returning pulse
6.1.902: And every fibre trembled, as with death
6.1.903: Life was commingled. Then, not limb by limb,
6.1.904: With toil and strain, but rising at a bound
6.1.905: Leaped from the earth erect the living man.
6.1.906: Fierce glared his eyes uncovered, and the life
6.1.907: Was dim, and still upon his face remained
6.1.908: The pallid hues of hardly parted death.
6.1.909: Amazement seized upon him, to the earth
6.1.910: Brought back again: but from his lips tight drawn
6.1.911: No murmur issued; he had power alone
6.1.912: When questioned to reply. 'Speak,' quoth the hag,
6.1.913: As I shall bid thee; great shall be thy gain
6.1.914: If true thine answers, freed for evermore
6.1.915: From all Haemonian art. Such burial place
6.1.916: Shall now be thine, and on thy funeral pyre
6.1.917: Such fatal woods shall burn, such chant shall sound,
6.1.918: 'That to thy ghost no more or magic song
6.1.919: Or spell shall reach, and thy Lethaean sleep
6.1.920: Shall never more be broken in a death
6.1.921: ' From me received anew: for such reward
6.1.922: ' Think not this second life enforced in vain.
6.1.923: ' Obscure may be the answers of the gods
6.1.924: ' By priestess spoken at the holy shrine;
6.1.925: ' But whoso braves the oracles of death
6.1.926: ' In search of truth, should gain a sure response.
6.1.927: ' Then speak, I pray thee. Let the hidden fates
6.1.928: ' Tell through thy voice the mysteries to come.'
6.1.929: Thus spake she, and her words by mystic force
6.1.930: Gave him his answer; but with gloomy mien,
6.1.931: And tears swift flowing, thus he made reply:
6.1.932: 'Called from the margin of the silent stream
6.1.933: I saw no fateful sisters spin the threads.
6.1.934: 'Yet know I this, that 'mid the Roman shades
6.1.935: 'Reigns fiercest discord; and this impious war
6.1.936: 'Destroys the peace that ruled the fields of death.
6.1.938: 'In paths diverse the Roman chieftains leave
6.1.939: 'And thus disclose the fates. The blissful ghosts
6.1.940: Bear visages of sorrow. Sire and son
6.1.941: 'The Decii, who gave themselves to death
6.1.943: 'And great Camillus, wept; and Sulla's shade
6.1.945: 'The scion of his race about to fall
6.1.946: ' In sands of Libya: Cato, greatest foe
6.1.947: ' To Carthage, grieves for that indignant soul
6.1.948: ' Which shall disdain to serve. Brutus alone
6.1.949: ' In all the happy ranks I smiling saw,
6.1.950: ' First consul when the kings were thrust from Rome.
6.1.951: ' The chains were fallen from boastful Catiline.
6.1.952: ' Him too I saw rejoicing, and the pair
6.1.953: ' Of Marii, and Cethegus' naked arm.
6.1.954: ' The Drusi, heroes of the people, joyed,
6.1.955: ' In laws immoderate; and the famous pair
6.1.956: ' Of greatly daring brothers: guilty bands
6.1.957: ' By bars eternal shut within the doors
6.1.958: ' That close the prison of hell, applaud the fates,
6.1.959: 'Claiming the plains Elysian: and the King
6.1.960: ' Throws wide his pallid halls, makes hard the points
6.1.961: ' Of craggy rocks, and forges iron chains,
6.1.962: ' The victor's punishment. But take with thee
6.1.963: 'This comfort, youth, that there a calm abode,
6.1.964: ' And peaceful, waits thy father and his house.
6.1.965: ' Nor let the glory of a little span
6.1.966: ' Disturb thy boding heart: the hour shall come
6.1.967: ' When all the chiefs shall meet. Shrink not from death,
6.1.968: ' But glorying in the greatness of your souls,
6.1.969: ' E'en from your humble sepulchres descend,
6.1.970: ' And tread beneath your feet, in pride of place,
6.1.971: ' The wandering phantoms of the gods of Rome.
6.1.972: ' Which chieftain's tomb by Tiber shall be laved,
6.1.973: ' And which by Nile; their fate, and theirs alone,

7.1.420: Your brands in Caesar's blood, and thus shall give
7.1.421: Another sanction to the laws of Rome,

7.1.425: Of all these mingled peoples and of Rome
7.1.426: Disproves an angry heaven. See here combined
7.1.427: 'All means of victory. Noble men have sought
7.1.428: 'Unasked the risks of war. Our soldiers boast
7.1.429: 'Ancestral statues. If to us were given
7.1.431: Or patriot Decius to devote his life,
7.1.432: 'Here would they take their stand. From furthest east
7.1.433: 'All nations gathered, cities as the sand
7.1.434: 'Unnumbered, give their aid: a world complete

7.1.458: At these his words, indignant at the thought,
7.1.459: And Rome rose up within them, and to die
7.1.462: Moved either host to battle, one in fear
7.1.463: And one in hope of empire. These hands shall do
7.1.464: Such work as not the rolling centuries,
7.1.465: Not all mankind, though free from sword and war,
7.1.466: Shall e'er make good. Nations that were to live
7.1.467: This fight shall crush, and peoples pre-ordained
7.1.468: To make the history of the coming world
7.1.469: Shall come not to the birth. The Latin names
7.1.470: Shall sound as fables in the ears of men,
7.1.471: And ruins loaded with the dust of years
7.1.472: Shall hardly mark her cities. Alba's hill,
7.1.473: Home of our gods, no human foot shall tread,
7.1.474: Save of some Senator at the nightly feast
7.1.476: Serves his high office. Void and desolate
7.1.477: Are Veii, Cora and Laurentum's hold;
7.1.478: Yet not the tooth of envious time destroyed
7.1.480: That rased their citadels. Where now has fled
7.1.481: The teeming life that once Italia knew?
7.1.482: Not all the earth can furnish her with men:
7.1.483: Untenanted her dwellings and her fields:
7.1.484: Slaves till her soil: one city holds us all:
7.1.485: Crumbling to ruin, the ancestral roof
7.1.486: Finds none on whom to fall; and Rome herself,
7.1.487: Void of her citizens, draws within her gates
7.1.488: The dregs of all the world. That none might wage
7.1.489: A civil war again, thus deeply drank
7.1.490: Pharsalia's fight the life-blood of her sons.
7.1.491: Dark in the calendar of Rome for aye,
7.1.492: The days when Allia and Cannae fell:
7.1.493: And shall Pharsalus' morn, darkest of all,
7.1.494: Stand on the page unmarked? Alas, the fates!
7.1.495: Not plague nor pestilence nor famine's rage,
7.1.496: Not cities given to the flames, nor towns
7.1.497: Trembling at shock of earthquake shall weigh down
7.1.498: Such heroes lost, when Fortune's ruthless hand
7.1.499: Lops at one blow the gift of centuries,
7.1.500: Leaders and men embattled. How great art thou,
7.1.501: Rome, in thy fall! Stretched to the widest bounds
7.1.502: War upon war laid nations at thy feet
7.1.503: Till flaming Titan nigh to either pole
7.1.504: Beheld thine empire; and the furthest east
7.1.505: Was almost thine, till day and night and sky
7.1.506: For thee revolved, and all the stars could see
7.1.507: Throughout their course was Roman. But the fates
7.1.508: In one dread day of slaughter and despair
7.1.509: Turned back the centuries and spoke thy doom.
7.1.510: And now the Indian fears the axe no more
7.1.511: Once emblem of thy power, now no more
7.1.512: The girded Consul curbs the Getan horde,
7.1.513: Or in Sarmatian furrows guides the share:
7.1.514: Still Parthia boasts her triumphs unavenged:
7.1.515: Foul is the public life; and Freedom, fled
7.1.516: To furthest Earth beyond the Tigris stream,
7.1.517: And Rhine's broad river, wandering at her will
7.1.518: 'Mid Teuton hordes and Scythian, though by sword
7.1.519: Sought, yet returns not. Would that from the day
7.1.520: When Romulus, aided by the vulture's flight,
7.1.521: Ill-omened, raised within that hateful grove
7.1.522: Rome's earliest walls, down to the crimsoned field
7.1.523: In dire Thessalia fought, she ne'er had known
7.1.524: Italia's peoples! Did the Bruti strike
7.1.525: In vain for liberty? Why laws and rights
7.1.526: Sanctioned by all the annals designate
7.1.527: With consular titles? Happier far the Medes
7.1.528: And blest Arabia, and the Eastern lands
7.1.529: Held by a kindlier fate in despot rule!
7.1.530: That nation serves the worst which serves with shame.
7.1.531: No guardian gods watch over us from heaven:
7.1.532: Jove is no king; let ages whirl along
7.1.533: In blind confusion: from his throne supreme
7.1.534: Shall he behold such carnage and restrain
7.1.535: His thunderbolts? On Mimas shall he hurl
7.1.536: His fires, on Rhodope and OEta's woods
7.1.538: This life to Cassius' hand? On Argos fell
7.1.539: At grim Thyestes' feast untimely night
7.1.540: By him thus hastened; shall Thessalia's land
7.1.541: Receive full daylight, wielding kindred swords
7.1.542: In fathers' hands and brothers'? Careless of men
7.1.543: Are all the gods. Yet for this day of doom
7.1.544: Such vengeance have we reaped as deities
7.1.545: May give to mortals; for these wars shall raise
7.1.546: Our parted Caesars to the gods; and Rome
7.1.547: Shall deck their effigies with thunderbolts,
7.1.548: And stars and rays, and in the very fanes
7.1.549: Swear by the shades of men.
7.1.551: They seize the space that yet delays the fates
7.1.552: Till short the span dividing. Then they gaze
7.1.553: For one short moment where may fall the spear,
7.1.554: What hand may deal their death, what monstrous task
7.1.555: Soon shall be theirs; and all in arms they see,
7.1.556: In reach of stroke, their brothers and their sires
7.1.557: With front opposing; yet to yield their ground
7.1.558: It pleased them not. But all the host was dumb
7.1.559: With horror; cold upon each loving heart,
7.1.560: Awe-struck, the life-blood pressed; and all men held
7.1.561: With arms outstretched their javelins for a time,
7.1.562: Poised yet unthrown. Now may th' avenging gods
7.1.563: Allot thee, Crastinus, not such a death
7.1.564: As all men else do suffer! In the tomb
7.1.565: May'st thou have feeling and remembrance still!
7.1.566: For thine the hand that first flung forth the dart,
7.1.567: Which stained with Roman blood Thessalia's earth.
7.1.568: Madman! To speed thy lance when Caesar's self
7.1.569: Still held his hand! Then from the clarions broke
7.1.570: The strident summons, and the trumpets blared
7.1.571: Responsive signal. Upward to the vault
7.1.572: The sound re-echoes where nor clouds may reach
7.1.573: Nor thunder penetrate; and Haemus' slopes
7.1.576: Groan, and Pangaean cliffs, till at their rage
7.1.577: Borne back from all the earth they shook for fear.
7.1.578: Unnumbered darts they hurl, with prayers diverse;
7.1.579: Some hope to wound: others, in secret, yearn
7.1.580: For hands still innocent. Chance rules supreme,
7.1.581: And wayward Fortune upon whom she wills
7.1.582: Makes fall the guilt. Yet, for the hatred bred
7.1.583: By civil war suffices spear nor lance,
7.1.584: Urged on their flight afar: the hand must grip
7.1.585: The sword and drive it to the foeman's heart.
7.1.586: But while Pompeius' ranks, shield wedged to shield,
7.1.587: Were ranged in dense array, and scarce had space
7.1.588: To draw the blade, came rushing at the charge
7.1.589: Full on the central column Caesar's host,
7.1.590: Mad for the battle. Man nor arms could stay
7.1.591: The crash of onset, and the furious sword
7.1.592: Clove through the stubborn panoply to the flesh,
7.1.593: There only stayed. One army struck-their foes
7.1.594: Struck not in answer; Magnus' swords were cold,
7.1.595: But Caesar's reeked with slaughter and with guilt.
7.1.596: Nor Fortune lingered, but decreed the doom
7.1.597: Which swept the ruins of a world away.
7.1.598: Soon as withdrawn from all the spacious plain,
7.1.599: Pompeius' horse was ranged upon the flanks;
7.1.600: Passed through the outer files, the lighter armed
7.1.601: Of all the nations joined the central strife,
7.1.602: With divers weapons armed, but all for blood
7.1.603: Of Rome athirst: then blazing torches flew,
7.1.604: Arrows and stones, and ponderous balls of lead
7.1.605: Molten by speed of passage through the air.
7.1.606: There Ituraean archers and the Mede
7.1.607: Winged forth their shafts unaimed, till all the sky
7.1.608: Grew dark with missiles hurled; and from the night
7.1.609: Brooding above, Death struck his victims down.
7.1.610: Guiltless such blow, while all the crime was heaped
7.1.611: Upon the Roman spear. In line oblique
7.1.612: Behind the standards Caesar in reserve
7.1.613: Had placed some companies of foot, in fear
7.1.614: The foremost ranks might waver. These at his word,
7.1.615: No trumpet sounding, break upon the ranks
7.1.616: Of Magnus' horsemen where they rode at large
7.1.617: Flanking the battle. They, unshamed of fear
7.1.618: And careless of the fray, when first a steed
7.1.619: Pierced through by javelin spurned with sounding hoof
7.1.620: The temples of his rider, turned the rein,
7.1.621: And through their comrades spurring from the field
7.1.622: In panic, proved that not with warring Rome
7.1.625: There stood the victim, and the victor's arm
7.1.626: Wearied of slaughter. Oh, that to thy plains,
7.1.627: Pharsalia, might suffice the crimson stream
7.1.628: From hosts barbarian, nor other blood
7.1.629: Pollute thy fountains' sources! these alone
7.1.630: Shall clothe thy pastures with the bones of men!
7.1.631: Or if thy fields must run with Roman blood
7.1.632: Then spare the nations who in times to come
7.1.635: Through all the army, and the favouring fates
7.1.636: Decreed for Caesar's triumph: and the war
7.1.637: Ceased in the wider plain, though still ablaze
7.1.638: Where stood the chosen of Pompeius' force,
7.1.639: Upholding yet the fight. Not here allies
7.1.640: Begged from some distant king to wield the sword:
7.1.641: Here were the Roman sons, the sires of Rome,
7.1.642: Here the last frenzy and the last despair:
7.1.643: Here, Caesar, was thy crime: and here shall stay
7.1.644: My Muse repelled: no poesy of mine
7.1.645: Shall tell the horrors of the final strife,
7.1.646: Nor for the coming ages paint the deeds
7.1.647: Which civil war permits. Be all obscured
7.1.648: In deepest darkness! Spare the useless tear
7.1.649: And vain lament, and let the deeds that fell
7.1.650: In that last fight of Rome remain unsung.
7.1.651: But Caesar adding fury to the breasts
7.1.652: Already flaming with the rage of war,
7.1.653: That each might bear his portion of the guilt
7.1.654: Which stained the host, unflinching through the ranks
7.1.655: Passed at his will. He looked upon the brands,
7.1.656: These reddened only at the point, and those
7.1.657: Streaming with blood and gory to the hilt:
7.1.658: He marks the hand which trembling grasped the sword,
7.1.659: Or held it idle, and the cheek that grew
7.1.660: Pale at the blow, and that which at his words
7.1.661: Glowed with the joy of battle: midst the dead
7.1.662: He treads the plain and on each gaping wound
7.1.663: Presses his hand to keep the life within.
7.1.664: Thus Caesar passed: and where his footsteps fell
7.1.665: As when Bellona shakes her crimson lash,
7.1.666: Or Mavors scourges on the Thracian mares
7.1.667: When shunning the dread face on Pallas' shield,
7.1.668: He drives his chariot, there arose a night
7.1.669: Dark with huge slaughter and with crime, and groans
7.1.670: As of a voice immense, and sound of arms
7.1.671: As fell the wearer, and of sword on sword
7.1.672: Crashed into fragments. With a ready hand
7.1.673: Caesar supplies the weapon and bids strike
7.1.674: Full at the visage; and with lance reversed
7.1.675: Urges the flagging ranks and stirs the fight.
7.1.676: Where flows the nation's blood, where beats the heart,
7.1.677: Knowing, he bids them spare the common herd,
7.1.678: But seeks the senators-thus Rome he strikes,
7.1.679: Thus the last hold of Freedom. In the fray,
7.1.680: Then fell the nobles with their mighty names
7.1.681: Of ancient prowess; there Metellus' sons,
7.1.683: Not once nor twice the conquerors of kings,
7.1.684: First of all men, Pompeius' name except,
7.1.687: Where was thy sword? Veiled by a common helm
7.1.688: Unknown thou wanderest. Thy country's pride,
7.1.689: Hope of the Senate, thou (for none besides);
7.1.690: Thou latest scion of that race of pride,
7.1.691: Whose fearless deeds the centuries record,
7.1.692: Tempt not the battle, nor provoke the doom!
7.1.693: Awaits thee on Philippi's fated field
7.1.694: Thy Thessaly. Not here shalt thou prevail
7.1.695: 'Gainst Caesar's life. Not yet hath he surpassed
7.1.696: The height of power and deserved a death
7.1.697: Noble at Brutus' hands-then let him live,
7.1.700: Lay all the honour of Rome; no common stream
7.1.701: Mixed with the purple tide. And yet of all
7.1.702: Who noble fell, one only now I sing,
7.1.703: Thee, brave Domitius. Whene'er the day
7.1.704: Was adverse to the fortunes of thy chief
7.1.705: Thine was the arm which vainly stayed the fight.
7.1.706: Vanquished so oft by Caesar, now 'twas thine
7.1.707: Yet free to perish. By a thousand wounds
7.1.708: Came welcome death, nor had thy conqueror power
7.1.709: Again to pardon. Caesar stood and saw
7.1.710: The dark blood welling forth and death at hand,
7.1.711: And thus in words of scorn: ' And dost thou lie,
7.1.713: 'Thee his successor, thee? Why leavest thou then
7.1.714: His standards helpless?' But the parting life
7.1.715: Still faintly throbbed within Domitius' breast,
7.1.716: Thus finding utterance: 'Yet thou hast not won
7.1.717: Thy hateful prize, for doubtful are the fates;
7.1.718: 'Nor thou the master, Caesar; free as yet,
7.1.719: 'With great Pompeius for my leader still,
7.1.720: ' Warring no more, I seek the silent shades,
7.1.721: Yet with this hope in death, that thou subdued
7.1.722: 'To Magnus and to me in grievous guise
7.1.723: 'Mayst pay atonement.' So he spake: no more;
7.1.724: Then closed his eyes in death.
7.1.726: When thus a world was perishing, the tear
7.1.727: Meet for each fate, or sing the wound that reft
7.1.728: Each life away. One spurned upon the soil
7.1.729: His vitals as they trailed; one faced the foe
7.1.730: And as the sword struck deep into his throat
7.1.731: Breathed forth his life: another fell to earth
7.1.732: Prone at the stroke; one stood though shorn of limb;
7.1.733: Glanced from this breast unharmed the quivering spear;
7.1.734: That it transfixed to earth. Here from the veins
7.1.735: Spouted the life-blood, till the foeman's arms
7.1.736: Were crimsoned. One his brother slew, nor dared
7.1.737: To spoil the corse, till severed from the neck
7.1.738: He flung the head afar. Another dashed
7.1.739: Full in his father's teeth the fatal sword,
7.1.740: By murderous frenzy striving to disprove
7.1.741: His kinship with the slain. Yet for each death
7.1.742: We find no separate dirge, nor weep for men
7.1.743: When peoples fell. Thus, Rome, thy doom was wrought
7.1.744: At dread Pharsalus. Not, as in other fields,
7.1.745: By soldiers slain, or captains; here were swept
7.1.746: Whole nations to the death; Assyria here,
7.1.747: Achaia, Pontus; and the blood of Rome
7.1.748: Gushing in torrents forth, forbade the rest
7.1.749: To stagnate on the plain. Nor life was reft,
7.1.750: Nor safety only then; but reeled the world
7.1.751: And all her manifold peoples at the blow
7.1.752: In that day's battle dealt; nor only then
7.1.753: Felt, but in all the times that were to come.
7.1.754: Those swords gave servitude to every age
7.1.755: That shall be slavish; by our sires was shaped
7.1.756: For us our destiny, the despot yoke.
7.1.757: Yet have we trembled not, nor feared to bare
7.1.758: Our throats to slaughter, nor to face the foe:
7.1.759: We bear the penalty for others' shame,
7.1.760: Such be our doom; yet, Fortune, sharing not
7.1.761: In that last battle, 'twas our right to strike
7.1.762: One blow for freedom ere we served our lord.
7.1.763: Now saw Pompeius, grieving, that the gods
7.1.764: Had left his side, and knew the fates of Rome
7.1.765: Passed from his governance; yet all the blood
7.1.766: That filled the field scarce brought him to confess
7.1.767: His fortunes fled. A little hill he sought
7.1.768: Whence to descry the battle raging still
7.1.769: Upon the plain, which when he nearer stood
7.1.770: The warring ranks concealed. Thence did the chief
7.1.771: Gaze on unnumbered swords that flashed in air
7.1.772: And sought his ruin; and the tide of blood
7.1.773: In which his host had perished. Yet not as those
7.1.774: Who, prostrate fallen, would drag nations down
7.1.775: To share their evil fate, Pompeius did.
7.1.776: Still were the gods thought worthy of his prayers
7.1.777: To give him solace, in that after him
7.1.778: Might live his Romans. 'Spare, ye gods,' he said,
7.1.779: Nor lay whole peoples low; my fall attained,
7.1.780: The world and Rome may stand. And if ye need
7.1.781: More bloodshed, here on me, my wife, and sons
7.1.782: 'Wreak out your vengeance-pledges to the fates
7.1.783: Such have we given. Too little for the war
7.1.784: Is our destruction? Doth the carnage fail,
7.1.785: The world escaping? Magnus' fortunes lost,
7.1.786: Why doom all else beside him? ' Thus he cried,
7.1.787: And passed amid his standards, and recalled
7.1.788: His vanquished host that rushed on fate declared.
7.1.789: Not for his sake such carnage should be wrought.
7.1.790: So thought Pompeius; nor the foeman's sword
7.1.791: He feared, nor death; but lest upon his fall
7.1.792: To quit their chief his soldiers might refuse,
7.1.793: And o'er his prostrate corpse a world in arms
7.1.794: Might find its ruin: or perchance he wished
7.1.795: From Caesar's eager eyes to veil his death.
7.1.796: In vain, unhappy! for the fates decree
7.1.797: He shall behold, shorn from the bleeding trunk,
7.1.798: Again thy visage. And thou, too, his spouse,
7.1.799: Beloved Cornelia, didst cause his flight;
7.1.800: Thy longed-for features; yet he shall not die
7.1.803: Though fearing not the weapons at his back,
7.1.804: Pompeius fled, his mighty soul prepared
7.1.805: To meet his final doom. He saw thy field,
7.1.806: Pharsalia, tearless and without a groan;
7.1.807: For solemn grief and majesty of mien
7.1.808: Were in his face, as for the woes of Rome.
7.1.809: No pride in him the day of victory found,
7.1.810: Nor rout shall find despair; alike in days
7.1.811: When fickle Fortune triple triumph gave
7.1.812: And when she fled, her lord.
7.1.814: Of thine impending fate, thou partest free
7.1.815: To muse upon the happy days of yore.
7.1.816: Hope now has fled; but in the fleeting past
7.1.817: How wast thou great! Seek thou the wars no more,
7.1.818: And call the gods to witness that for thee
7.1.819: Henceforth no man shall die. The fights to come
7.1.820: On Afric's mournful shore, by Pharos' stream
7.1.821: And fateful Munda, and the final scene
7.1.822: Of dire Pharsalia's battle are not thine.
7.1.823: Thy name no more shall stir the world to war,
7.1.824: But those great rivals biding with us yet,
7.1.825: Caesar and Liberty; and not for thee
7.1.826: When thou hadst fled the field, but for itself
7.1.827: The dying Senate still upheld the fight.
7.1.828: Find'st thou not solace thus to quit the field
7.1.829: Nor witness all the horrors of its close?
7.1.830: Look back upon the crimsoned ranks of war,
7.1.831: The rivers turbid with ensanguined stream;
7.1.832: Then pity thou thy kinsman. How shall he
7.1.833: Enter the city, who on such a field
7.1.834: Finds happiness? Whate'er in lands unknown
7.1.835: Thine exiled lot, whate'er the Pharian king
7.1.836: May place upon thee, trust thou in the gods;
7.1.837: Trust the long story of the favouring fates:
7.1.838: 'Twere worse to conquer. Then forbid the tear,
7.1.839: The nation's grief, the weeping of mankind,
7.1.840: And let the world adore thee in defeat
7.1.841: As in thy triumphs. With unaltered gaze
7.1.842: Look down upon the kings, thy subjects still;
7.1.843: Look on the realms and cities which they hold,
7.1.844: Egypt and Libya, gifts from thee of yore;
7.1.845: And choose the country that befits thy death.
7.1.846: Larissa first was witness of thy fall,
7.1.847: Thy noble mien, as victor of the fates;
7.1.848: And loud in sorrow, yet with gifts of price
7.1.849: Fit for a conqueror flung back her gates
7.1.850: And poured her citizens forth. ' Our homes and fanes
7.1.851: To thee are open; would it were our lot
7.1.852: With thee to perish; of thy mighty name
7.1.853: Still much survives and conquered by thyself,
7.1.854: Thyself alone, still couldst thou to the war
7.1.855: All nations call and challenge fate again.'
7.1.856: But thus he spake: 'To cities nor to men
7.1.857: Avails the conquered aught: then pledge your faith
7.1.858: To him who has the victory.' Caesar still
7.1.859: Trod deep in piles of slaughter on the field,
7.1.860: His country's vitals, while his daughter's spouse
7.1.861: Thus gave him kingdoms. But Pompeius fled
7.1.862: 'Mid sobs and groans and blaming of the gods
7.1.863: For this their fierce commandment; and he fled
7.1.864: Full of the fruits and knowledge of the love
7.1.865: The peoples bore him, which he knew not his
7.1.868: Flowed deep enough upon the fatal field,
7.1.869: Caesar gave mercy to the meaner crowd
7.1.870: Whose deaths were vain. But that the hostile camp
7.1.871: Might not recall the foe, nor calm of night
7.1.872: Banish their fears, he bids his cohorts dash,
7.1.873: While Fortune glowed and terror filled the plain,
7.1.874: Straight on the ramparts of the conquered foe.
7.1.875: Light was the task to urge them to the spoil
