8.1.720: Rapt to the boat was Magnus, of himself
8.1.721: No longer master, and the miscreant crew
8.1.722: Unsheathed their swords; which when the chieftain saw
8.1.723: He swathed his visage, for he scorned unveiled
8.1.724: To yield his life to fortune; closed his eyes
8.1.725: And held his breath within him, lest some word,
8.1.726: Or sob escaped, might mar the deathless fame
8.1.727: His deeds had won. And when within his side
8.1.728: Achillas plunged his blade, nor sound nor cry
8.1.729: He gave, but calm consented to the blow
8.1.730: And proved himself in dying; in his breast
8.1.731: These thoughts revolving: ' In the years to come
8.1.732: ' Men shall make mention of our Roman toils,
8.1.733: ' Gaze on this boat, ponder the Pharian faith;
8.1.734: ' And think upon thy fame and all the years
8.1.735: ' While Fortune smiled: but for the ills of life
8.1.736: ' How thou couldst bear them, this men shall not know
8.1.737: ' Save by thy death. Then weigh thou not the shame
8.1.738: ' That waits on thine undoing. Whoso strikes,
8.1.739: ' The blow is Caesar's. Men may tear this frame
8.1.740: 'And cast it mangled to the winds of heaven;
8.1.741: 'Yet have I prospered, nor can all the gods
8.1.742: ' Call back my triumphs. Life may bring defeat,
8.1.743: 'But death no misery. If my spouse and son
8.1.745: ' I suffer: admiration at my death
8.1.746: 'Shall prove their love.' So did Pompeius die,
8.1.747: And so kept guard upon his thoughts in death.
8.1.748: His spouse, less patient to behold the crime
8.1.749: Than to endure it, filled the airs with cries;
8.1.750: '0, husband, whom my wicked self hath slain!
8.1.751: 'That lonely isle apart thy bane hath been
8.1.752: 'And stayed thy coming. Caesar to the Nile
8.1.753: 'Has won before us; for what other hand
8.1.754: 'May do such work? But whosoe'er thou art
8.1.755: 'Sent from the gods with power, for Caesar's ire,
8.1.756: 'Or thine own sake, to slay, thou dost not know
8.1.757: 'Where lies the heart of Magnus. Thou dost haste
8.1.758: To deal the blow as he would have it fall.
8.1.759: 'Let me die first, and let him seeing bear
8.1.760: 'An agony no less than death can bring.
8.1.761: 'No freedom mine from blame of war. Alone
8.1.762: Of Roman wives, through oceans and through camps,
8.1.763: Fearing no fates, I followed him afield;
8.1.764: And in defeat when even monarchs feared
8.1.765: Received my husband. Did I then deserve
8.1.766: Thus to be left of thee, and didst thou seek
8.1.767: To spare me? And when rushing on thine end
8.1.768: Was I to live? Without the monarch's help
8.1.769: Death shall be mine, either by headlong leap
8.1.770: Beneath the waters; or some sailor's hand
8.1.771: Shall bind around this neck the fatal cord;
8.1.772: Or else some comrade, worthy of his chief,
8.1.773: Drive to my heart his blade for Magnus' sake,
8.1.774: And claim the service done to Caesar's arms.
8.1.775: What! does your cruelty withhold my fate?
8.1.776: Ah! still he lives, nor is it mine as yet
8.1.777: To win this freedom; they forbid me death,
8.1.778: Kept for the victor's triumph.' Thus she spake,
8.1.779: While friendly hands upheld her fainting form;
8.1.780: And sped the trembling vessel from the shore.
8.1.781: Men say that Magnus, when the deadly blows
8.1.782: Fell thick upon him, lost nor form divine,
8.1.783: Nor venerated mien; and as they gazed
8.1.784: Upon his lacerated head they marked
8.1.785: Still on his features anger with the gods.
8.1.786: For fierce Septimius in the very blow
8.1.787: Made yet more black his crime-unwound the folds
8.1.788: That swathed the face, and seized the noble head
8.1.789: And drooping neck ere yet was fled the life:
8.1.790: Then placed upon the bench; and with his blade
8.1.791: Slow at its hideous task, and blows unskilled
8.1.792: Hacked through the flesh and brake the knotted bone;
8.1.793: For yet man had not learned by swoop of sword
8.1.794: Deftly to lop the neck. Achillas claimed
8.1.795: The gory head dissevered. What! shalt thou
8.1.796: A Roman soldier, while thy blade yet reeks
8.1.797: From Magnus' slaughter, play the second part
8.1.798: To this base varlet of the Pharian king?
8.1.799: Nor bear thyself the bleeding trophy home?
8.1.800: Then, that the impious boy (ah! shameful fate)
8.1.801: Might know the features of the hero slain,
8.1.802: Seized by the locks, the dread of kings, which waved
8.1.803: Upon his stately front, on Pharian pike
8.1.804: The head was lifted; while almost the life
8.1.805: Gave to the tongue its accents, and the eyes
8.1.806: Were yet scarce glazed: that head at whose command
8.1.807: Was peace or war, that tongue whose eloquent tones
8.1.808: Would move assemblies, and that noble brow
8.1.809: On which were showered the rewards of Rome.
8.1.810: Nor to the tyrant did the sight suffice
8.1.811: To prove the murder done. The perishing flesh,
8.1.812: The tissues, and the brain he bids remove
8.1.813: By art nefarious: the shrivelled skin
8.1.814: Draws tight upon the bone; and poisonous juice
8.1.815: Gives to the face its lineaments in death.
8.1.816: Last of thy race, thou base degenerate boy,
8.1.817: About to perish soon, and yield the throne
8.1.818: To thine incestuous sister; while the Prince
8.1.819: From Macedon here in consecrated vault
8.1.820: Now rests, and ashes of the kings are closed
8.1.821: In mighty pyramids, and lofty tombs
8.1.822: Of thine unworthy fathers mark the graves;
8.1.823: Shall Magnus' body hither and thither borne
8.1.824: Be battered, headless, by the ocean wave?
8.1.825: Too much it troubled thee to guard the corse
8.1.827: To witness! Such the fate which Fortune kept
8.1.828: With prosperous Pompeius to the end.
8.1.829: 'Twas not for him in evil days some ray
8.1.830: Of light to hope for. Shattered from the height
8.1.831: Of power in one short moment to his death!
8.1.832: Years of unbroken victories balanced down
8.1.833: By one day's carnage! In his happy time
8.1.834: Heaven did not harass him, nor did she spare
8.1.835: In misery. Long Fortune held the hand
8.1.836: That dashed him down. Now beaten by the sands,
8.1.837: Torn upon rocks, the sport of ocean's waves
8.1.838: Poured through its wounds, his headless carcase lies,
8.1.839: Save by the lacerated trunk unknown.
8.1.840: Yet ere the victor touched the Pharian sands
8.1.841: Some scanty rites to Magnus Fortune gave,
8.1.842: Lest he should want all burial. Pale with fear
8.1.843: Came Cordus, hasting from his hiding place;
8.1.844: Quaestor, he joined Pompeius on thy shore,
8.1.845: Idalian Cyprus, bringing in his train
8.1.846: A cloud of evils. Through the darkening shades
8.1.847: Love for the dead compelled his trembling steps,
8.1.848: Hard by the margin of the deep to search
8.1.849: And drag to land his master. Through the clouds
8.1.850: The moon shone sadly, and her rays were dim;
8.1.851: But by its hue upon the hoary main
8.1.852: He knew the body. In a fast embrace
8.1.853: He holds it, wrestling with the greedy sea,
8.1.854: And deftly watching for a refluent wave
8.1.855: Gains help to bring his burden to the land.
8.1.856: Then clinging to the loved remains, the wounds
8.1.857: Washed with his tears, thus to the gods he speaks,
8.1.858: And misty stars obscure: 'Here, Fortune, lies
8.1.859: Pompeius, thine: no costly incense rare
8.1.860: Or pomp of funeral he dares to ask;
8.1.861: Nor that the smoke rise heavenward from his pyre
8.1.862: With eastern odours rich; nor that the necks
8.1.863: Of pious Romans bear him to the tomb,
8.1.864: Their parent; while the forums shall resound
8.1.865: ' With dirges; nor that triumphs won of yore
8.1.866: 'Be borne before him; nor for sorrowing hosts
8.1.867: 'To cast their weapons forth. Some little shell
8.1.868: He begs as for the meanest, laid in which
8.1.869: His mutilated corse may reach the flame.
8.1.870: Grudge not his misery the pile of wood
8.1.871: ' Lit by this menial hand. Is't not enough
8.1.873: ' Weeps not beside him at his obsequies,
8.1.874: ' Nor with a last embrace shall place the torch
8.1.875: ' Beneath her husband dead, but on the deep
8.1.878: He sees the pyre of some ignoble youth
8.1.879: Deserted of his own, with none to guard:
8.1.880: And quickly drawing from beneath the limbs
8.1.881: Some glowing logs, ' Whoe'er thou art,' he said,
8.1.882: Neglected shade, uncared for, dear to none,
8.1.883: Yet happier than Pompeius in thy death,
8.1.884: Pardon I ask that this my stranger hand
8.1.885: ' Should violate thy tomb. Yet if to shades
8.1.886: 'Be sense or memory, gladly shalt thou yield
8.1.887: 'This from thy pyre to Magnus. 'Twere thy shame,
8.1.888: 'Blessed with due burial, if his remains
8.1.889: Were homeless.' Speaking thus, the wood aflame
8.1.890: Back to the headless trunk at speed he bore,
8.1.891: Which hanging on the margin of the deep,
8.1.892: Almost the sea had won. In sandy trench
8.1.893: The gathered fragments of a broken boat,
8.1.894: Trembling, he placed around the noble limbs.
8.1.895: No pile above the corse nor under lay,
8.1.896: Nor was the fire beneath. Then as he crouched
8.1.897: Beside the blaze, ' 0, greatest chief,' he cried,
8.1.899: 'If to be tossed unburied on the deep
8.1.900: Rather than these poor rites thy shade prefer,
8.1.901: 'From these mine offices thy mighty soul
8.1.902: Withdraw, Pompeius. Injuries dealt by fate
8.1.903: Command this duty, lest some bird or beast
8.1.904: 'Or ocean monster, or fierce Caesar's wrath
8.1.905: 'Should venture aught upon thee. Take the fire;
8.1.906: All that thou canst; by Roman hand at least
8.1.908: 'To loved Hesperia's land, not here shall rest
8.1.909: 'Thy sacred ashes; but within an urn
8.1.910: Cornelia, from this humble hand received,
8.1.911: Shall place them. Here upon a meagre stone
8.1.912: We draw the characters to mark thy tomb.
8.1.913: These letters reading may some kindly friend
8.1.914: 'Bring back thine head, dissevered, and may grant
8.1.915: 'Full funeral honours to thine earthly frame.'
8.1.916: Then did he cherish the enfeebled fire
8.1.917: Till Magnus' body mingled with its flames.
8.1.918: But now the harbinger of coming dawn
8.1.919: Had paled the constellations: he in fear
8.1.920: Seeks for his hiding place. Whom dost thou dread,
8.1.921: Madman, what punishment for such a crime,
8.1.922: For which thy fame by rumour trumpet-tongued
8.1.923: Has been sent down to ages? Praise is thine
8.1.924: For this thy work, at impious Caesar's hands;
8.1.925: Sure of a pardon, go; confess thy task,
8.1.926: And beg the head dissevered. But his work
8.1.927: Was still unfinished, and with pious hand
8.1.928: (Fearing some foe) he seizes on the bones
8.1.929: Now half consumed, and sinews; and the wave
8.1.930: Pours in upon them, and in shallow trench
8.1.931: Commits them to the earth; and lest some breeze
8.1.932: Might bear away the ashes, or by chance
8.1.933: Some sailor's anchor might disturb the tomb,
8.1.934: A stone he places, and with stick half burned
8.1.935: Traces the sacred name: Here Magnus lies.
8.1.936: And art thou, Fortune, pleased that such a spot
8.1.937: Should be his tomb which even Caesar's self
8.1.938: Had chosen, rather than permit his corse
8.1.939: To rest unburied? Why, with thoughtless hand
8.1.940: Confine his shade within the narrow bounds
8.1.941: Of this poor sepulchre? Where the furthest sand
8.1.942: Hangs on the margin of the baffled deep
8.1.943: Cabined he lies; yet where the Roman name
8.1.944: Is known, and Empire, such in truth shall be
8.1.945: The boundless measure of his resting-place.
8.1.946: Blot out this stone, this proof against the gods!
8.1.947: OEta finds room for Hercules alone,
8.1.948: And Nysa's mountain for the Bromian god;
8.1.949: Not all the lands of Egypt should suffice
8.1.950: For Magnus dead: and shall one Pharian stone
8.1.951: Mark his remains? Yet should no turf disclose
8.1.952: His title, peoples of the earth would fear
8.1.953: To spurn his ashes, and the sands of Nile
8.1.954: No foot would tread. But if the stone deserves
8.1.955: So great a name, then add his mighty deeds:
8.1.956: Write Lepidus conquered and the Alpine war,
8.1.957: And fierce Sertorius by his aiding arm
8.1.958: O'erthrown; the chariots which as knight he drove;
8.1.959: Cilician pirates driven from the main,
8.1.960: And Commerce safe to nations; Eastern kings
8.1.961: Defeated and the barbarous Northern tribes;
8.1.962: Write that from arms he ever sought the robe;
8.1.963: Write that content upon the Capitol
8.1.964: Thrice only triumphed he, nor asked his due.
8.1.965: What mausoleum were for such a chief
8.1.966: A fitting monument? This paltry stone
8.1.967: Records no syllable of the lengthy tale
8.1.968: Of honours: and the name which men have read
8.1.969: Upon the sacred temples of the gods,
8.1.970: And lofty arches built of hostile spoils,
8.1.971: On desolate sands here marks his lowly grave
8.1.972: With characters obscure, such as erect
8.1.973: No traveller could read, and Roman guest
8.1.974: Without a hand to guide would pass unseen.
8.1.975: Thou land of Egypt, doomed to bear a part
8.1.976: In civil warfare, not unreasoning sang
8.1.977: High Cumae's prophetess, when she forbad
8.1.978: The stream Pelusian to the Roman arms,
8.1.979: And all the banks which in the summer-tide
8.1.980: Are covered by his flood. What grievous curse
8.1.981: Shall I call down upon thee? May the Nile
8.1.982: Turn back his water to his source, thy fields
8.1.983: Want for the winter rain, and all the land
8.1.984: Crumble to desert wastes! We in our fanes
8.1.985: Have known thine Isis and thy hideous gods,
8.1.986: Half hounds, half human, and the drum that bids
8.1.987: To sorrow, and Osiris, whom thy dirge
8.1.988: Proclaims for man. Thou, Egypt, in thy sand
8.1.989: Our dead containest. Nor, though her temples now
8.1.990: Serve a proud master, has Rome yet required
8.1.991: Pompeius' ashes: in a foreign land
8.1.992: Still lies her chief. But though men feared at first
8.1.993: The victor's ire, now, Rome, at length receive
8.1.994: Thy Magnus' bones, if still the restless wave
8.1.995: Has not prevailed upon that hated shore.
8.1.996: Shall men have fear of tombs and dread to move
8.1.997: The dust of those who should be with the gods?
8.1.998: 0, may my country place the crime on me,
8.1.999: If crime it be, to violate such a tomb
8.1.1000: Of such a hero, and to bear his dust
8.1.1001: Home to Ausonia. Happy, happy he
8.1.1002: Who bears such holy office in his trust!
8.1.1003: Haply when famine rages in the land
8.1.1004: Or burning southern winds, or fires abound
8.1.1005: And earthquake shocks, and Rome shall pray an end
8.1.1006: From angry heaven-by the gods' command,
8.1.1007: In council given, shalt thou be transferred
8.1.1008: To thine own city, and the priest shall bear
8.1.1009: Thy sacred ashes to their last abode.
8.1.1010: Who now may seek beneath the raging Crab
8.1.1011: Or hot Syene's waste, or Thebes athirst
8.1.1012: Under the rainy Pleiades, to gaze
8.1.1013: On Nile's broad stream; or whoso may exchange
8.1.1014: On the Red Sea or in Arabian ports
8.1.1015: Some Eastern merchandise, shall turn in awe
8.1.1016: To view the venerable stone that marks
8.1.1017: Thy grave, Pompeius; and shall worship more
8.1.1018: Thy dust commingled with the arid sand,
8.1.1019: Thy shade though exiled, than the fane upreared
8.1.1020: On Casius' mount to Jove! In temples shrined
8.1.1021: And gold, thy memory were viler deemed:
8.1.1022: Fortune lies with thee in thy lowly tomb
8.1.1023: And makes thee rival of Olympus' king.
8.1.1024: More awful is that stone by Libyan seas
8.1.1025: Lashed, than are Conquerors' altars. There a god
8.1.1026: Rests in dark earth to whom all men shall bow
8.1.1027: More than to gods Tarpeian: and his name
8.1.1028: Shall shine the brighter in the days to come
8.1.1029: For that no marble tomb about him stands
8.1.1030: Nor lofty monument. That little dust
8.1.1031: Time soon shall scatter and the tomb shall fall
8.1.1032: And all the proofs shall perish of his death.
8.1.1033: And happier days shall come when men shall gaze
8.1.1034: Upon the stone, nor yet believe the tale:
8.1.1035: And Egypt's fable, that she holds the grave
8.1.1036: Of great Pompeius, be believed no more
8.1.1037: Than Crete's which boasts the sepulchre of Jove.

9.1.1: YET in those ashes on the Pharian shore,
9.1.2: In that small heap of dust, was not confined
9.1.3: So great a shade; but from th' ignoble pyre
9.1.4: And limbs half burnt sprang forth and sought the sky
9.1.5: Where dwells the Thunderer. Black the space of air
9.1.6: Upreaching to the poles that bear on high
9.1.7: The constellations in their nightly round;
9.1.8: There 'twixt the orbit of the moon and earth
9.1.9: Abide those lofty spirits, half divine,
9.1.10: Who by their blameless lives and fire of soul
9.1.11: Are fit to tolerate the pure expanse
9.1.12: That bounds the lower ether: there shall dwell,
9.1.13: Where nor the monument encased in gold,
9.1.14: Nor richest incense, shall suffice to bring
9.1.15: The buried dead, in union with the spheres,
9.1.16: Pompeius' spirit. When with heavenly light
9.1.17: His soul was filled, first on the wandering stars
9.1.18: And fixed orbs he bent his wondering gaze;
9.1.19: Then saw what darkness veils our earthly day
9.1.20: And scorned the insults heaped upon his corse.
9.1.21: Next o'er Emathian plains he winged his flight,
9.1.22: And ruthless Caesar's standards, and the fleet
9.1.23: Tossed on the deep: in Brutus' blameless breast
9.1.24: Tarried awhile, and roused his angered soul
9.1.25: To reap the vengeance; last possessed the mind
9.1.28: Were poised and balanced, nor the war had given
9.1.29: The world its master, hated both the chiefs,
9.1.30: But followed Magnus for the Senate's cause
9.1.31: And for his country: now in all his heart
9.1.32: Was bound to Magnus, since Pharsalia's field.
9.1.33: Shorn of her guardian his country found
9.1.34: In him her guide; the people's trembling limbs
9.1.35: He cherished with new hope, and weapons gave
9.1.36: Back to the craven hands that cast them forth.
9.1.37: Nor yet for empire did he wage the war
9.1.38: Nor fearing slavery: nor in arms achieved
9.1.39: Aught for himself: freedom, since Magnus fell,
9.1.40: The aim of all his host. And lest the foe
9.1.41: In rapid course triumphant should collect
9.1.42: His scattered bands, he sought Corcyra's gulfs
9.1.43: Concealed, and bore in thousand ships away
9.1.44: The fragments of the ruin wrought in Thrace.
9.1.45: Who in such mighty navy had believed
9.1.46: A host defeated sailed upon the main
9.1.47: Thronging the sea with keels? Round Malea's cape
9.1.48: And Taenarus open to the shades below
9.1.49: And fair Cythera's isle, th' advancing fleet
9.1.50: Sweeps o'er the yielding wave, by northern breeze
9.1.51: Borne past the Cretan shores. But Phycus dared
9.1.52: Refuse her harbour, and th' avenging hand
9.1.53: Left her in ruins. Thus with gentle airs
9.1.54: They glide along the main and reach the shore
9.1.55: From Palinurus named; for not alone
9.1.56: On seas Italian, Pilot of the deep,
9.1.57: Hast thou thy monument; and Libya too
9.1.58: Claims that her tranquil harbours pleased thy soul.
9.1.59: Then in the distance on the main arose
9.1.60: The shining canvas of a stranger fleet,
9.1.61: Or friend or foe they knew not. Yet they dread
9.1.62: In every keel the presence of that chief
9.1.63: Their fear-compelling conqueror. But in truth
9.1.64: That navy tears and sorrow bore, and woes
9.1.67: Cornelia prayed her stepson and the crew
9.1.68: To stay their flight, lest haply from the shore
9.1.69: Back to the sea might float the headless corse;
9.1.70: And when the flame arising marked the place
9.1.71: Of that unhallowed rite, ' Fortune, didst thou
9.1.72: Judge me unfit,' she cried, ' to light the pyre
9.1.73: 'To cast myself upon the hero dead,
9.1.74: 'The lock to sever, and compose the limbs
9.1.75: 'Tossed by the cruel billows of the deep,
9.1.76: To shed a flood of tears upon his wounds,
9.1.77: To fill my robe with ashes from his urn,
9.1.78: And scatter in the temples of the gods
9.1.79: All that I could, his dust? That pyre bestows
9.1.80: No honour, haply by some Pharian hand
9.1.81: Piled up in insult to his mighty shade.
9.1.82: Happy the Crassi lying on the waste
9.1.83: Unburied. To the greater shame of heaven
9.1.84: ' Pompeius has such funeral. And shall this
9.1.85: ' For ever be my lot? her husbands slain
9.1.86: ' Cornelia ne'er enclose within the tomb,
9.1.87: ' Nor shed the tear beside the urn that holds
9.1.88: ' The ashes of the loved? Yet for my grief
9.1.89: ' What boots or monument or ordered pomp?
9.1.90: ' Dost thou not, impious, upon thy heart
9.1.91: · Pompeius' image, and upon thy soul
9.1.92: ' Bear ineffaceable? Dust closed in urns
9.1.93: ' Is for the wife who would survive her lord,
9.1.94: ' Not such as thee, Cornelia! And yet
9.1.95: 'Yon scanty light that glimmers from afar
9.1.96: ' Upon the Pharian shore, somewhat of thee
9.1.97: ' Recalls, Pompeius! Now the flame sinks down
9.1.98: ' And smoke drifts up across the eastern sky
9.1.99: ' Bearing thine ashes, and the rising wind
9.1.100: ' Sighs hateful in the sail. To me no more
9.1.101: ' Dearer than this whatever land has given
9.1.102: ' Pompeius victory, nor the frequent car
9.1.103: ' That carried him in triumph to the hill;
9.1.104: ' Gone is that happy husband from my thoughts;
9.1.105: ' Here did I lose the hero whom I knew;
9.1.106: ' Here let me stay; his presence shall endear
9.1.107: ' The sands of Nile where fell the fatal blow.
9.1.108: ' Thou, Sextus, brave the chances of the war
9.1.109: 'And bear Pompeius' standard through the world.
9.1.110: ' For thus thy father spake within mine ear:
9.1.111: ' " When sounds my fatal hour let both my sons
9.1.112: ' " Urge on the war; nor let some Caesar find
9.1.113: ' " Room for an empire, while shall live on earth
9.1.114: ' " Still one in whom Pompeius' blood shall run.
9.1.115: ' " This your appointed task; all cities strong
9.1.116: ' " In freedom of their own, all kingdoms urge
9.1.117: ' " To join the combat; for Pompeius calls.
9.1.118: ' " Nor shall a chieftain of that famous name
9.1.119: ' ' Ride on the seas and fail to find a fleet.
9.1.120: ' Urged by his sire's unconquerable will
9.1.121: ' " And mindful of his rights, mine heir shall rouse
9.1.122: ' " All nations to the conflict. One alone,
9.1.123: ' " (Should he contend for freedom) may ye serve;

9.1.156: ' Not Caesar wrought his death, nor any chief
9.1.157: ' Worthy to cause the ruin of our sire.
9.1.158: ' He fell by order of that shameful king
9.1.159: ' Who rules o'er Nilus; trusting to the gods

9.1.162: ' I saw them pierce our noble father's breast;

9.1.164: ' So fell a deed would dare, on Egypt's strand

9.1.177: ' The gods: I weep the part preserved by men.'

9.1.180: Flamed into fury: ' Launch our navies forth,
9.1.181: ' Ye sailors, from the shore, by stalwart arms

9.1.184: ' So great a prize; to lay in earth the limbs

9.1.201: 'Fallen and perished, shalt possess the land.'

9.1.214: Ill-fated Magnus' spoils, his arms of price,

9.1.227: Nought else so gratified, not all the blame

9.1.231: 'Gone is a citizen who though no peer
9.1.232: 'Of those who disciplined the state of yore
9.1.233: In due submission to the bounds of right,
9.1.234: 'Yet in this age irreverent of law
9.1.235: 'Has played a noble part. Great was his power,
9.1.236: 'But freedom safe: when all the plebs was prone
9.1.237: 'To be his slaves, he chose the private gown;
9.1.238: 'So that the Senate ruled the Roman state,
9.1.239: 'Its chief was Cato: nought by right of arms
9.1.240: 'He e'er demanded: willing took he gifts
9.1.241: 'Yet from a willing giver: wealth was his
9.1.242: Vast, yet the coffers of the State he filled
9.1.243: 'Beyond his own. He seized upon the sword,
9.1.244: 'Knew when to sheath it; war did he prefer
9.1.245: 'To arts of peace, yet armed loved peace the more.
9.1.246: 'Pleased took he power, pleased he laid it down:
9.1.247: 'Chaste was his home and simple, by his wealth
9.1.248: 'Untarnished. Mid the peoples great his name
9.1.249: And venerated: to his native Rome
9.1.250: He wrought much good. True faith in liberty
9.1.251: Long since with Marius and Sulla fled:
9.1.252: Now when Pompeius has been reft away
9.1.254: Shall seize the despot on Imperial power,
9.1.255: 'Unshamed shall cringe the Senate. Happy he
9.1.256: Who with disaster found his latest breath
9.1.257: 'And met the Pharian sword prepared to slay.
9.1.258: Life might have been his lot, in despot rule,
9.1.259: Prone at his kinsman's throne. Best gift of all
9.1.260: 'The knowledge how to die; next, death compelled.
9.1.261: If cruel Fortune doth reserve for me
9.1.262: An alien conqueror, may Juba be
9.1.263: As Ptolemaeus. So he take my head
9.1.264: My body grace his triumph, if he will.'
9.1.265: More than had Rome resounded with his praise
9.1.266: Words such as these gave honour to the shade
9.1.267: Of that most noble dead. Meanwhile the crowd
9.1.268: Weary of warfare, since Pompeius' fall,
9.1.269: Broke into discord, as their ancient chief
9.1.270: Cilician called them to desert the camp.
9.1.271: They seize upon their ships and float the wave;
9.1.272: But Cato hailed them from the nearest shore;
9.1.273: ' Untamed Cilician, is thy course now set
9.1.274: ' For Ocean theft again; Pompeius gone,
9.1.275: ' Pirate art thou once more? ' Then all the air
9.1.276: Hummed with the murmur of the throng; and one
9.1.277: Resolved on flight thus answered, ' Pardon, chief,
9.1.278: ' Twas love of Magnus, not of civil war,
9.1.279: ' That led us to the fight: his side was ours:
9.1.280: ' With him whom all the world preferred to peace,
9.1.281: ' Our cause is perished. Let us seek our homes
9.1.282: ' Long since unseen, our children and our wives.
9.1.283: If nor the rout on dread Pharsalia's field
9.1.284: Nor yet Pompeius' death shall close the war,
9.1.285: Whence comes the end? Our span of life is fled:
9.1.286: Give death safe haven, give old age his pyre.
9.1.287: Scarce even to its captains civil strife
9.1.288: Concedes due burial. Nor in our defeat
9.1.289: Does Fortune threaten us with the savage yoke

9.1.291: And with her rights, I leave thee. Who had been
9.1.292: Second to Magnus living, he shall be
9.1.293: My first hereafter: to that sacred shade
9.1.294: Be the prime honour. Chance of war appoints
9.1.295: My lord but not my leader. Thee alone
9.1.296: I followed, Magnus; after thee the fates.
9.1.297: 'Nor have I right to hope for victory now,
9.1.298: Nor wish: our Thracian array is fled
9.1.300: Of fortune rules the world; and none but he
9.1.301: Has power to keep or save. That civil war
9.1.302: Which while Pompeius lived was loyalty
9.1.303: Is impious now. Let country lead thee on,
9.1.304: 'Cato, and public right; but let us seek
9.1.305: ' The standards of the Consul.' Thus he spake

9.1.309: For all the shore was stirring with a crowd
9.1.310: Athirst for slavery. But burst these words
9.1.311: From Cato's blameless breast: ' Then with like vows
9.1.312: ' As Caesar's rival host ye too did seek
9.1.313: ' A lord and master! not for Rome the fight,
9.1.314: But for Pompeius! For that now no more
9.1.315: 'Ye fight for tyranny, but for yourselves,
9.1.316: 'Not for some despot chief, ye live and die;
9.1.317: ' Since now 'tis safe to conquer and no lord
9.1.318: ' Shall rob you, victors, of a world subdued-
9.1.319: ' Ye flee the war, and on your abject necks
9.1.320: 'Feel for the absent yoke; nor can endure
9.1.321: ' Without a despot! Yet to men the prize
9.1.322: ' Were worth the danger. Magnus might have used
9.1.323: ' To evil ends your blood; refuse ye now,
9.1.324: ' With liberty so near, your country's call?
9.1.325: ' Now lives one tyrant only of the three;
9.1.326: ' Thus far in favour of the laws have wrought

9.1.328: ' Not you, degenerate! Begone, and spurn
9.1.329: ' This gift of Ptolemaeus. Who would think

9.1.332: ' First turned your backs. Then flee in safety, flee!
9.1.333: ' By neither battle nor blockade subdued
9.1.334: ' Caesar shall give you life! 0 slaves most base,
9.1.335: ' Your former master slain, ye seek his heir!
9.1.336: ' Why doth it please you not yet more to earn
9.1.337: 'Than life and pardon? Bear across the sea
9.1.339: ' And both his sons; outstrip the Pharian gift.
9.1.340: ' Nor spare this head, which, laid before the feet

9.1.342: 'A full reward. Thus, cowards, shall ye learn
9.1.343: ' In that ye followed me how great your gain.
9.1.344: ' Quick to your task and purchase thus with blood
9.1.345: 'Your claim on Caesar. 'Tis a dastard crime;
9.1.348: The parting vessels. So when bees in swarm

9.1.386: When first the billows to the fleet gave way,

9.1.397: Of ocean; others lightened of their masts
9.1.398: Shook off the tempest; but a sweeping tide
9.1.399: Hurried them southwards, victor of the gale.
9.1.400: Some freed of shallows on a bank were forced
9.1.401: Which broke the deep: their ship in part was fast,
9.1.402: Part hanging on the sea; their fates in doubt.
9.1.403: Fierce rage the waves till hems them in the land;
9.1.404: Nor Auster's force in frequent buffets spent
9.1.405: Prevails upon the shore. High from the main,
9.1.406: By seas inviolate, one bank of sand
9.1.407: Far from the coast arose; there watched in vain

9.1.410: Some portion, but the major part by helm
9.1.411: And rudder guided, and by pilots' hands
9.1.412: Who knew the devious channels, safe at length
9.1.413: Floated the marsh of Triton loved (as saith
9.1.414: The fable) by that god, whose sounding shell
9.1.415: All seas and shores re-echo; and by her,
9.1.416: Pallas, who springing from her father's head
9.1.417: First lit on Libya, nearest land to heaven,
9.1.418: (As by its heat is proved); here on the brink
9.1.419: She stood, reflected in the placid wave
9.1.420: And called herself Tritonis. Lethe's flood
9.1.421: Flows silent near, in fable from a source

9.1.423: Here, too, that garden of the Hesperids,
9.1.424: Its boughs all golden, where of old his watch
9.1.425: The sleepless dragon held. Shame be on him
9.1.426: Who calls upon the poet for the proof
9.1.427: Of that which in the ancient days befell;
9.1.428: But here were golden groves by yellow growth
9.1.429: Weighed down in richness, here a maiden band
9.1.430: Were guardians; and a serpent, on whose eyes
9.1.431: Sleep never fell, was coiled around the trees,
9.1.432: Whose branches bowed beneath their ruddy load.
9.1.433: But great Alcides stripped the goodly boughs
9.1.434: Of all their riches, left them poor and light,
9.1.435: And bore the shining fruit to Argos' king.
9.1.436: Driven on the Libyan realms, more fruitful here,
9.1.437: Pompeius stayed the fleet, nor further dared
9.1.438: To Garamantian waves. But Cato's soul
9.1.439: Leaped in his breast, impatient of delay,
9.1.440: To pass the Syrtes by a landward march,
9.1.441: And trusting to their swords, 'gainst tribes unknown
9.1.442: To lead his legions. And the storm which closed
9.1.443: The main to navies gave them hope of rain;
9.1.444: Nor biting frosts they feared, in Libyan clime;
9.1.445: Nor suns too scorching in the falling year.
9.1.446: Thus ere they trod the deserts, Cato spake:
9.1.447: ' Ye men of Rome, who through mine arms alone
9.1.448: ' Can find the death ye covet, and shall fall
9.1.449: ' With pride unbroken should the fates command,
9.1.450: ' Meet this your weighty task, your high emprise
9.1.451: ' With hearts resolved to conquer. For we march
9.1.452: ' On sterile wastes, burnt regions of the world;
9.1.453: ' Scarce are the wells, and Titan from the height
9.1.454: ' Burns pitiless, unclouded; and the slime
9.1.455: ' Of poisonous serpents fouls the dusty earth.
9.1.456: ' Yet shall men venture for the love of laws
9.1.457: ' And country perishing, upon the sands
9.1.458: ' Of trackless Libya; men who brave in soul
9.1.459: ' Rely not on the end, and in attempt
9.1.460: ' Will risk their all. 'Tis not in Cato's thoughts
9.1.461: ' On this our enterprise to lead a band
9.1.462: ' Blind to the truth, unwitting of the risk.
9.1.463: ' Nay, give me comrades for the danger's sake,
9.1.464: ' Whom I shall see for honour and for Rome
9.1.465: ' Bear up against the worst. But whoso needs
9.1.466: ' A pledge of safety, to whom life is sweet,
9.1.467: ' Let him by fairer journey seek his lord.
9.1.468: ' First be my foot upon the sand; on me
9.1.469: ' First strike the burning sun; across my path
9.1.470: ' The serpent void his venom; by my fate
9.1.471: ' Know ye your perils. Let him only thirst
9.1.472: ' Who sees me at the spring: who sees me seek
9.1.473: ' The shade, alone sink fainting in the heat;
9.1.474: ' Or whoso sees me ride before the ranks
9.1.475: ' Plodding their weary march: such be the lot
9.1.476: ' Of each, who, toiling, finds in me a chief
9.1.477: ' And not a comrade. Snakes, thirst, burning sand
9.1.478: 'The brave man welcomes, and the patient breast
9.1.479: ' Finds happiness in labour. By its cost
9.1.480: ' Courage is sweeter; and this Libyan land
9.1.481: ' Such cloud of ills can furnish as might make
9.1.482: 'Men flee unshamed.' 'Twas thus that Cato spake,
9.1.483: Kindling the torch of valour and the love
9.1.484: Of toil: then reckless of his fate he strode
9.1.485: The desert path from which was no return:
9.1.486: And Libya ruled his destinies, to shut
9.1.487: His sacred name within a narrow tomb.
9.1.488: One-third of all the world, if fame we trust,
9.1.489: Is Libya; yet by winds and sky she proves
9.1.490: Equal to Europe; for the shores of Nile
9.1.491: No more than Scythian Tanais are remote
9.1.492: From furthest Gades, where with bending coast,
9.1.493: Yielding a place to Ocean, Europe parts
9.1.494: From Afric shores. Yet falls the larger world
9.1.495: To Asia only. From the former two
9.1.496: Issues the Western wind; but Asia's right
9.1.497: Touches the Southern limits and her left
9.1.498: The Northern tempest's home, and of the East
9.1.499: She's mistress to the rising of the Sun.
9.1.500: All that is fertile of the Afric lands
9.1.501: Lies to the west, but even here abound
9.1.502: No wells of water: though the Northern wind,
9.1.503: Infrequent, leaving us with skies serene,
9.1.504: Falls there in showers. Not gold nor wealth of brass
9.1.505: It yields the seeker; pure and unalloyed
9.1.506: Down to its lowest depths is Libyan soil.
9.1.507: Yet citron forests to Maurusian tribes
9.1.508: Were riches, had they known; but they, content,
9.1.509: Lived 'neath the shady foliage, till gleamed
9.1.510: The axe of Rome amid the virgin grove,
9.1.511: To bring from furthest limits of the world
9.1.512: Our banquet tables and the fruit they bear.
9.1.513: But suns excessive and a scorching clime
9.1.514: Burn all the glebe beside the shifting sands:
9.1.515: There die the harvests on the crumbling mould;
9.1.516: No root finds sustenance, nor kindly Jove
9.1.517: Makes rich the furrow nor matures the vine.
9.1.518: Sleep binds all nature and the tract of sand
9.1.519: Lies ever fruitless, save that by the coast
9.1.520: The hardy Nasamon plucks a scanty grass.
9.1.521: Unclothed their race, and living on the woes
9.1.522: Worked by the cruel Syrtes on the world.
9.1.523: He dwells a spoiler by the sandy waves,
9.1.524: And while no ships unlade upon his shore,
9.1.525: Grows rich by wrecks-his only trade with man.
9.1.526: By such a path at hardy Cato's word

9.1.529: More than on ocean waves; for Auster's force

9.1.531: And yet more fraught with mischief: neither crags
9.1.532: Repelled his strength, nor lofty mountains tamed

9.1.535: O'er the defenceless earth. Nor merely dust

9.1.540: Reft by the tempest, and the native huts
9.1.541: From roof to base were hurried on the blast.
9.1.542: Not higher, when some all-devouring flame
9.1.543: Has seized upon its prey, in volumes dense

9.1.552: By not resisting stood, and blasts that whirled

9.1.556: Through all the regions of the boundless sky;
