9.1.558: Where men may fear the weapons from the heaven
9.1.559: There falling, as the armour of the gods,
9.1.560: Nor deem them ravished from a soldier's arm.
9.1.561: 'Twas thus on Numa by the sacred fire
9.1.562: Those shields descended which our chosen priests
9.1.563: Bear on their shoulders; from some warlike race
9.1.564: By tempest rapt, to be the prize of Rome.
9.1.565: While thus the tempest whirled the earth aloft
9.1.566: Prone fell the host, and wound their garments tight,
9.1.567: And gripped the soil; but hardly thus prevailed.
9.1.568: Weight had not held them safe; the raging blast
9.1.569: Piles heaps upon them, their recumbent limbs
9.1.570: Are whelmed in sand. At length they struggling rose
9.1.571: Back to their feet, when lo! around them stood,
9.1.572: Forced by the storm, a growing bank of earth
9.1.573: Which held them motionless. And from afar
9.1.574: Where walls lay prostrate, mighty stones were hurled,
9.1.575: Thus piling ills on ills in wondrous form:
9.1.576: No dwellings had they seen, yet at their feet
9.1.577: Beheld the ruins. All the earth was hid
9.1.578: In vast envelopment, nor found they guide
9.1.579: Save from the stars, which as in middle deep
9.1.580: Flamed o'er them wandering: yet some were hid
9.1.581: Beneath the circle of the Libyan earth
9.1.582: Which tending downwards hid the Northern sky.
9.1.583: When warmth dispersed the tempest-driven air,
9.1.584: And rose upon the earth the flaming day,
9.1.585: Bathed were their limbs in sweat, but parched and dry
9.1.586: Their gaping lips; when to a scanty spring
9.1.587: Far off beheld they came, whose meagre drops
9.1.588: All gathered in the hollow of a helm
9.1.589: They offered to their chief. Caked were their throats
9.1.590: With dust, and panting; and one little drop
9.1.591: Had made him envied. 'Wretch, and dost thou deem
9.1.592: Me wanting in a brave man's heart? ' he cried,
9.1.593: ' Me only in this throng? And have I seemed
9.1.594: 'Tender, unfit to bear the morning heat?
9.1.595: He who would quench his thirst 'mid such a host,
9.1.596: 'Doth most deserve its pangs.' Then in his wrath
9.1.597: Dashed down the helmet, and the scanty spring,
9.1.598: Thus by their leader spurned, sufficed for all.
9.1.599: Now had they reached that temple which possess,
9.1.600: Sole in all Libya, th' untutored tribes
9.1.601: Of Garamantians. Here holds his seat
9.1.602: (So saith the story) a prophetic Jove,
9.1.603: Wielding no thunderbolts, nor like to ours;
9.1.604: The Libyan Hammon of the curved horn.
9.1.605: No wealth adorns his fane by Afric tribes
9.1.606: Bestowed, nor glittering hoard of Eastern gems.
9.1.607: Though rich Arabians, Ind and Ethiop
9.1.608: Know him alone as Jove, still he is poor
9.1.609: Holding his shrine by riches undefiled
9.1.610: Through time; and pure as gods of olden days
9.1.611: He spurns the wealth of Rome. That here sone god
9.1.613: That buds in Libya-for that which grows
9.1.614: Upon the arid dust which Leptis parts
9.1.615: From Berenice, knows no leaves; alone
9.1.616: Hammon uprears a wood; a fount the cause
9.1.617: Which with its waters binds the crumbling soil.
9.1.618: Yet shall the Sun when poised upon the height
9.1.619: Strike through the foliage: hardly can the tree
9.1.620: Protect its trunk, and to a little space
9.1.621: His rays draw in the circle of the shade.
9.1.622: Here have men found the spot where that high band
9.1.624: The zodiac stars: not here oblique their course,
9.1.625: Nor Scorpion rises straighter than the Bull,
9.1.626: Nor to the Scales does Ram give back his hours,
9.1.627: Nor does Astraea bid the Fishes sink
9.1.628: More slowly down: but watery Capricorn
9.1.629: Is equal with the Crab, and with the Twins
9.1.630: The Archer; neither does the Lion rise
9.1.631: Above Aquarius. But the race that dwells
9.1.632: Beyond the fervour of the Libyan fires
9.1.633: Sees to the South that shadow which with us
9.1.634: Falls to the North: slow Cynosura sinks
9.1.635: For them below the deep; and, dry with us,
9.1.636: The Wagon plunges; far from either pole,
9.1.637: No star they know that does not seek the nain,
9.1.638: But all the constellations in their course
9.1.639: Whirl to their vision through the middle sky.
9.1.640: Before the doors the Eastern peoples stood
9.1.641: Seeking from horned Jove to know their fates:
9.1.642: Yet to the Roman chief they yielded place,
9.1.643: Whose comrades prayed him to entreat the gods
9.1.644: Famed through the Libyan world, and judge the voice
9.1.645: Renowned from distant ages. First of these
9.1.647: 'The voice and counsel of this mighty god
9.1.648: 'Has offered as we march; from such a guide
9.1.649: 'To know the issues of the war, and learn
9.1.650: 'To track the Syrtes. For to whom on earth
9.1.651: 'If not to blameless Cato, shall the gods
9.1.652: Entrust their secret truths? Thou at the least
9.1.653: 'Their faithful follower through life hast been.
9.1.654: 'Lo! thou hast liberty to speak with Jove.
9.1.655: Ask impious Caesar's fates, and learn the laws
9.1.656: 'That wait our country in the future days:
9.1.657: 'Whether the people shall be free to use
9.1.658: 'Their rights and customs, or the civil war
9.1.659: 'For us is wasted. To thy sacred breast,
9.1.660: 'Lover of virtue, take the voice divine;
9.1.661: 'Demand what virtue is and guide thy steps
9.1.664: Of godlike thoughts borne in his quiet breast,
9.1.665: This answer uttered, worthy of the shrines:
9.1.666: 'What, Labienus, dost thou bid me ask?
9.1.667: 'Whether in arms and freedom I should wish
9.1.668: ' To perish, rather than endure a king?
9.1.669: ' Is longest life worth aught? And doth its term
9.1.670: ' Make difference? Can violence to the good
9.1.671: Do injury? Do Fortune's threats avail
9.1.672: Outweighed by virtue? Doth it not suffice
9.1.673: To aim at deeds of bravery? Can fame
9.1.674: Grow by achievement? Nay! No Hammon's voice
9.1.675: Shall teach us this more surely than we know.
9.1.676: Bound are we to the gods; no voice we need;
9.1.677: They live in all our acts, although the shrine
9.1.678: Be silent: at our birth and once for all
9.1.679: What may be known the author of our being
9.1.680: Revealed; nor chose these thirsty sands to chaunt
9.1.681: 'To few his truth, whelmed in the dusty waste.
9.1.682: God has his dwelling in all things that be,
9.1.683: In earth and air and sea and starry vault,
9.1.684: In virtuous deeds; in all that thou canst see,
9.1.685: In all thy thoughts contained. Why further, then,
9.1.686: Seek we our deities? Let those who doubt
9.1.687: And halting, tremble for their coming fates,
9.1.688: Go ask the oracles. No mystic words,
9.1.689: Make sure my heart, but surely coming Death.
9.1.690: " Coward alike and brave, we all must die.
9.1.691: Thus hath Jove spoken: seek to know no more.'
9.1.692: Thus Cato spoke, and faithful to his creed
9.1.693: He parted from the temple of the god
9.1.694: And left the oracle of Hammon dumb.
9.1.695: Bearing his javelin, as one of them
9.1.696: He strode afoot before the panting troops:
9.1.697: No bending neck, no litter bore his form.
9.1.698: He bade them not, but showed them how to toil.
9.1.699: Spare in his sleep, the last to sip the spring,
9.1.700: When at some rivulet to quench their thirst
9.1.701: The eager ranks pressed onward, he alone
9.1.702: Until the humblest follower might drink
9.1.703: Stood motionless. If for the truly good
9.1.704: Is fame, and virtue by the deed itself,
9.1.705: Not by successful issue, should be judged,
9.1.706: Yield, famous ancestors! Fortune, not worth
9.1.707: Gained you your glory. But such name as his
9.1.708: Who ever merited by successful war
9.1.709: Or slaughtered peoples? Rather would I lead
9.1.710: With him his triumphs through the pathless sands
9.1.711: And Libya's bounds, than in Pompeius' car
9.1.712: Three times ascend the Capitol, or break
9.1.713: The proud Jugurtha. Rome! in him behold
9.1.714: His country's father, worthiest of thy vows;
9.1.715: A name by which men shall not blush to swear,
9.1.716: Whom, shouldst thou break the fetters from thy neck,
9.1.717: Thou mayst in distant days decree divine.
9.1.718: Now was the heat more dense, and through that clime
9.1.719: Than which no further on the Southern side
9.1.720: The gods permit, they trod; and scarcer still
9.1.721: The water, till in middle sands they found
9.1.722: One copious fountain; but its brimming wave
9.1.723: Was thronged with serpents which it hardly held,
9.1.724: And thirsty asps were pressing on the marge.
9.1.725: But when the chieftain saw that speedy fate
9.1.726: Was on the host, if they should leave the well
9.1.727: Untasted, ' Vain,' he cried, your fear of death.
9.1.728: ' Drink, nor delay: 'tis from the threatening tooth
9.1.729: " Men draw their deaths, and fatal from the fang
9.1.730: ' Issues the juice if mingled with the blood;
9.1.731: ' The cup is harmless.' Then he sipped the fount,
9.1.732: Still doubting, and in all the Libyan waste
9.1.733: There only was he first to touch the stream.
9.1.734: Why fertile thus in death the pestilent air
9.1.735: Of Libya, what poison in her soil
9.1.736: Her several nature mixed, my care to know
9.1.737: Has not availed: but from the days of old
9.1.738: A fabled story has deceived the world.
9.1.739: Far on her limits, where the burning shore
9.1.740: Admits the ocean fervid from the sun
9.1.741: Plunged in its waters, lay Medusa's fields
9.1.742: Untilled; nor forests shaded, nor the plough
9.1.743: Furrowed the soil, which by its mistress' gaze
9.1.744: Was hardened into stone: Phorcus, her sire.
9.1.745: Malevolent nature from her body first
9.1.746: Drew forth these noisome pests; first from her jaws
9.1.747: Issued the sibilant rattle of serpent tongues;
9.1.748: Clustered around her head the poisonous brood
9.1.749: Like to a woman's hair, wreathed on her neck
9.1.750: Which gloried in their touch; their glittering heads
9.1.751: Advanced towards her; and her tresses kempt
9.1.752: Dripped down with viper's venom. This alone
9.1.753: Thou hast, accursed one, which men can see
9.1.754: Unharmed; for who upon that gaping mouth
9.1.755: Looked and could dread? Whom suffered she to die
9.1.756: Who saw her face? He rushed upon his fate
9.1.757: And ere he feared was stricken to the death.
9.1.758: Perished the limbs while living, and the soul
9.1.759: Grew stiff and stark ere yet it fled the frame.
9.1.760: Men have been frenzied by the Furies' locks,
9.1.761: Not killed; and Cerberus at Orpheus' song
9.1.762: Ceased from his hissing, and Alcides saw
9.1.763: The Hydra ere he slew. This monster born
9.1.764: Brought horror with her birth upon her sire
9.1.765: Phorcus, in second order God of Waves,
9.1.766: And upon Ceto and the Gorgon brood,
9.1.767: Her sisters. She could treat the sea and sky
9.1.768: With deadly calm unknown, and from the world
9.1.769: Bid cease the soil. Borne down by instant weight
9.1.770: Fowls fell from air, and beasts were fixed in stone.
9.1.771: Whole Ethiop tribes who tilled the neighbouring lands
9.1.772: Rigid in marble stood. The Gorgon sight
9.1.773: No creature bore and even her serpents turned
9.1.774: Back from her visage. Atlas in his place
9.1.775: Beside the Western columns, by her look
9.1.776: Was turned to granite; and when Phlegra's brood
9.1.777: Gigantic, serpent-tailed, were feared of heaven,
9.1.778: She made them mountains, and the Gorgon head
9.1.779: Borne on Athena's bosom closed the war.
9.1.780: Here born of Danae and the golden shower,
9.1.781: Floating on wings Parrhasian, by the god
9.1.782: Arcadian given, author of the lyre
9.1.783: And wrestling art, came Perseus, swooping down
9.1.784: From heaven. Cyllenian Harpe did he bear
9.1.785: Still crimson from another monster slain,
9.1.786: The guardian of the heifer loved by Jove.
9.1.787: This to her winged brother Pallas lent
9.1.788: Price of the monster's head: by her command
9.1.789: He sought the limits of the Libyan land,
9.1.790: Poised o'er Medusa's realm, with head averse
9.1.791: Towards the rising sun: a burnished shield
9.1.792: Of yellow brass upon his other arm,
9.1.793: Her gift, her bore: in which she bade him see
9.1.794: The fatal face unscathed. Nor yet in sleep
9.1.795: Lay all the monster, for such total rest
9.1.796: To her were death-so fated: serpent locks
9.1.797: In vigilant watch, some reaching forth defend
9.1.798: Her head, while others lay upon her face
9.1.799: And slumbering eyes. Then hero Perseus shook
9.1.800: Though turned averse; trembled his dexter hand:
9.1.801: But Pallas held, and the descending blade
9.1.802: Shore the broad neck whence sprang the viper brood.
9.1.803: What visage bore the Gorgon as the steel
9.1.804: Thus reft her life! what poison from her throat
9.1.805: Breathed! from her eyes what venom of death distilled!
9.1.806: The goddess dared not look, and Perseus' face
9.1.807: Had frozen, averse, had not Athena veiled
9.1.808: With coils of writhing snakes the features dead.
9.1.809: Then with the Gorgon head the hero flew
9.1.810: Uplifted on his wings and sought the sky.
9.1.811: Shorter had been his voyage through the midst
9.1.812: Of Europe's cities; but Athena bade
9.1.813: To spare her peoples and their fruitful lands;
9.1.814: For who when such an airy courser passed
9.1.815: Had not looked up to heaven? Western winds
9.1.816: Now sped his pinions, and he took his course
9.1.817: O'er Libya's regions, from the stars and suns
9.1.818: Veiled by no culture. Phoebus' nearer track
9.1.819: There burns the soil, and loftiest on the sky
9.1.820: There falls the night, to shade the wandering moon,
9.1.821: If e'er forgetful of her course oblique,
9.1.822: Straight through the stars, nor bending to the North
9.1.823: Nor to the South, she hastens. Yet that earth,
9.1.824: In nothing fertile, void of fruitful yield,
9.1.825: Drank in the poison of Medusa's blood,
9.1.826: Dripping in dreadful dews upon the soil,
9.1.827: And in the crumbling sands by heat matured.
9.1.828: Where first within the dust the venom germ
9.1.829: Took life, an asp was reared of turgid neck
9.1.830: And sleep compelling: thick the poison drop
9.1.831: That was his making, in no fang of snake
9.1.832: More closely pressed. Greedy of warmth it seeks
9.1.833: No frozen world itself, nor haunts the sands
9.1.834: Beyond the Nile; yet has our thirst of gain
9.1.835: No shame nor limit, and this Libyan death,
9.1.836: This fatal pest we purchase for our own.
9.1.837: Haemorrhois huge spreads out his scaly coils,
9.1.838: Who suffers not his hapless victims' blood
9.1.839: To stay within their veins. Chersydros sprang
9.1.840: To life, to dwell within the doubtful marsh
9.1.841: Where land nor sea prevails. A cloud of spray
9.1.842: Marked fell Chelyder's track: and Cenchris rose
9.1.843: Straight gliding to his prey, his belly tinged
9.1.844: With various spots unnumbered, more than those
9.1.845: Which paint the Theban marble; horned snakes
9.1.846: With spines contorted: like to torrid sand
9.1.848: Sole of all serpents Scytale to shed
9.1.849: In vernal frosts his slough; and thirsty Dipsas;
9.1.850: Dread Amphisbaena with his double head
9.1.851: Tapering; and Natrix who in bubbling fount
9.1.852: Fuses his venom. Greedy Prester swells
9.1.853: His foaming jaws; Pareas, head erect
9.1.854: Furrows with tail alone his sandy path;
9.1.855: Swift Jaculus there, and Seps whose poisonous juice
9.1.856: Makes liquid bone and flesh: and there upreared
9.1.857: His regal head, and frighted from his track
9.1.858: With sibilant terror all the subject swarm,
9.1.859: Baneful ere darts his poison, Basilisk
9.1.860: In sands deserted king. Ye serpents too
9.1.861: Who in all other regions harmless glide
9.1.862: Adored as gods, and bright with golden scales,
9.1.863: Are deadly here: for Afric air inhaled
9.1.864: Bestows malignant gift, as poised on wings
9.1.865: Whole herds of kine ye follow, and with coils
9.1.866: Encircling close, crush in the mighty bull.
9.1.867: Nor does the elephant in his giant bulk,
9.1.868: Nor aught, find safety; and ye need no fang
9.1.869: Nor poison, to compel the fatal end.
9.1.870: Amid these pests undaunted Cato urged
9.1.871: His desert journey on. His hardy troops
9.1.872: Beneath his eyes, pricked by a scanty wound,
9.1.873: In strangest forms of death unnumbered fall.
9.1.874: Tyrrhenian Aulus, bearer of a flag,
9.1.875: Trod on a Dipsas; quick with head reversed
9.1.876: The serpent struck; no mark betrayed the tooth:
9.1.877: The aspect of the wound nor threatened death,
9.1.878: Nor any evil; but the poison germ
9.1.879: In silence working as consuming fire
9.1.880: Absorbed the moisture of his inward frame,
9.1.881: Draining the natural juices that were spread
9.1.882: Around his vitals; in his arid jaws
9.1.883: Set flame upon his tongue: his wearied limbs
9.1.884: No sweat bedewed; dried up, the fount of tears
9.1.885: Fled from his eyelids. Tortured by the fire
9.1.886: Nor Cato's sternness, nor of his sacred charge
9.1.887: The honour could withhold him; but he dared
9.1.888: To dash his standard down, and through the plains
9.1.889: Raging, to seek for water that might slake
9.1.890: The fatal venom thirsting at his heart.
9.1.891: Plunge him in Tanais, in Rhone and Po,
9.1.892: Pour on his burning tongue the flood of Nile,
9.1.893: Yet were the fire unquenched. So fell the fang
9.1.894: Of Dipsas in the torrid Libyan lands;
9.1.895: In other climes less fatal. Next he seeks
9.1.896: Amid the sands, all barren to the depths,
9.1.897: For moisture: then returning to the shoals
9.1.898: Laps them with greed-in vain-the briny draught
9.1.899: Scarce quenched the thirst it made. Nor knowing yet
9.1.900: The poison in his frame, he steels himself
9.1.901: To rip his swollen veins and drink the gore.
9.1.902: Cato bids lift the standard, lest his troops
9.1.903: May find in thirst a pardon for the deed.
9.1.904: But on Sabellus' yet more piteous death
9.1.905: Their eyes were fastened. Clinging to his skin
9.1.906: A Seps with curving tooth, of little size,
9.1.907: He seized and tore away, and to the sands
9.1.908: Pierced with his javelin. Small the serpent's bulk;
9.1.909: None deals a death more horrible in form.
9.1.910: For swift the flesh dissolving round the wound
9.1.911: Bared the pale bone; swam all his limbs in blood;
9.1.912: Wasted the tissue of his calves and knees:
9.1.913: And all the muscles of his thighs were thawed
9.1.914: In black distilment, and the membrane sheath
9.1.915: Parted, that bound his vitals, which abroad
9.1.916: Flowed upon earth: yet seemed it not that all
9.1.917: His frame was loosed, for by the venomous drop
9.1.918: Were all the bands that held his muscles drawn
9.1.919: Down to a juice; the framework of his chest
9.1.920: Was bare, its cavity, and all the parts
9.1.921: Hid by the organs of life, that make the man.
9.1.922: So by unholy death there stood revealed
9.1.923: His inmost nature. Head and stalwart arms,
9.1.924: And neck and shoulders, from their solid mass
9.1.925: Melt in corruption. Not more swiftly flows
9.1.926: Wax at the sun's command, nor snow compelled
9.1.927: By southern breezes. Yet not all is said:
9.1.928: For so to noxious humours fire consumes
9.1.929: Our fleshly frame; but on the funeral pyre
9.1.930: What bones have perished? These dissolve no less
9.1.931: Than did the mouldered tissues, nor of death
9.1.932: Thus swift is left a trace. Of Afric pests
9.1.933: Thou bear'st the palm for hurtfulness: the life
9.1.934: They snatch away, thou only with the life
9.1.937: Not this by melting! for a Prester's fang
9.1.938: Nasidius struck, who erst in Marsian fields
9.1.939: Guided the plough. Upon his face there burns
9.1.940: A redness as of flame: swollen the skin,
9.1.941: His features hidden, swollen all his limbs
9.1.942: Till more than human: and his definite frame
9.1.943: One tumour huge conceals. A ghastly gore
9.1.944: Is puffed from inwards as the virulent juice
9.1.945: Courses through all his body; which, thus grown,
9.1.946: His corselet holds not. Not in caldron so
9.1.947: Boils up to mountainous height the steaming wave;
9.1.948: Nor in such bellying curves does canvas bend
9.1.949: To Eastern tempests. Now the ponderous bulk
9.1.950: Rejects the limbs, and as a shapeless trunk
9.1.951: Burdens the earth: and there, to beasts and birds
9.1.952: A fatal feast, his comrades leave the corse;
9.1.953: Nor dare to place, yet swelling, in the tomb.
9.1.954: But for their eyes the Libyan pests prepared
9.1.955: More dreadful sights. On Tullus great in heart,
9.1.956: And bound to Cato with admiring soul,
9.1.957: A fierce Haemorrhois fixed. From every limb,
9.1.958: (As from a statue saffron spray is showered
9.1.959: In every part) there spouted forth for blood
9.1.960: A sable poison: from the natural pores
9.1.961: Of moisture, gore profuse; his mouth was filled
9.1.962: And gaping nostrils, and his tears were blood.
9.1.963: Brimmed full his veins; his very sweat was red;
9.1.966: In sleep was victim, for around his heart
9.1.967: Stood still the blood congealed: no pain he felt
9.1.968: Of venomous tooth, but swift upon him fell
9.1.969: Death, and he sought the shades; more swift to kill
9.1.970: No draught in poisonous cups from ripened plants
9.1.971: Of direst growth Sabaean wizards brew.
9.1.972: Lo! Upon branchless trunk a serpent, named
9.1.973: By Libyans Jaculus, rose in coils to dart
9.1.974: His venom from afar. Through Paullus' brain
9.1.975: It rushed, nor stayed; for in the wound itself
9.1.976: Was death. Then did they know how slowly flies,
9.1.977: Flung from a sling, the stone; how gently speed
9.1.978: Through air the shafts of Scythia. What availed,
9.1.979: Murrus, the lance by which thou didst transfix
9.1.980: A Basilisk? Swift through the weapon ran
9.1.981: The poison to his hand: he drew his sword
9.1.982: And severed arm and shoulder at a blow:
9.1.983: Then gazed secure upon his severed hand
9.1.984: Which perished as he looked. So hadst thou died,
9.1.985: And such had been thy fate!
9.1.987: A scorpion had strength o'er death and fate?
9.1.988: Yet with his threatening coils and barb erect
9.1.989: He won the glory of Orion slain;
9.1.990: So bear the stars their witness. And who would fear
9.1.991: Thy haunts, Salpuga? Yet the Stygian Maids
9.1.992: Have given thee power to snap the fatal threads.
9.1.993: Thus nor the day with brightness, nor the night
9.1.994: With darkness gave them peace. The very earth
9.1.995: On which they lay they feared; nor leaves nor straw
9.1.996: They piled for couches, but upon the ground
9.1.997: Unshielded from the fates they laid their limbs,
9.1.998: Cherished beneath whose warmth in chill of night
9.1.999: The frozen pests found shelter; in whose jaws
9.1.1000: Harmless the while, the lurking venom slept.
9.1.1001: Nor did they know the measure of their march
9.1.1002: Accomplished, nor their path; the stars in heaven
9.1.1003: Their only guide. ' Return, ye gods,' they cried,
9.1.1004: In frequent wail, ' the arms from which we fled.
9.1.1005: ' Give back Thessalia. Sworn to meet the sword
9.1.1006: ' Why, lingering, fall we thus? In Caesar's place
9.1.1007: ' The thirsty Dipsas and the horned snake
9.1.1008: ' Now wage the warfare. Rather let us seek
9.1.1009: ' That region by the horses of the sun
9.1.1010: ' Scorched, and the zone most torrid: let us fall
9.1.1011: 'Slain by some heavenly cause, and from the sky
9.1.1012: ' Descend our fate! Not, Africa, of thee
9.1.1013: ' Complain we, nor of Nature. From mankind
9.1.1014: ' Cut off, this quarter, teeming thus with pests
9.1.1015: ' She gave to snakes, and to the barren fields
9.1.1016: ' Denied the husbandman, nor wished that men
9.1.1017: 'Should perish by their venom. To the realms
9.1.1018: ' Of serpents have we come. Hater of men,
9.1.1019: ' Receive thy vengeance, whoso of the gods
9.1.1020: ' Severed this region upon either hand,
9.1.1021: ' With death in middle space. Our march is set
9.1.1022: 'Through thy sequestered kingdom, and the host
9.1.1023: ' Which knows thy secret seeks the furthest world.
9.1.1024: ' Perchance some greater wonders on our path
9.1.1025: ' May still await us; in the waves be plunged
9.1.1026: ' Heaven's constellations, and the lofty pole
9.1.1027: 'Stoop from its height. By further space removed
9.1.1028: ' No land, than Juba's realm; by rumour's voice
9.1.1029: ' Drear, mournful. Haply for this serpent land
9.1.1030: ' There may we long, where yet some living thing
9.1.1031: ' Gives consolation. Not my native land
9.1.1032: ' Nor European fields I hope for now
9.1.1033: ' Lit by far other suns, nor Asia's plains.
9.1.1034: ' But in what land, what region of the sky,
9.1.1035: ' Where left we Africa? But now with frosts
9.1.1036: ' Cyrene stiffened: have we changed the laws
9.1.1037: ' Which rule the seasons, in this little space?
9.1.1038: ' Cast from the world we know, 'neath other skies
9.1.1039: ' And stars we tread; behind our backs the home
9.1.1040: ' Of southern tempests: Rome herself perchance
9.1.1041: ' Now lies beneath our feet. Yet for our fates
9.1.1042: ' This solace pray we, that on this our track
9.1.1043: ' Pursuing Caesar with his host may come.'
9.1.1044: Thus was their stubborn patience of its plaints
9.1.1045: Disburdened. But the bravery of their chief
9.1.1046: Forced them to bear their toils. Upon the sand,
9.1.1047: All bare, he lies and dares at every hour
9.1.1048: Fortune to strike: he only at the fate
9.1.1049: Of each was present, flew to every call;
9.1.1050: And roused their hearts to fight the poison germ.
9.1.1051: Not life he brings them, but the strength in death
9.1.1052: To die without a groan-to groan were shame
9.1.1053: When he was witness-over him what power
9.1.1054: Had plague or venom? In a comrade's breast
9.1.1055: They see him conquer anguish; and they learn,
9.1.1056: Gazing on him, how weak the power of pain.
9.1.1057: Some aid from Fortune, weary of their woes,
9.1.1058: At length they gained. Of all who till the earth
9.1.1059: The Psyllians only are by snakes unharmed.
9.1.1060: Potent as herbs their song; safe is their blood,
9.1.1061: Nor gives admission to the poison germ
9.1.1062: E'en when the chant has ceased. Their home itself
9.1.1063: Placed in such venomous tract and serpent-thronged
9.1.1064: Gained them this vantage, and a truce with death,
9.1.1065: Else could they not have lived. Such is their trust
9.1.1066: In purity of blood, that newly born
9.1.1067: Each babe they prove by test of deadly asp
9.1.1068: For foreign lineage. So the bird of Jove
9.1.1069: Turns his new fledglings to the rising sun
9.1.1070: And such as gaze upon the beams of day
9.1.1071: With eyes unwavering, for the use of heaven
9.1.1072: He rears; but such as blink at Phoebus' rays
9.1.1073: Casts from the nest. Thus of unmixed descent
9.1.1074: The babe who, dreading not the serpent touch,
9.1.1075: Plays in his cradle with the deadly snake.
9.1.1076: Nor with their own immunity from harm
9.1.1077: Contented do they rest, but watch for guests
9.1.1078: Who need their help against the noisome plague.
9.1.1079: Now to the Roman standards are they come,
9.1.1080: And when the chieftain bade the tents be fixed,
9.1.1081: First all the sandy space within the lines
9.1.1082: With song they purify and magic words
9.1.1083: From which all serpents flee: next round the camp
9.1.1084: In widest circuit from a kindled fire
9.1.1086: And juice distils from Syrian galbanum;
9.1.1087: Then mournful tamarisk, costum from the East,
9.1.1089: From Thrace, and leaves of fennel feed the flames,
9.1.1090: And thapsus brought from Eryx: and they burn
9.1.1091: Larch, southern-wood and antlers of a deer
9.1.1092: Which lived afar. From these in densest fumes,
9.1.1093: Deadly to snakes, a pungent smoke arose;
9.1.1094: And thus in safety passed the night away.
9.1.1095: But should some victim feel the fatal fang
9.1.1096: Upon the march, then of this magic race
9.1.1097: Were seen the wonders; with saliva first
9.1.1098: They smear the limb, whose silent working keeps
9.1.1099: The venom in the wound. From foaming mouth
9.1.1100: Next with continuous cadence would they pour
9.1.1101: Unceasing chants-nor breathing space nor pause-
9.1.1102: Else spreads the poison: nor does fate permit
9.1.1103: A moment's silence. Oft from the black flesh
9.1.1104: Flies forth the pest beneath the magic song:
9.1.1105: But should it linger nor obey the voice,
9.1.1106: Repugnant to the summons, on the wound
9.1.1107: Prostrate they lay their lips and from the depths
9.1.1108: Now paling draw the venom. In their mouths,
9.1.1109: Sucked from the freezing flesh, they hold the death,
9.1.1110: Then spew it forth; and from the taste shall know
9.1.1111: The nature of the snake whose bite they cure.
9.1.1112: Thus helped, the Roman host with lighter heart
9.1.1113: Trod through the barren fields in lengthy march.
9.1.1114: Twice veiled the moon her light and twice renewed;
9.1.1115: Yet still, with waning or with growing orb
9.1.1116: Saw Cato's steps upon the sandy waste.
9.1.1117: But more and more beneath their feet the dust
9.1.1118: Began to harden, till the Libyan tracts
9.1.1119: Once more were earth, and in the distance rose
9.1.1120: Some groves of scanty foliage, and huts
9.1.1121: Of plastered straw unfashioned: and their hearts
9.1.1122: Leaped at the prospect of a better land.
9.1.1123: How fled their sorrow! how with growing joy
9.1.1124: They met the savage lion in the path!
9.1.1125: In tranquil Leptis first they found retreat:
9.1.1126: And passed a winter free from heat and rain.
9.1.1127: When Caesar sated with Emathia's slain
9.1.1128: Forsook the battlefield, all other cares
9.1.1129: Neglected, he pursued his kinsman fled,
9.1.1130: On him alone intent: by land his steps
9.1.1131: He traced in vain; then, rumour for his guide,
9.1.1132: He crossed the sea and reached the Thracian strait
9.1.1133: For love renowned; where on the mournful shore
9.1.1134: Rose Hero's tower, and Helle born of cloud
9.1.1135: Took from the rolling waves their former name.
9.1.1136: Nowhere with shorter space the sea divides
9.1.1137: Europe from Asia; though Pontus parts
9.1.1138: By scant division from Byzantium's hold
9.1.1139: Chalcedon oyster-rich: and small the strait
9.1.1140: Through which Propontis pours the Euxine wave.
9.1.1141: Then marvelling at their ancient fame, he seeks
9.1.1142: Sigeum's sandy beach and Simois' stream,
9.1.1143: Rhoeteum noble for its Grecian tomb,
9.1.1144: And all the heroes' shades, the theme of song.
9.1.1145: Next by the town of Troy burnt down of old
9.1.1146: Now but a memorable name, he turns
9.1.1147: His steps, and searches for the mighty stones
9.1.1148: Relics of Phoebus' wall. But bare with age
9.1.1149: Forests of trees and mouldering trunks oppressed
9.1.1150: Assaracus' palace, and with wearied roots
9.1.1151: Possessed the ancient temples of the gods.
9.1.1152: All Pergamus with densest brake was veiled
9.1.1153: And even her stones were perished. He beheld
9.1.1154: Thy rock, Hesione; the hidden grove,
9.1.1155: Anchises' nuptial chamber; and the cave
9.1.1156: Where sat the arbiter; the spot from which
9.1.1157: Was snatched the beauteous youth; the mountain lawn
9.1.1158: Where mourned OEnone. Not a stone but told
9.1.1159: The story of the past. A little stream
9.1.1160: Scarce trickling through the arid plain he passed,
9.1.1161: Nor knew 'twas Xanthus: deep in grass he placed,
9.1.1162: Careless, his footstep; but the herdsman cried
9.1.1163: Thou tread'st the dust of Hector.' Stones confused
9.1.1164: Lay at his feet in sacred shape no more:
9.1.1165: 'Look on the altar of Jove,' thus spake the guide,
9.1.1166: God of the household, guardian of the home.'
9.1.1167: O sacred task of poets, toil supreme,
9.1.1168: Which rescuing all things from allotted fate
9.1.1169: Dost give eternity to mortal men!
9.1.1170: Grudge not the glory, Caesar, of such fame.
9.1.1171: For if the Latian Muse may promise aught,
9.1.1172: Long as the heroes of the Trojan time
9.1.1173: Shall live upon the page of Smyrna's bard,
9.1.1174: So long shall future races read of thee
9.1.1175: In this my poem; and Pharsalia's song
9.1.1176: Live unforgotten in the age to come.
9.1.1177: When by the ancient grandeur of the place
9.1.1178: The chieftain's sight was filled, of gathered turf
9.1.1179: Altars he raised: and as the sacred flame
9.1.1180: Cast forth its odours, these not idle vows
9.1.1181: Gave to the gods, 'Ye deities of the dead,
9.1.1182: ' Who watch o'er Phrygian ruins: ye who now
9.1.1183: Lavinia's homes inhabit, and Alba's height:
9.1.1184: Gods of my sire AEneas, in whose fanes
9.1.1185: The Trojan fire still burns: pledge of the past
9.1.1187: Unseen of men! here in your ancient seat,
9.1.1189: 'I call upon you and with pious hand
9.1.1190: Burn frequent offerings. To my emprise
9.1.1191: Give prosperous ending! Here shall I replace
9.1.1192: 'The Phrygian peoples, here in glad return
9.1.1194: And from these stones shall rise a Roman Troy.'
9.1.1195: He seeks his fleet, and eager to regain
9.1.1196: Time spent at Ilium, to the favouring breeze
9.1.1197: Spreads all his canvas. Past rich Asia borne,
9.1.1198: Rhodes soon he left while foamed the sparkling main
9.1.1199: Beneath his keels; nor ceased the wind to stretch
9.1.1200: His bending sails, till on the seventh night
9.1.1201: The Pharian beam proclaimed Egyptian shores.
9.1.1202: But day arose, and veiled the nightly lamp
9.1.1203: Ere rode his barks on waters safe from storm.
9.1.1204: Then Caesar saw that tumult held the shore,
9.1.1205: And mingled voices of uncertain sound
9.1.1206: Struck on his ear: and trusting not himself
9.1.1207: To doubtful kingdoms, of uncertain troth,
9.1.1208: He kept his ships from land. But from the king
9.1.1209: Came his vile minion forth upon the wave,
9.1.1210: Bearing his dreadful gift, Pompeius' head,
9.1.1211: Wrapped in a covering of Pharian wool.
9.1.1212: First took he speech and thus in shameless words
9.1.1213: Commends the murder: ' Conqueror of the world,
9.1.1214: First of the Roman race, and, what as yet
9.1.1215: Thou dost not know, safe by thy kinsman slain;
9.1.1216: This gift receive from the Pellaean king,
9.1.1217: Sole trophy absent from the Thracian field,
9.1.1218: 'To crown thy toils on land and on the deep.
9.1.1219: Here in thine absence have we placed for thee
9.1.1220: 'An end upon the war. Here Magnus came
9.1.1221: To mend his fallen fortunes; on our swords
9.1.1222: 'Here met his death. With such a pledge of faith
9.1.1223: Here have we bought thee, Caesar; with his blood
9.1.1224: Seal we this treaty. Take the Pharian realm
9.1.1225: Sought by no bloodshed, take the rule of Nile,
9.1.1226: Take all that thou wouldst give for Magnus' life:
9.1.1227: And hold him vassal worthy of thy camp
9.1.1228: 'To whom the fates against thy son-in-law
9.1.1229: 'Such power entrusted; nor hold thou the deed
9.1.1231: And so the merit. Guest ancestral he
9.1.1232: Who was its victim; who, his sire expelled,
9.1.1233: ' Gave back to him the sceptre. For a deed
9.1.1234: ' So great, thou'lt find a name-or ask the world.
9.1.1235: ' If 'twas a crime, thou must confess the debt
9.1.1236: 'To us the greater, for that from thy hand
9.1.1239: Unveiled the head. Now had the hand of death
9.1.1240: Passed with its changing touch upon the face:
9.1.1241: Nor at first sight did Caesar on the gift
9.1.1242: Pass condemnation; nor avert his gaze,
9.1.1243: But dwelt upon the features till he knew
9.1.1244: The crime accomplished. Then when truth was sure
9.1.1245: The loving father rose, and tears he shed
9.1.1246: Which flowed at his command, and glad in heart
9.1.1247: Forced from his breast a groan: thus by the flow
9.1.1248: Of feigned tears and grief he hoped to hide
9.1.1249: His joy else manifest: and the ghastly boon
9.1.1250: Sent by the king disparaging, professed
9.1.1251: Rather to mourn his son's dissevered head,
9.1.1252: Than count it for a debt. For thee alone,
9.1.1253: Magnus, he durst not fail to find a tear:
9.1.1254: He, Caesar, who with mien unaltered spurned
9.1.1255: The Roman Senate, and with eyes undimmed
9.1.1256: Looked on Pharsalia's field. O fate most hard!
9.1.1257: Didst thou with impious war pursue the man
9.1.1258: Whom 'twas thy lot to mourn? No kindred ties,
9.1.1259: No memory of thy daughter and her son
9.1.1260: Touch on thy heart? Didst think perchance that grief
9.1.1261: Might help thy cause 'mid lovers of his name?
9.1.1262: Or haply, moved by envy of the king,
9.1.1263: Griev'st that to other hands than thine was given
9.1.1264: To shed the captive's life-blood? and complain'st
9.1.1265: Thy vengeance perished and the conquered chief
9.1.1266: Snatched from thy haughty hand? Whate'er the cause
9.1.1267: That urged thy grief, 'twas far removed from love.
9.1.1268: Was this forsooth the object of thy toil
9.1.1269: O'er lands and oceans, that without thy ken
9.1.1270: He should not perish? Nay! but well was reft
9.1.1271: From thine arbitrament his fate. What crime
9.1.1272: Did cruel Fortune spare, what depth of shame
9.1.1273: To Roman honour! since she suffered not,
9.1.1274: Perfidious traitor, while yet Magnus lived,
9.1.1277: To gain their credence in his sembled grief:
9.1.1278: Hence from my sight with his detested gift,
9.1.1279: Thou minion, to thy king. Worse does your crime
9.1.1280: Deserve from Caesar than from Magnus' hands.
9.1.1281: The only prize that civil war affords
9.1.1282: Thus have we lost-to bid the conquered live.
9.1.1283: If but the sister of this Pharian king
9.1.1284: Were not by him detested, by the head
9.1.1285: Of Cleopatra had I paid this gift.
9.1.1286: Such were the fit return. Why did he draw
9.1.1287: His separate sword, and in the toil that's ours
9.1.1288: Mingle his weapons? In Thessalia's field
9.1.1289: Gave we such right to the Pellaean blade?
9.1.1290: Such licence did your mutual kingdom gain?
9.1.1291: Magnus as partner in the rule of Rome
9.1.1292: I had not brooked; and shall I tolerate
9.1.1293: Thee, Ptolemaeus? In vain with civil wars
9.1.1294: Thus have we roused the nations, if there be
9.1.1295: Now any might but Caesar's, if any land
9.1.1296: Yet owns you masters. From your shore I'd turn
9.1.1297: The prows of Latium; but fame forbids,
9.1.1298: Lest men should whisper that I did not damn
9.1.1299: This deed of blood, but feared the Pharian land.
9.1.1300: Nor think ye to deceive; victorious here
9.1.1301: I stand: else had my welcome at your hands
9.1.1302: Been that of Magnus; and that neck were mine
9.1.1303: But for Pharsalia's chance. At greater risk
9.1.1304: So seems it, than we dreamed of, took we arms;
9.1.1305: Exile, and Magnus' threats, and Rome I knew,
9.1.1306: Not Ptolemaeus. But we spare the boy:
9.1.1307: Pass by the murder. Let the princeling know
9.1.1308: We give no more than pardon for his crime.
9.1.1309: And now in honour of the mighty dead,
9.1.1310: Not merely that the earth may hide your guilt,
9.1.1311: Lay ye the chieftain's head within the tomb;
9.1.1312: ' With proper sepulture appease his shade
9.1.1313: 'And place his scattered ashes in an urn.
9.1.1314: Thus may he know my coming, and may hear
9.1.1315: Affection's accents, and my fond complaints.
9.1.1316: Me sought he not, but rather, for his life,
9.1.1317: This Pharian vassal; snatching from mankind
9.1.1318: The happy morning which had shown the world
9.1.1319: A peace between us. But my prayers to heaven
9.1.1320: No favouring answer found; that arms laid down
9.1.1322: I might embrace thee, begging thee to grant
9.1.1323: 'Thine ancient love to Caesar, and thy life.
9.1.1324: 'Thus for my labours with a worthy prize
9.1.1325: 'Content, thine equal, bound in faithful peace,
9.1.1326: 'I might have brought thee to forgive the gods
9.1.1327: 'For thy disaster; thou hadst gained for me
9.1.1330: No comrade in his tears; nor did the host
9.1.1331: Give credit to his grief. Deep in their breasts
9.1.1332: They hide their groans, and gaze with joyful front
9.1.1333: (O famous Freedom! ) on the deed of blood:
9.1.1334: And dare to laugh when mighty Caesar wept.

10.1.1: WHEN Caesar, following those who bore the head,
10.1.2: First trod the shore accursed, with Egypt's fates
10.1.3: His fortunes battled, whether Rome should pass
10.1.4: In crimson conquest o'er the guilty land,
10.1.5: Or Memphis' arms should ravish from the world
10.1.6: Victor and vanquished: and the warning shade
10.1.7: Of Magnus saved his kinsman from the sword.
10.1.8: By that dread crime assured, his standards borne
10.1.9: Before, he marched upon the Pharian town;
10.1.10: But when the people, jealous of their laws,
10.1.11: Murmured against the fasces, Caesar knew
10.1.12: Their minds were adverse, and that not for him
10.1.13: Was Magnus' murder wrought. And yet with brow
10.1.14: Dissembling fear, intrepid, through the shrines
10.1.15: Of Egypt's gods he strode, and round the fane
10.1.16: Of ancient Isis; bearing witness all
10.1.17: To Macedon's vigour in the days of old.
10.1.18: Yet did nor gold nor ornament restrain
10.1.19: His hasting steps, nor worship of the gods,
10.1.20: Nor city ramparts: but in greed of gain
10.1.21: He sought the cave dug out amid the tombs.
10.1.22: The madman offspring there of Philip lies,
10.1.23: The famed Pellaean robber, Fortune's friend,
10.1.24: Snatched off by fate, in vengeance for the world.
10.1.25: In sacred sepulchre the hero's limbs,
10.1.26: Which should be scattered o'er the earth, repose,
10.1.27: Still spared by Fortune to these tyrant days:
10.1.28: For in a world to freedom once recalled,
10.1.29: All men had mocked the dust of him who set
10.1.30: The baneful lesson that so many lands
10.1.31: Can serve one master. Macedon he left
10.1.32: His home obscure; Athena he despised,
10.1.33: The conquest of his sire, and spurred by fate
10.1.34: Through Asia rushed with havoc of mankind,
10.1.35: Plunging his sword through peoples; red with blood
10.1.36: Unknown to them Euphrates, Ganges ran.
10.1.37: Curse of all earth, fell star of evil fate
10.1.38: To every nation! On the outer sea
10.1.39: He launched his fleet to sail the ocean wave:
10.1.40: Nor flame nor flood nor sterile Libyan sands
10.1.41: Stayed back his course, nor Hammon's pathless shoals;
10.1.42: Far to the west, where downward slopes the world
10.1.43: He would have led his armies, and the poles
10.1.44: Had compassed, and had drunk the fount of Nile:
10.1.45: But came his latest day; such end alone
10.1.46: Could nature place upon the madman king,
10.1.47: Who jealous in death as when he won the world
10.1.48: His empire with him took, nor left an heir.
10.1.49: Thus every city to the spoiler's hand
10.1.50: Was victim made. Yet in his fall was his
10.1.51: Babylon; and Parthia feared him. Shame on us
10.1.52: That Eastern nations dreaded more the lance
10.1.53: Of Macedon than now the Roman spear.
10.1.54: True that we rule beyond where takes its rise
10.1.55: The burning southern breeze, beyond the homes
10.1.56: Of western winds, and to the northern star;
10.1.57: But towards the rising of the sun, we yield
10.1.58: To him who kept the Arsacids in awe;
10.1.59: And puny Pella held as province sure
10.1.60: The Parthia fatal to our Roman arms.
10.1.61: Now from the stream Pelusian of the Nile,
10.1.62: Was come the boyish king, taming the rage
10.1.63: Of his effeminate people: pledge of peace;
10.1.64: And Caesar safely trod Pellean halls;
10.1.65: When Cleopatra bribed her guard to break
10.1.66: The harbour chains, and borne in little boat
10.1.69: Fury of Latium; to the bane of Rome
10.1.70: Unchaste. For as the Spartan queen of yore
10.1.71: By fatal beauty Argos urged to strife
10.1.72: And Ilium's homes, so Cleopatra roused
10.1.73: Italia's frenzy. By her drum she called
10.1.74: Down on the Capitol terror (if to speak
10.1.75: Such word be lawful); mixed with Roman arms
10.1.76: Coward Canopus, hoping she might lead
10.1.77: A Pharian triumph, Caesar in her train;
10.1.78: And 'twas in doubt upon Leucadian waves
10.1.79: Whether a woman, not of Roman blood,
10.1.80: Should hold the world in awe. Such lofty thoughts
10.1.81: Seized on her soul upon that night in which
10.1.82: The wanton daughter of Pellean kings
10.1.83: First shared our leaders' couches. Who shall blame
10.1.84: Antonius for the madness of his love,
10.1.85: When Caesar's haughty breast drew in the flame?
10.1.86: Who red with carnage, 'mid the clash of arms,
10.1.87: In palace haunted by Pompeius' shade,
10.1.88: Gave place to love; and in adulterous bed,
10.1.89: Magnus forgotten, from the Queen impure,
10.1.90: To Julia gave a brother: on the bounds
10.1.92: His foe to gather: while in dalliance base
10.1.93: He waited on his mistress, and to her
10.1.94: Pharos would give; for her would conquer all.
10.1.95: Then Cleopatra, trusting to her charms,
10.1.96: Tearless approached him, though in form of grief;
10.1.97: Her tresses loose as though in sorrow torn,
10.1.98: So best becoming her; and thus began:
10.1.99: 'If, mighty Caesar, aught to noble birth
10.1.100: ' Be due, give ear. Of Lagian race am I
10.1.101: ' Offspring illustrious; from my father's throne
10.1.102: 'Cast forth to banishment; unless thy hand
10.1.103: 'Restore to me the sceptre: then a Queen
10.1.104: ' Falls at thy feet embracing. To our race
10.1.105: ' Bright star of justice thou Nor first shall I
10.1.106: ' As woman rule the cities of the Nile;
10.1.107: ' For, neither sex preferring, Pharos bows
10.1.108: 'To queenly governance. Of my parted sire
10.1.109: ' Read the last words, by which 'tis mine to share
10.1.110: ' With equal rights the kingdom and the bed.
10.1.111: 'And the boy loves his sister, were he free;
10.1.112: ' But his affections and his sword alike
10.1.113: ' Pothinus orders. Nor wish I myself
10.1.114: ' To wield my father's power; but this my prayer:
10.1.115: ' Save from this foul disgrace our royal house,
10.1.116: ' Bid that the king shall reign, and from the court
10.1.117: 'Remove this hateful varlet, and his arms.
10.1.118: 'How swells his bosom for that his the hand
10.1.119: 'That shore Pompeius' head! And now he threats
10.1.120: Thee, Caesar, also; which the Fates avert!
10.1.121: Shame on the earth and thee that Magnus' death
10.1.122: Should be Pothinus' triumph or his guilt.'
10.1.123: Her words were nothing to his stubborn ear;
10.1.124: Her face achieved the prayer, her wanton smile,
10.1.125: The long voluptuous night of shame untold:
10.1.126: So did she bribe her judge; so Caesar fell.
10.1.127: When she had purchased at so vast a price
10.1.128: Peace from the chief, the joys of such a peace
10.1.129: A feast proclaimed. There in full pomp the Queen
10.1.130: Displayed her luxuries, as yet unknown
10.1.131: To Roman manners. Spacious rose the hall
10.1.132: Like to such fane as this corrupted age
10.1.133: Shall scarcely rear: the lofty ceiling shone
10.1.134: With richest tracery, the beams were bound
10.1.135: In golden coverings; no scant veneer
10.1.136: Lay on its walls, but built in solid blocks
10.1.137: Of marble, gleamed the palace. Agate stood
10.1.138: In sturdy columns, bearing up the roof;
10.1.139: Onyx and porphyry on the spacious floor
10.1.140: Were trodden 'neath the foot; the mighty gates
10.1.141: Of Maroe's ebony throughout were formed,
10.1.142: No mere adornment; ivory clothed the hall,
10.1.143: Studded with emerald spots; upon the doors
10.1.144: Gleamed polished tortoise shells from Indian seas:
10.1.145: And gems of price and yellow jasper shone
10.1.146: On couch and coverlet, whose greater part
10.1.147: Dipped more than once within the vats of Tyre
10.1.148: Had drunk their juice; and part were feathered gold;
10.1.149: Part crimson dyed, in manner as are passed
10.1.150: Through Pharian leash the threads. There waited slaves
10.1.151: In number as a people, some in ranks
10.1.152: By different blood distinguished, some by age;
10.1.153: This band with Libyan, that with auburn hair
10.1.154: Red so that Caesar on the banks of Rhine
10.1.155: None such had witnessed; some with features scorched
10.1.156: By torrid suns, their locks in twisted coils
10.1.157: Drawn from their foreheads. Eunuchs too were there,
10.1.158: Unhappy race; and on the other side
10.1.159: Men of full age whose cheeks with growth of hair
10.1.162: Lay kings, and Caesar in the midst supreme.
10.1.163: There in her fatal beauty lay the Queen
10.1.164: Thick daubed with unguents, nor with throne content
10.1.165: Nor with her brother spouse; laden she lay
10.1.166: On neck and hair with all the Red Sea spoils,
10.1.167: And faint beneath the weight of gems and gold.
10.1.168: Her snowy breast shone through Sidonian lawn
10.1.169: Which woven close by shuttles of the East
10.1.170: The art of Nile had loosened. Ivory feet
10.1.171: Bore citron tables brought from woods that wave
10.1.172: On Atlas, such as Caesar never saw
10.1.173: When Juba was his captive. Blind in soul
10.1.174: By madness of ambition, thus to fire
10.1.175: By such profusion of her wealth, the mind
10.1.176: Of Caesar armed, her guest in civil war!
10.1.177: Not though he aimed with pitiless hand to grasp
10.1.178: The riches of a world; not though were here
10.1.179: Those ancient leaders of the simple age,
10.1.180: Fabricius or Curius stern of soul,
10.1.181: Or he who, Consul, left in sordid garb
10.1.182: His Tuscan plough, could all their several hopes
10.1.183: Have risen to such spoil. On plates of gold
10.1.184: They piled the banquet sought in earth and air
10.1.185: And from the deepest seas and Nilus' waves,
10.1.186: Through all the world; in craving for display,
10.1.187: No hunger urging. Frequent birds and beasts,
10.1.188: Egypt's high gods, they placed upon the board:
10.1.189: In crystal goblets water of the Nile
10.1.190: They handed, and in massive cups of price
10.1.191: Was poured the wine; no juice of Mareot grape,
10.1.192: But noble vintage of Falernian growth
10.1.193: Which seasons few in Meroe's famous vats
10.1.194: Had mellowed as with age. Upon their brows
10.1.195: Chaplets were placed of roses ever young
10.1.196: With glistening nard entwined; and in their locks
10.1.197: Was cinnamon infused, not yet in air
10.1.198: Its fragrance perished, nor in foreign climes;
10.1.199: And rich amomum from the neighbouring fields.
10.1.200: Thus Caesar learned the booty of a world
10.1.201: To lavish, and his breast was shamed of war
10.1.202: Waged with his son-in-law, from whose defeat
10.1.203: His spoils were meagre, and he longed to find
10.1.204: A cause of battle with the Pharian realm.
10.1.205: When of the banquet and of wine and feast
10.1.206: They wearied and their pleasure found an end,
10.1.207: Caesar drew out in colloquy the night
10.1.208: Thus with Achoreus, on the highest couch
10.1.209: With linen ephod as a priest begirt:
10.1.210: 'O thou devoted to all sacred rites,
10.1.211: 'Loved by the gods, as proves thy length of days,
10.1.212: 'Tell, if thou wilt, whence sprang the Pharian race;
10.1.213: 'How lie their lands, the manners of their tribes,
10.1.214: 'The form and worship of their deities.
10.1.215: 'Expound the sculptures on your ancient fanes:
10.1.216: 'Reveal your gods if willing to be known:
10.1.217: 'If to th' Athenian sage your fathers taught
10.1.219: ' To bear in trust the secrets of the world?
10.1.220: ' True, by the rumour of my kinsman's flight
10.1.221: ' Here was I drawn; yet also by your fame:
10.1.222: ' And even in the midst of war's alarms
10.1.223: ' The stars and heavenly spaces have I conned;
10.1.224: 'Nor shall Eudoxus' year excel mine own.
10.1.225: ' But though such ardour burns within my breast,
10.1.226: ' Such zeal to know the truth, yet my chief wish
10.1.227: ' To learn the source of your mysterious flood
10.1.228: ' Through ages hidden: give me certain hope
10.1.229: ' To see the fount of Nile-and civil war
10.1.230: ' I quit for ever.' He spake, and then the priest:
10.1.231: ' The secrets, Caesar, of our mighty sires
10.1.232: ' Kept from the common people until now
10.1.233: ' I hold it right to utter. Some may deem
10.1.234: ' That silence on these wonders of the earth
10.1.235: ' Were greater piety. But to the gods
10.1.236: ' I hold it grateful that their handiwork
10.1.237: ' And sacred edicts should be known to men.
10.1.238: ' A different power by the primal law,
10.1.239: ' Each star possesses: these alone control
10.1.240: ' The movement of the sky, with adverse force
10.1.241: ' Opposing: while the sun divides the year,
10.1.242: ' And day from night, and by his potent rays
10.1.243: ' Forbids the stars to pass their stated course.
10.1.244: ' The moon by her alternate phases sets
10.1.245: ' The varying limits of the sea and shore.
10.1.246: ' Neath Saturn's sway the zone of ice and snow
10.1.247: ' Has passed; while Mars in lightning's fitful flames
10.1.248: ' And winds abounds: beneath high Jupiter
10.1.249: ' Unvexed by storms abides a temperate air;
10.1.250: ' And fruitful Venus' star contains the seeds
10.1.251: ' Of all things. Ruler of the boundless deep
10.1.252: ' The god Cyllenian: whene'er he holds
10.1.253: ' That part of heaven where the Lion dwells
10.1.254: ' With neighbouring Cancer joined, and Sirius star
10.1.255: ' Flames in its fury; where the circular path
10.1.256: ' (Which marks the changes of the varying year)
10.1.257: ' Gives to hot Cancer and to Capricorn
10.1.258: ' Their several stations, under which doth lie
10.1.259: ' The fount of Nile, he, master of the waves,
10.1.260: ' Strikes with his beam the waters. Forth the stream
10.1.261: ' Brims from his fount, as Ocean when the moon
10.1.262: ' Commands an increase; nor shall curb his flow
10.1.263: ' Till night wins back her losses from the sun.
10.1.264: ' Vain is the ancient faith that Ethiop snows
10.1.265: ' Send Nile abundant forth upon the lands.
10.1.266: ' Those mountains know nor northern wind nor star.
10.1.267: ' Of this are proof the breezes of the South,
10.1.268: ' Fraught with warm vapours, and the people's hue
10.1.269: ' Burned dark by suns: and 'tis in time of spring,
10.1.270: ' When first are thawed the snows, that ice-fed streams
10.1.271: ' In swollen torrents tumble; but the Nile
10.1.272: ' Nor lifts his wave before the Dog star burns;
10.1.273: ' Nor seeks again his banks, until the sun
10.1.274: ' In equal balance measures night and day.
10.1.275: ' Nor are the laws that govern other streams
10.1.276: ' Obeyed by Nile. For in the wintry year
10.1.277: 'Were he in flood, when distant far the sun,
10.1.278: ' His waters lacked their office; but he leaves
10.1.279: ' His channel when the summer is at height,
10.1.280: ' Tempering the torrid heat of Egypt's clime.
10.1.281: ' Such is the task of Nile; thus in the world
10.1.282: ' He finds his purpose, lest exceeding heat
10.1.283: ' Consume the lands: and rising thus to meet
10.1.285: ' By Cancer burnt gives ear; nor curbs his wave
10.1.286: ' Till the slant sun and Meroe's lengthening shades
10.1.287: ' Proclaim the autumn. Who shall give the cause?
10.1.288: ' 'Twas Parent Nature's self which gave command
10.1.289: ' Thus for the needs of earth should flow the Nile.
10.1.290: ' Vain too the fable that the western winds
10.1.291: ' Control his current, in continuous course
10.1.292: ' At stated seasons governing the air;
10.1.293: ' Or hurrying from Occident to South
10.1.294: ' Clouds without number which in misty folds
10.1.295: ' Press on the waters; or by constant blast,
10.1.296: ' Forcing his current back whose several mouths
10.1.297: ' Burst on the sea;-so, forced by seas and wind,
10.1.298: 'Men say, his billows pour upon the land.
10.1.299: ' Some speak of hollow caverns, breathing holes
10.1.300: ' Deep in the earth, within whose mighty jaws
10.1.302: ' From northern cold to southern climes are drawn;
10.1.303: 'And when hot Meroe pants beneath the sun,
10.1.304: ' Then, say they, Ganges through the silent depths
10.1.305: ' And Padus pass: and from a single fount
10.1.306: ' The Nile arising not in single streams
10.1.307: ' Pours all the rivers forth. And rumour says
10.1.308: ' That when the sea which girdles in the world
10.1.309: ' O'erflows, thence rushes Nile, by lengthy course,
10.1.310: ' Softening his saltness. More, if it be true
10.1.311: ' That ocean feeds the sun and heavenly fires,
10.1.312: ' Then Phoebus journeying by the burning Crab
10.1.313: ' Sucks from its waters more than air can hold
10.1.314: ' Upon his passage-this the cool of night
10.1.315: ' Pours on the Nile. If, Caesar, 'tis my part
10.1.316: ' To judge such difference, 'twould seem that since
10.1.317: ' Creation's age has passed, earth's veins by chance
10.1.318: ' Some waters hold, and shaken cast them forth:
10.1.319: ' But others took when first the globe was formed
10.1.320: ' A sure abode; by Him who framed the world
10.1.321: ' Fixed with the Universe. And, Roman, thou,
10.1.322: ' In thirsting thus to know the source of Nile,
10.1.323: ' Dost as the Pharian and Persian kings
10.1.324: ' And those of Macedon; nor any age
10.1.325: ' Refused the secret, but the place prevailed
10.1.326: ' Remote by nature. Greatest of the kings
10.1.328: ' To Nile its mystery, and to furthest earth
10.1.329: ' Sent chosen Ethiops whom the crimson zone
10.1.330: ' Stayed in their further march, while flowed his stream
10.1.331: ' Warm at their feet. Sesostris westward far
10.1.332: ' Reached, to the ends of earth; and necks of kings
10.1.333: ' Bent 'neath his chariot yoke: but of the springs
10.1.334: ' Which fill your rivers, Rhone and Po, he drank,
10.1.335: 'Not of the fount of Nile. Cambyses king
10.1.336: 'In madman quest led forth his host to where
10.1.337: 'The long-lived races dwell: then famine struck,
10.1.338: 'Ate of his dead and, Nile unknown, returned.
10.1.339: No lying rumour of thy hidden source
10.1.340: 'Has e'er made mention; wheresoe'er thou art
10.1.341: 'Yet art thou sought, nor yet has nation claimed
10.1.342: 'In pride of place thy river as its own.
10.1.343: ' Yet shall I tell, so far as has the god,
10.1.344: ' Who veils thy fountain, given me to know,
10.1.345: 'Thy progress. Daring to upraise thy banks
10.1.346: ''Gainst fiery Cancer's heat, thou tak'st thy rise
10.1.347: 'Beneath the zenith: straight towards the north
10.1.348: 'And mid Bootes flowing; to the couch
10.1.349: 'Bending, or to the risings, of the sun
10.1.351: 'To Araby's peoples and to Libyan sands.
10.1.352: 'By Seres first beheld, yet know they not
10.1.353: Whence art thou come; and with no native stream
10.1.354: Strik'st thou the Ethiop fields. Nor knows the world
10.1.355: 'To whom it owes thee. Nature ne'er revealed
10.1.357: 'Nor did she wish thee to be seen of men
10.1.358: ' While still a tiny rivulet, but preferred
10.1.359: ' Their wonder to their knowledge. Where the sun
10.1.360: ' Stays at his limit, dost thou rise in flood
10.1.361: ' Untimely; such thy right: to other lands
10.1.362: ' Bearing thy winter: and by both the poles
10.1.363: ' Thou only wanderest. Here men ask thy rise
10.1.364: ' And there thine ending. Meroe rich in soil
10.1.366: 'Thy broad expanse, rejoicing in the leaves
10.1.367: 'Of groves of ebony, which though spreading far
10.1.368: 'Their branching foliage, by no breadth of shade
10.1.370: 'Pass from the Lion to the fervid earth.
10.1.371: 'Next dost thou journey onwards past the realm
10.1.372: 'Of burning Phoebus, and the sterile sands,
10.1.373: 'With equal volume; now with all thy strength
10.1.374: 'Gathered in one, and now in devious streams
10.1.375: 'Parting the bank that crumbles at thy touch.
10.1.376: 'Then by our kingdom's gates, where Philae parts
10.1.378: ' The sluggish bosom of thy flood recalls
10.1.379: ' Thy wandering currents, which through desert wastes
10.1.380: ' Flow gently on to where the merchant track
10.1.381: ' Divides the Red Sea waters from our own.
10.1.382: ' Who, gazing, Nile, upon thy tranquil flow,
10.1.383: ' Could picture how in wild array of foam
10.1.384: ' (Where shelves the earth) thy billows shall be plunged
10.1.385: ' Down the steep cataracts, in fuming wrath
10.1.386: ' That rocks should bar the passage of thy stream
10.1.387: ' Free from its source? For whirled on high the spray
10.1.388: ' Aims at the stars, and trembles all the air
10.1.389: With rush of waters; and with sounding roar
10.1.390: The foaming mass down from the summit pours
10.1.391: In hoary waves victorious. Next an isle
10.1.392: In all our ancient lore "untrodden" named
10.1.393: Stems firm thy torrent; and the rocks we call
10.1.394: Springs of the river, for that here are marked
10.1.395: The earliest tokens of the coming flood.
10.1.396: With mountain shores now nature hems thee in
10.1.397: And shuts thy waves from Libya; in the midst
10.1.398: Hence do thy waters run, till Memphis first
10.1.399: Forbids the barrier placed upon thy stream
10.1.400: And gives thee access to the open fields.'
10.1.401: Thus did they pass, as though in peace profound,
10.1.402: The nightly watches. But Pothinus' mind,
10.1.404: Was frenzied still; since great Pompeius fell
10.1.405: No deed to him was crime; his rabid soul
10.1.406: Th' avenging goddesses and Magnus' shade
10.1.407: Stirred to fresh horrors; and a Pharian hand
10.1.408: No less was worthy, as he deemed, to shed
10.1.409: That blood which Fortune purposed should bedew
10.1.410: The conquered fathers: and the fell revenge
10.1.411: Due to the senate for the civil war
10.1.412: This hireling almost snatched. Avert, ye fates,
10.1.413: Far hence the shame that not by Brutus' hand
10.1.414: This blow be struck! Shall thus the tyrant's fall,
10.1.415: Just at our hands, become a Pharian crime.
10.1.416: Reft of example? To prepare a plan
10.1.417: (Fated to fail) he dares; nor veils in fraud
10.1.418: A plot for murder, but with open war
10.1.419: Attacks th' unconquered chieftain: from his crimes
10.1.420: He gained such courage as to send command
10.1.421: To lop the head of Caesar, and to join
10.1.422: In death the kinsmen chiefs. These words by night
10.1.423: His faithful servants to Achillas bear,
10.1.424: His foul associate, whom the boy had made
10.1.425: Chief of his armies, and who ruled alone
10.1.426: O'er Egypt's land and o'er himself her king:
10.1.427: ' Now lay thy limbs upon the sumptuous couch
10.1.428: ' And sleep in luxury, for the Queen hath seized
10.1.429: 'The palace; nor alone by her betrayed,
10.1.430: ' But Caesar's gift, is Pharos. Dost delay
10.1.431: ' Nor hasten to the chamber of thy Queen?
10.1.432: ' Thou only? Married to the Latian chief,
10.1.433: 'The impious sister now her brother weds
10.1.434: ' And hurrying from rival spouse to spouse
10.1.435: ' Hath Egypt won, and plays the bawd for Rome.
10.1.436: ' By amorous potions she has won the man:
10.1.437: ' Then trust the boy! Yet give him but a night
10.1.438: ' In her enfondling arms, and drunk with love
10.1.439: ' Thy life and mine he'll barter for a kiss.
10.1.440: ' We for his sister's charms by cross and flame
10.1.441: ' Shall pay the penalty: nor hope of aid;
10.1.442: ' Here stands adulterous Caesar, here the King
10.1.443: ' Her spouse: how hope we from so stern a judge
10.1.444: ' To gain acquittal? Shall she not condemn
10.1.445: 'Those who ne'er sought her favours? By the deed
10.1.446: We dared together and lost, by Magnus' blood
10.1.447: ' Which wrought the bond between us, be thou swift
10.1.448: ' With hasty tumult to arouse the war:
10.1.449: ' Dash in with nightly band, and mar with death
10.1.450: ' Their shameless nuptials: on the very bed
10.1.451: With either lover smite the ruthless Queen.
10.1.452: ' Nor let the fortunes of the Western chief
10.1.453: ' Make pause our enterprise. We share with him
10.1.454: ' The glory of his empire o'er the world.
10.1.455: ' Pompeius fallen makes us too sublime,
10.1.456: There lies the shore that bids us hope success:
10.1.457: Ask of our power from the polluted wave,
10.1.458: And gaze upon the scanty tomb which holds
10.1.459: Not all Pompeius' ashes. Peer to him
10.1.460: Was he whom now thou fearest. Noble blood,
10.1.461: ' True, is not ours: what boots it? Nor are realms
10.1.462: ' Nor wealth of peoples given to our command.
10.1.463: 'Yet have we risen to a height of power
10.1.464: For deeds of blood, and Fortune to our hands
10.1.465: Attracts her victims. Lo! a nobler now
10.1.466: Lies in our compass, and a second death
10.1.467: Hesperia shall appease; for Caesar's blood,
10.1.468: Shed by these hands, shall give us this, that Rome
10.1.469: Shall love us, guilty of Pompeius' fall.
10.1.470: Why fear these titles, why this chieftain's strength?
10.1.471: For shorn of these, before your swords he lies
10.1.472: A common soldier. To the civil war
10.1.473: This night shall bring completion, and shall give
10.1.474: To peoples slain fit offerings, and send
10.1.475: That life the world demands beneath the shades.
10.1.476: Rise then in all your hardihood and smite
10.1.477: This Caesar down, and let the Roman youths
10.1.478: Strike for themselves, and Lagos for its King.
10.1.479: No do thou tarry: full of wine and feast
10.1.480: Thou'lt fall upon him in the lists of love;
10.1.481: Then dare the venture, and the heavenly gods
10.1.482: Shall grant of Cato's and of Brutus' prayers
10.1.485: To hear the voice that counselled him to crime.
10.1.486: No sounding clarion summoned, as is wont,
10.1.487: His troops to arms; nor trumpet blare betrayed
10.1.488: Their nightly march: but rapidly he seized
10.1.489: All needed instruments of blood and war.
10.1.490: Of Latian race the most part of his train,
10.1.491: Yet to barbarian customs were their minds
10.1.492: By long forgetfulness of Rome debased:
10.1.493: Else had it shamed to serve the Pharian King;
10.1.494: But now his vassal and his minion's word
10.1.495: Compel obedience. Those who serve in camps
10.1.496: Lose faith and love of kin: their pittance earned
10.1.497: Makes just the deed: and for their sordid pay,
10.1.498: Not for themselves, they threaten Caesar's life.
10.1.499: Where finds the piteous destiny of the realm
10.1.500: Rome with herself at peace? The host withdrawn
10.1.501: From dread Thessalia raves on Nilus' banks
10.1.502: As all the race of Rome. What more had dared,
10.1.503: With Magnus welcomed, the Lagean house?
10.1.504: Each hand must render to the gods their due,
10.1.505: Nor son of Rome may cease from civil war;
10.1.506: By Heaven's command our state was rent in twain;
10.1.507: Nor love for husband nor regard for sire
10.1.508: Parted our peoples. 'Twas a slave who stirred
10.1.509: Afresh the conflict, and Achillas grasped
10.1.510: In turn the sword of Rome: nay more, had won,
10.1.511: Had not the fates adverse restrained his hand
10.1.514: Ripe for their plot were met; the spacious hall
10.1.515: Still busied with the feast. So might have flowed
10.1.516: Into the kingly cups a stream of gore,
10.1.517: And in mid banquet fallen Caesar's head.
10.1.518: Yet did they fear lest in the nightly strife
10.1.520: So did they trust the sword-might slay the King.
10.1.521: Thus stayed the deed, for in the minds of slaves
10.1.522: The chance of doing Caesar to the death
10.1.523: Might bear postponement: when the day arose
10.1.524: Then should he suffer; and a night of life
10.1.525: Thus by Pothinus was to Caesar given.
10.1.526: Now from the Casian rock looked forth the Sun
10.1.527: Flooding the land of Egypt with a day
10.1.528: Warm from its earliest dawn, when from the walls
10.1.529: Not wandering in disorder are they seen,
10.1.530: But drawn in close array, as though to meet
10.1.531: A foe opposing; ready to receive
10.1.532: Or give the battle. Caesar, in the town
10.1.533: Placing no trust, within the palace courts
10.1.534: Lay in ignoble hiding place, the gates
10.1.535: Close barred: nor all the kingly rooms possessed,
10.1.536: But in the narrowest portion of the space
10.1.537: He drew his band together. There in arms
10.1.538: They stood, with dread and fury in their souls.
10.1.539: He feared attack, indignant at his fear.
10.1.540: Thus will a noble beast in little cage
10.1.541: Imprisoned, fume, and break upon the bars
10.1.542: His teeth in frenzied wrath; nor more would rage
10.1.543: The flames of Vulcan in Sicilian depths
10.1.544: Should Etna's top be closed. He who but now
10.1.545: By Haemus' mount against Pompeius chief,
10.1.546: Italia's leaders and the Senate line,
10.1.547: His cause forbidding hope, looked at the fates
10.1.548: He knew were hostile, with unfaltering gaze,
10.1.549: Now fears before the crime of hireling slaves,
10.1.550: And in mid palace trembles at the blow:
10.1.551: He whom nor Scythian nor Alaun had dared
10.1.552: To violate, nor the Moor who aims the dart
10.1.553: Upon his victim slain, to prove his skill.
10.1.554: The Roman world but now did not suffice
10.1.555: To hold him, nor the realms from furthest Ind
10.1.556: To Tyrian Gades. Now, as puny boy,
10.1.557: Or woman, trembling when a town is sacked,
10.1.558: Within the narrow corners of a house
10.1.559: He seeks for safety; on the portals closed
10.1.560: His hope of life: and with uncertain gait
10.1.561: He treads the halls; yet not without the King;
10.1.562: In purpose, Ptolemaeus, that thy life
10.1.563: For his shall give atonement; and to hurl
10.1.564: Thy severed head among the servant throng
10.1.565: Should darts and torches fail. So story tells
10.1.566: The Colchian princess with sword in hand,
10.1.567: And with her brother's neck bared to the blow,
10.1.568: Waited her sire, avenger of his realm
10.1.569: Despoiled, and of her flight. In the imminent risk
10.1.570: Caesar, in hopes of peace, an envoy sent
10.1.571: To the fierce vassals, from their absent lord
10.1.572: Bearing a message, thus: ' At whose command
10.1.573: Wage ye the war?' But not the laws which bind
10.1.574: All nations upon earth, nor sacred rights,
10.1.575: Availed to save or messenger of peace,
10.1.576: Or King's ambassador; or thee from crime
10.1.577: Such as befitted thee, thou land of Nile
10.1.578: Fruitful in monstrous deeds: not Juba's realm,
10.1.579: Vast though it be, nor Pontus, nor the land
10.1.580: Thessalian, nor the arms of Pharnaces,
10.1.581: Nor yet the tracts which chill Iberus girds,
10.1.582: Nor Libyan coasts such wickedness have dared,
10.1.583: As thou, and all thy minions. Closer now
10.1.584: War hemmed them in, and weapons in the courts,
10.1.586: Yet did no ram, fatal with single stroke,
10.1.587: Assail the portal, nor machine of war;
10.1.588: Nor flame they called in aid; but blind of plan
10.1.589: They wander purposeless, in separate bands
10.1.590: Around the circuit, nor at any spot
10.1.591: With strength combined attempt to breach the wall.
10.1.592: The fates forbad, and Fortune from their hands
10.1.593: Held fast the palace as a battlement.
10.1.594: Nor failed they to attack from ships of war
10.1.595: The regal dwelling, where its frontage bold
10.1.596: Made stand apart the waters of the deep:
10.1.597: There, too, was Caesar's all-protecting arm;
10.1.598: For these at point of sword, and those with fire
10.1.599: He forces back, and though besieged he dares
10.1.600: To storm th' assailants: and as lay the ships
10.1.601: Joined rank to rank, bids drop upon their sides
10.1.602: Lamps drenched with reeking tar. Nor slow the fire
10.1.603: To seize the hempen cables and the decks
10.1.604: Oozing with melting pitch; the oarsman's bench
10.1.605: All in one moment, and the topmost yards
10.1.606: Burst into flame: half merged the vessels lay
10.1.607: While swam the foemen, all in arms, the wave;
10.1.608: Nor fell the blaze upon the ships alone,
10.1.609: But seized with writhing tongues the neighbouring homes,
10.1.610: And fanned to fury by the Southern breeze
10.1.611: Tempestuous, it leaped from roof to roof;
10.1.612: Not otherwise than on its heavenly track,
10.1.613: Unfed by matter, glides the ball of light,
10.1.616: Some of the forces to the city's aid
10.1.617: From the besieged halls. Nor Caesar gave
10.1.618: To sleep its season; swifter than all else
10.1.619: To seize the crucial moment of the war.
10.1.620: Quick in the darkest watches of the night
10.1.621: He leaped upon his ships, and Pharos seized,
10.1.622: Gate of the main; an island in the days
10.1.623: Of Proteus seer, now bordering the walls
10.1.624: Of Alexander's city. Thus he gained
10.1.625: A double vantage, for his foes were pent
10.1.626: Within the narrow entrance, which for him
10.1.627: And for his aids gave access to the sea.
10.1.628: Nor longer was Pothinus' doom delayed,
10.1.629: Yet not with cross or flame, nor with the wrath
10.1.630: His crime demanded; nor by savage beasts
10.1.631: Torn, did he suffer; but by Magnus' death,
10.1.632: Alas the shame! he fell; his head by sword
10.1.633: Hacked from his shoulders. Next by frauds prepared
10.1.634: By Ganymede her base attendant, fled
10.1.635: Arsinoe from the Court to Caesar's foes;
10.1.636: There in the absence of the King she ruled
10.1.637: As of Lagean blood: there at her hands,
10.1.638: The savage minion of the tyrant boy,
10.1.639: Achillas, fell by just avenging sword.
10.1.640: Thus did another victim to thy shade
10.1.641: Atone, Pompeius; but the gods forbid
10.1.642: That this be all thy vengeance! Not the King
10.1.643: Nor all the stock of Lagos for thy death
10.1.644: Would make fit sacrifice! So Fortune deemed;
10.1.645: And not till patriot swords shall drink the blood
10.1.646: Of Caesar, Magnus, shalt thou be appeased.
10.1.647: Still, though was slain the author of the strife,
10.1.648: Sank not their rage: with Ganymede for chief
10.1.649: Again they rush to arms; in deeds of fight
10.1.650: Again they conquer. So might that one day
10.1.651: Have witnessed Caesar's fate; so might its fame
10.1.654: Crushed on the narrow surface of the mole,
10.1.655: Prepared to throw his troops upon the ships,
10.1.656: Sudden upon him the surrounding foes
10.1.657: With all their terrors came. In dense array
10.1.658: Their navy lined the shores, while on the rear
10.1.659: The footmen ceaseless charged. No hope was left,
10.1.660: For flight was not, nor could the brave man's arm
10.1.661: Achieve or safety or a glorious death.
10.1.662: Not now were needed for great Caesar's fall,
10.1.663: Caught in the toils of nature, routed host
10.1.664: Or mighty heaps of slain: his only doubt
10.1.665: To fear or hope for death: while on his brain
10.1.666: Brave Scaeva's image flashed, now vainly sought,
10.1.667: Who on the wall by Epidamnus' fields
10.1.668: Earned fame immortal, and with single arm
10.1.669: Drove back Pompeius as he trod the breach.
